parties:
Mansur Ali (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Janata Bank and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J: This Rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiff No. 2 petitioner calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 28.5.87 of the court of Munsif, Satkhira passed in Title Suit No. 173 of 1984 should not be set aside.

2. Short facts relevant for the disposal of the rule are as follows:-The petitioner a plaintiff No. 2 along with 2 others namely opposite Parties Nos. 4 and 5. Shamsul Arefin and vied. Mostafa as plaintiff Nos. 1 and 3 filed Title Suit No. 173 of 1984 with a prayer for declaration that the order dated 24.11.70 made by the Vice President of the United Bank Limited at Khulna Zonal Office suspending the plaintiffs from their respective post is illegal and malafide and that the plaintiffs are in service from 24.11.70 till their reinstatement.

3. The case of the plaintiff-petitioner was that he was grade III officer of erstwhile United Bank Limited and was appointed as an officer in the Satkhira Branch of the Bank towards the last part of 1969. While the plaintiff petitioner and other plaintiffs were serving in the said Bank, the Vice President of the Bank lodged an FIR on 3.10.70 with the Satkhira Police Station against them alleging misappropriation. The plaintiffs were arrested and while they were in custody the Vice President of the Bank by order dated 24.11.70 suspended the plaintiff with effect from 24.11.70 for an indefinite period. The plaintiffs approached for their reinstatement in Janata Bank which succeeded the said United Bank under President's Order No. 26 of 1972. The criminal cases were registered as Sessions case Nos. 177, 178, 179 and 180 of 1981 and the Sessions Judge by his order dated 12.5.81 discharged the plaintiffs as the prosecution failed to produce any evidence against the plaintiffs. After being discharged the plaintiff-petitioner gave representation for his reinstatement but with no result. During the pendency of the suit the Assistant General Manager of the Janata Bank by his letter dated 3.11.86 dismissed the plaintiff from service. The subsequent order of dismissal dated 3.11.86 was also challenged by way of making a prayer for amendment of the plaint which was allowed.

4. The defendant Nos. 1, 2, and 3 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the allegations made in the FIR was not false and that the plaintiffs case is barred by limitation and that the suit is undervalued and the order of suspension was not withdrawn because of the pendency of the criminal case. The plaintiffs are not entitled to seek any relief in the court and that plaintiffs have also no cause of action for the suit. While the suit was pending the defendant filed a, petition praying for return of the plaint in view of the Administrative Tribunal Act VII of 1981 as amended up to date alleging that by reason of section 4 of the Act the case is not cognizable by the Civil Court and the plaintiffs relief lies in the Administrative Tribunal in consequence of the amendment made by Ordinance No. 23 of 1982, Ordinance No. 38 of 1985 and Ordinance No. 60 of 1984 by which the matters relating to the employee of the Janata Bank and other Banks were brought within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal.

<u>5. The learned Munsif after hearing the parties by his order dated 28.3.87 allowed the application and ordered that the plaint be returned and the suit be disposed of accordingly. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff has filed this application and obtained the instant rule. Opposite Party Nos. 1-3 by filing affidavit-in-opposition have controverted the statements and allegations made in the application:</u>

<u>6. At the outset Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali; the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, raised a preliminary objection as to the maintainability of the revision case under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before this court. The learned Advocate submits that the impugned order returning the plaint for presentation in the proper court is appealable under rule 1(a) of Order 43 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the appeal lies before the District Judge according to the valuation of the suit and there being provision of appeal the revision before the High Court Division without first moving the court of appeal below, is incompetent. The learned Advocate has referred to the provision of section 115 which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"The High Court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears to have exercised jurisdiction resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice."</u>

<u>The learned Advocate referred to the provision of Order 43 rule 1(a) of the Code which provides for an appeal from an order under rule 10 of Order VII of the Code returning the plaint to be presented in proper Court. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied on a number of decisions Viz, AIR 1975 (Karnatak) 200, 10 DLR, 633, 21 PLD (Karachi)(1969)349, 22 DLR (SC) 389 and 39 DLR, 306. In the case of Eagle Star Insurance Co. Ltd. and another Vs. The Gwalior Transport Ltd. and another reported in AIR 1975 (Karnatak) 200 it is held that any order directing the return of the plain., for presentation in the proper court had been clearly  made appealable under clause (a) of rule 1 of Order 43 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, one of the essential ingredients of section 115 of the Code relative to the absence of a right of appeal remains unfulfilled. It is also held that if right of appeal in respect of any order or decision or decree is conferred under any of the provisions of the Code, the jurisdiction under section 115 CPC would be clearly barred. In the case of Fazle Karim Khan Vs. Naderuzzaman and others reported in 10 DLR (1958) 632 it is held:</u>

<u>"High Court will not entertain a revision application which instead of being moved before the District Judge under the proviso to section 153(b) of Bangladesh Tenancy Act is moved before the High Court."</u>

<u>In the aforesaid decision the principle laid down is that when the Subordinate Judge and the Superior Court are vested with concurrent jurisdiction the case should be instituted in the court of lowest jurisdiction, otherwise, in cases, the provision as to appeal etc, as provided by the Code of Civil Procedure or any other Act, would be made nugatory and the superior court would be over crowded. This view is founded on the provision of section 15 and Order 7 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was also held that the proper court to move the petition was not the High Court but the District Judge. The next cited case is the case of Arts Council of Pakistan Vs. Raizuddin Pirzada reported in PLD (Karachi) 1969 P 349 wherein similar question arose and it was decided that the appeal could be filed in the District Court against the impugned order and, therefore, it was submitted that the revision was barred. After considering the relevant provision the learned Judge held:</u>

<u>"A plain reading of the section suggests that revision is barred only when there is right of appeal in this court, and not when the applicant has a right of appeal in a subordinate court."</u>

<u>In this said judgment the decision of the case of Charles S Brown Vs. Albert Donugh Hanson reported in AIR 1933 (Bom) 185 has been referred, wherein the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court while dealing with the question of maintainability of a revision case under section 115of the Code of Civil Procedure observed as follows :</u>

<u>"The order made by the learned Subordinate Judge was one in which an appeal was competent (in the District Court) and therefore it is excluded from the purview of this court in revision under section 115 CPC."</u>

<u>In reply to the submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party regarding maintainability or otherwise of revision against the order returning the plaint, Mr. MA Rahim, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has referred to section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides for filing revision case to the High Court from the order of any court subordinate to it for which "no appeal lies thereto" and submits that the word" thereto" should be interpreted to express and mean the High Court Division and, therefore, the revision may not lie against the order which is appealable to the High Court but the order for which appeal is provided before the District Judge is not excluded from the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has cited the case of Arts Council of Pakistan Vs. Reazuddin Pirzada reported in PLD 1969 (Kar) 349 wherein it was held that as the appeal could be filed before the High Court revision was barred. It was further held that a plain reading of the section suggest that revision is barred only when there is right of appeal before the High Court and not when the applicant has a right of appeal in a Subordinate Court. In the said case the decision reported in 1933 AIR (Born) 185 has been referred. In the above cited case while dismissing the revisional application the Division Bench of Bombay High Court made the following observation in respect of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure:</u>

<u>"The order made by the learned subordinate Judge is one in which an appeal was competent (in the District Court) and therefore one which is excluded from the purview of the court in revision by section 115 CPC."</u>

<u>Thus the decision of the above quoted case does not support the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. The next case cited by Mr. Rahim is the case of Wahid Sadeque and others Vs. Majibar Rahman Chowdhury and others reported in 42 DLR 220. In the said case the decision reported in PLD 1962 (Kar) 349 and the case of Zafar Ahmed Vs. Abdul Khaleque reported in PLD 1964 (Kar) 149 have been relied on. In paragraph 9 of the judgment of the case reported in 42 DLR 220 it is observed that revision is barred only when the same matter would be brought by way of appeal to the High Court. Though right of appeal was provided to the District Judge's court the forum of appeal could not be availed of as the Civil Court remained closed due to long vacation from 1st. December to 31 December, 1989 and as such the High Court Division assumed the revisional jurisdiction taking into consideration the circumstances of exceptional nature. Therefore, this cannot be accepted as a general principle for determining the point as to whether revision application lies to the High Court against the order from which appeal lies before the District Judge but the right has not been availed of by the aggrieved party.</u>

<u>7. Now let us have a look to the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the contruction of the section and the language used it cannot be said that restriction imposed relates only to the appeals when it lies to the High Court Division and there is no such restriction in filing a revision case out of the judgment and order against which appeal lies to the District Judge's Court. The determination of the point depends on the interpretation of the words "appeal lies thereto". In the decision reported in 10 DLR 632 the underlying principle has been interpreted to mean and indicate either both the subordinate court and the superior court concurrently and in such event the case should be filed in the lowest grade having jurisdiction and, if not availed of the revisional application will be barred.</u>

8. In the case of Municipal Committee Bahawalpur, through its Chairman Vs. Sh. Aziz Elahi, Ex-Chief Sanitary Inspector reported in 22 DLR (SC) 1970 page 389 it has been held that revision is incompetent where appeal against decree or order lies directly to the High Court or to the District Judge's Court.

9. In this respect the following provisions of sections 15 and 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure is called for consideration in the matter:

"15. Court in which suits to be instituted. Every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it.

16. Suits to be instituted where subject-matter situate, subject to the pecuniary or other limitations prescribed by any law."

In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner has cited the case of Arts Council of Pakistan Vs. Riazuddin Pirzada reported in PLD 1969 (Kar) 349 where the question arose and was considered that the appeal could be filed before the High Court and therefore, revision was barred. The learned Judge held: that a plain reading of this section suggest that revision is barred only when there is right of appeal to this court and not when the applicant has right of appeal in a Subordinate Court. In the said case decision of the case reported in AIR 1933 (Bom) 185 has been referred. There are diverse shades of opinion regarding the maintainability of a revisional application before the High Court against the order passed by the Subordinate Court against which appeal lies.

<u>10. A series of the judicial pronouncement support the view that if a decree or order in the nature of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure passed by the Court of first instance and made appealable under the Code, whether the appeal lies to the High Court or the District Judge, the revision would not be competent. The present case having been taken from the order passed by the court below for which appeal has been provide under Order 43 rule 1(a) CPC the revision is not maintainable, no matter whether the appeal has been provided for either before the District Judge or to the High Court Division. In the Municipal Committee, Bahawalpur, through its Chairman Vs. Sh. Aziz MN, Ex-Chief Sanitary Inspector reported in 22 DLR 389 it is held that:</u>

<u>"Revision is incompetent where appeal against a decree or order lies directly to the High Court or only after another appeal has been taken before the District Judge."</u>

The present case is one which does not fall within the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and hence the revision is found to be not maintainable and as such cannot be entertained. Thus the words "in which no appeal lies thereto" appearing in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been interpreted as follows:

"If framers of section 115 of the CP Code had been of the opinion that a revision would be incompetent only where an immediate appeal lay to the High Court, they would have used word "from" and not 'in' before the words" which no appeal lies thereto" in section 115 CPC."

To arrive at the decision Hamoodur Rahman CJ of erstwhile Supreme Court of Pakistan speaking for the court while considering the point placed reliance on series of decisions Viz. the case of Maharaja Bahadur Ram Ben Vijay Prashad Singh Vs. Kishan Singh and others reported in AIR 1944 (Patna) 54 and the case of Custodian of Evacuee Property, New Delhi Vs. Nasiruddin and others AIR 1962 (Punjab) 218  and the case of Vankalugiri Vs. The Hindu Religious Endowments Board (Madras) AIR 1949 PC 156, observed as follows :

"Where Sir John Beaumont, who wrote the opinion of the Board, pointed out, after referring to the relevant decision on the subject, that section 115 applies only to cases in which an appeal lies, and, where the Legislature has provided no right of appeal, the manifest intention is that the order of the trial Court, right or wrong, shall be final."

11. The next point urged by Mr. MA Rahim, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, is that the learned Munsif committed error of law in his decision in returning the plaint on the ground of absence of jurisdiction in view of the promulgation of the Administrative Tribunal Act VII of 1981 and subsequent amendment thereof vide Ordinance No. 23 of 1982. Ordinance No. 38 of 1985 and Ordinance No. 60 of 1984 in which the service matters of Janata Bank and other Banks were brought within the jurisdiction and scope of the Administrative Tribunal with effect from 25th September, 1984. The learned Advocate further submits that the Administrative Tribunal Act and the amendment thereof did not take away the jurisdiction of the Civil Court in respect of suits filed earlier to the amendment of the Administrative Tribunal Act by the employees of the Bank inasmuch as the dismissal order made on 3.11.86 with retrospective effect from 24.11.70 being incidental to and consequential of the order of suspension dated 24.11.70 the jurisdiction of the Munsif could not be ousted and thus the learned Munsif committed error of law in returning the plaint so as to drive the plaintiff to another litigation.

12. Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali, on the other hand, submits that the suit in which the order of suspension was challenged before the Administrative Tribunal Act as amended upto date came into force but order of dismissal from service of the Bank was made on 11.3.86 which is admittedly after the amendment and thus the order of dismissal has given rise to fresh cause of action at the time when Administrative Tribunal has already been set up as the appropriate and proper forum for dealing with the Matters relating to the service of the Bank employees. The learned Advocate further submits that as soon as the plaintiff was dismissed from service of the Bank on 11.3.86 the order of suspension automatically ceased to exist and the suit became infructuous and there is no alternative remedy and as such the learned court was quite justified in returning the plaint on the ground that the court has ceased to have the jurisdiction to try the suit. The learned Advocate further submits that the order of suspension and the order of dismissal arc two distinct and separate causes of action and hence by way of amendment a new cause of action could not be substituted for the previous one and the order of dismissal can effect from the date of filing of the suit.

13. From the scrutiny of the application and affidavit-in-opposition and other relevant papers it is found that the order of suspension was made on 24.11.70 and the suit was filed on 10.6.84. Though the Administrative Tribunal Act was promulgated on 1.2.81 and given effect to from 5.6.81. the Bank employees were brought within the scope and jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal on 25.9.84.

14. The law relating to the service of the employees under the Government and also under the Bank Administrative Tribunal Act VII of 1981 was promulgated on 5th of June, 1981 by which the Administrative Tribunal was established giving exclusive jurisdiction to it to hear and determine application made by any person in the service of the Republic in respect of the terms and conditions of the service and jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunal under section 4 of the Act which provides:

"(I) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine an application made by any person in the service of the Republic in respect of the terms and conditions or service including pension rights or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the Republic."

The person mentioned in sub-section (I) as above has been defined in sub-section (3) as follows:

"(3) In this section a "person in the service of the Republic" includes a person who is or has retired from such service, but does not include a person in defence service of Bangladesh."

By Administrative Tribunal Amendment Ordinance 1984 (Ordinance No. LX of 1984) the employees of the Banks have been brought within the jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunals set up under the Act.

15. Mr. Rahim the learned Advocate for the petitioner, very candidly concedes the legal position that after the introduction of the amended provision of the Administrative Tribunal Act the Bank employees like the government employees have also been brought within the scope and under the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal and as such no suit or proceeding can be instituted in the Civil Court after the date of amendment but his contention is that the suit filed before the amendment of the law relating to the Administrative Tribunal and found to have been pending are protected under section 13 of the Act which runs as follows:

"Saving—All suits, cases, applications and appeals, relating to any matter in respect of which a Tribunal has jurisdiction pending, immediately before the commencement of this Act, before any court shall be tried, heard and disposed of by such court, as if this Act had not come into force."

16. Referring to the above provision of the saving clause of the Act Mr. Rahim submits that the instant suit was filed before the amendment of the law, against the order of suspension of the petitioner from service and the suit was pending while the amendment came into operation and during the pendency of the suit the petitioner having been dismissed from service necessary amendment of the plaint was sought for and accordingly the prayer for amendment was allowed. The learned Advocate submits that the order of suspension from service is a continuing wrong justifying the application of the provision of section 23 of the Limitation Act. It is also submitted that the amendment of the plaint having been allowed in the suit pending from before, it takes effect from the date of filing of the suit and not from the date of filing of the petition for amendment or from the date of the order. Making a reference to the case reported in AIR (1919) (Born) 798 the learned Advocate submits that the act of suspension from service was a wrong constituted and continued till the order of dismissal from service was effected and hence the relief sought for in the suit by way of amending the plaint cannot be treated as barred by any law. In the case of Asizun Nessa Khatun Vs. Abul Hossain Bhuiya and others reported in 9 DLR 559 it is held :

"Whether the injury complained of is complete on a date, there is no continuing wrong even though the damage caused by that injury might continue. In such case the cause of action to the person injured arises, once and for all, at the time when the injury is inflicted, and the fact that the effects of the injury are felt by the aggrieved person on subsequent occasion, intermittently or even continuously, does not make the injury a continuing wrong so as to give him a fresh cause of action on each such occasion. If, however, the act is such that the injury itself is continuous, then there is a continuing wrong and the case is governed by section 23 of the Limitation Act." Mr. Sheik Razzaque Ali, the learned advocate for the opposite party, referred to section 22 of the Limitation Act and contended that amendment upon new cause of action particularly when it is barred by any law, cannot be allowed. In support of his argument the learned Advocate has cited the cases reported in AIR 1918(Cal) 145, AIR 1972 Rajasthan 241, AIR 1967 (SC) 96, AIR 1938 (Mad) 53, AIR 1938 (Raj) 125 and AIR 1935 (A11) 842.

17. In the case of AK Gupta and Sons Ltd. Vs. Damodar Corporation reported in AIR 1967 (SC) (Pat) 96 it is observed that in the matter of allowing amendment of pleading the general rule is that a party is not allowed by way of amendment to set up a new case or a new cause of action particularly when the suit on the new cause of action is barred. In the case of Tirkha Vs. Ghost Ram reported in AIR 1955 (All) 842 it is held:-

"The court has no right to direct the amendment of a plaint when it has u jurisdiction over the subject matter of the plaint."

In the case of Demur Mohtan Vs. Jagdip Mohon reported in AIR 1936 Patna 535 it is held:

"An amendment which involves a substantial alteration of the cause of action should not be permitted more specially when the suit was brought long after the period of limitation."

18. The learned Advocate for the opposite party contends that the civil Court ceased to have any jurisdiction to try the suit arising out the order of dismissal of the petitioner from service of the Bank and the order of dismissal cannot have retrospective effect. In favour of this proposition of law the learned Advocate has relied on the cases reported in AIR 1966 (Cal) 272(277) and 8 PLR (Dhaka) 820. The learned Advocate further submits that with the order of dismissal of the petitioner from service the cause of action arising out of the order of suspension ceased and a new cause of action has arisen which has been kept out of the general jurisdiction of the Civil Court by the Administrative Tribunal Act as amended by which a separate special forum has been set up for the settlement: of disputes relating to Bani employees and thus filing and entertainment of suit in the Civil Court has been prohibited by imposing a bar. It is also contended that the amendment made subsequent to the promulgation of the Act cannot be allowed and, if allowed cannot be given retrospective effect.

19. In support of the contention that when by a statute an authority is vested in another Tribunal with exclusive power over any subject matter, a Civil Court ceases to have any jurisdiction to try such suit having no jurisdiction. Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali has also refereed to Article 117(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh read with section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act 1981 and cited the cases reported in 33 DLR (AD) 143, 33 DLR (AD) 150, and BCR (Dac) 289 in support of his contention.

<u>20. From the submission made by the learned Advocate of the respective parties and the decisions cited it has become clear that amendment sought for to replace a cause of action, after it has ceased to exist, by a separate, distinct and new cause of action so as to change the nature of the suit and the cause of action will not be allowed and if allowed, can not relate back to the date of the filing of the suit. Furthermore, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court having been vested in the Administrative Tribunal by the promulgation of special statute the jurisdiction of Civil Court in respect of Bank Employees has been ousted and in that view of the matter the plaint was rightly returned by the Civil Court for presentation to the proper Court/Tribunal having jurisdiction.</u>

21. Having regard to the facts and circumstances and law involved in the case I do not find that the learned court below has committed any error of law in his decision in returning the plaint for presentation in the proper court. For the reasons stated I am of the view that the impugned order of the learned Munsif does not call for interference at this stage.

In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment: Syed Amirul Islam J: This revisional application at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against an order dated 12.11.91 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and 1st Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong, in Money Suit No. 52 of 1988, disallowing the plaintiffs application for rejection of counter claim of the defendants. 2. The facts, as are relevant for disposal of the application, may be stated as follows: 3. The Sonali Bank, Agrabad Branch, Chittagong filed the aforesaid money suit for realisation of an amount of Taka 1,98,48,632.70 being the principal amount of loan including interest as on 31.1.88 with a further prayer of pendente lite interest @ 20% per annum on and from the date of filing till the realisation of the decretal dues with cost and other charges. Ultimately on 31.10.90 the case was transferred to the 1st Artha Rin Adalat. Chittagong by virtue of amendment of section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat in 1990, 4. The defendant opposite parties appeared and filed a joint written statement on 29.8.91. In the said written statement they admitted the loan but disputed the claims of the plaintiffs and also made a counter claim of Taka 2,67,04,706.91 against the plaintiff petitioner on different counts as damages and compensation. 5. The plaintiff petitioner on 19.10.91 filed an application in the trial Court for rejecting the prayer of counter claim on the ground that Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 empowers only Bank and some other specified Financial Institutions to institute suit for recovery of loan and since the defendants do not answer the said description they cannot file a counter claim in Artha Rin Adalat. The said application dated 19.10.91 was heard by the trial Court on 12.11.91 and the said application of the plaintiff was rejected by the trial Court holding that the counter claim was made under the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure which is applicable in the proceedings of Artha Rin Adalat In the present Rule the plaintiff petitioner calls in question the legality and propriety of the said order of the trial Court. 6. Mr. Khairul Haque, the learned Advocate, appears for the petitioner and submits that Artha Rin Adalat is a special Court set up for special purpose of speedy recovery of loans by the Banks and specified Financial Institutions only and the Artha Rin Adalat has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the claim of any other person. He further submits that Artha Rin Adalat has jurisdiction to adjudicate in the matter of recovery of loans of the aforesaid Institutions only and not in respect of any other kinds of claim which do not come within the definition of (loan) as defined in section 2 (kha) of the Act and, as such, the counter claim is not entertainable. 7. Mr. Hasan Arif, the learned Advocate, who appears for the defendant opposite parties, submits that Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 (hereinafter called the 'Act') is a procedural law and it does not create any forum i.e. Artha Rin Adalat has got no independent existence of its own. He draws our attention to section 3 of the Act and submits that the provisions of the Act is complementary and not derogatory to other laws and, as such, section 3 if read with section 5(4) and 5(5) of the Act will show that Artha Rin Adalat is an ordinary civil Court as contemplated in the Civil Procedure Code and the Civil Procedure Code is applicable in its entirety to the proceedings of the Artha Rin Adalat unless they are repugnant to the express. provisions of the Act. He further argues by referring to Order 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that even the Civil Procedure Code also provides special procedure on negotiable Instrument and the special procedure has been extended by the Act. and therefore, the Artha Rin Adalat is very much a civil Court under the Civil Courts Act, 1887, as well as under the Civil Procedure Code. His next submission is that section 7 of the Act by providing special procedure for appeal simply restricts the scope of Order 41 and section 94 of the Civil Procedure Code. His final argument is that section 6 of the Act provides that the proceeding, order, Judgment and decree of Artha Rin Adalat shall not be called in question before any court or authority save as provided by section 7 of the Act and as such section 6 prohibits revision to the High Court Division. Before we take up the above noted points for consideration it would be pertinent to note that the Act has come up for consideration in various cases in the past before this court as well as before the Appellate Division. It appears that all the points that have been agitated before us have already been considered in different cases except the last point. To cut the matter short it may be stated that it has already been held by the Appellate Division in the case of Mr. Zahirul Islam vs. National Bank Ltd. and others in CPSLA No. 251 and 318 of 1993 reported in 1994 (11) BLT SC (AD) 23 that Artha Rin Adalat is a special forum created by a special law for adjudication of suits which can be filed by a Bank or a Financial Institution for recovery of its loan. 8. Similarly, in the case of MAC Proprietor, Mahtabuddin Chowdhury and another vs. Agrani Bank reported in 14 BLD (1994) 195, a Division Bench of the High Court Division after considering different provisions of the Act held that "This Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a special law under which courts were constituted with their own forum of appeal. So, by way of interpretating the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 5, it can be found that this is an ordinary civil Court for all practical purposes and all the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable in the proceeding". 9. Finally, in the case of Sultan Alam @ SA Badal vs. Rupali Bank reported in 46 DLR 292 this Bench after considering the provisions of the Act held that the nature and function of Artha Rin Adalat coupled with its power and authority clearly indicate that it is a special forum of limited jurisdiction and not an ordinary civil Court and cannot review its judgement under the provision or Order 47 rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code. From the finding and observations of the aforesaid cases it is clear that the submissions of Mr. Arif that the Act did not create a forum or that the Artha Rin Adalat is an ordinary civil Court and that the Civil Procedure Code applies in its entirety to the proceeding of the said Court is negatived. 10. Now let us consider the final submission of Mr. Arif that a revision does not lie from an order of the Artha Rin Adalat. Let us examine and see if his submission has got any substance. It may be stated that in construing the word "final" in many decisions of the Superior Courts of this subcontinent, it has been held that the word "final" does not necessarily take away revisional power, as "final" means not appealable but open to revision. In considering the scope of section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, the Full Bench of the Madras High Court in the case of Parthasaradhi Nadu vs. Koteswara Rao 47 Mad. 369 (FB) observed "it is further argued that the fact that the decision of this Judge is, by section 57 of the Act (Local Boards Act) and by the rules, final, precludes any revision. There is really no authority adduced in support of that proposition and, in my judgment, it would be quite contrary to the whole object and intention of section 115, Civil Procedure Code, so to hold. The section only applies where there is no appeal". This decision has been followed in 1950 Mad. 730. 11. In construing the word "final" which occurs in section 29(6) of the East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act it was held that the word means that the order of Rent Controller was, subject to the result of an appeal to the District Judge, final. It does not take away the jurisdiction of the High Court to interfere with the District Judge's order under section 115 Civil Procedure Code. 12. In considering section 43 of the Wakfs Ord., 1962, the Supreme Court in the case of Amir Sultan vs. Md. K Alam, 29 DLR (SC) 295 observed that "Though his decision has been made final which precludes any further appeal from his decision, such finality as attaches thereto does not oust the revisional power of the High Court". In interpreting similar provision as embodied in Article 29(4) of the Local Govt. (Union Parishad) Ord. 1983, the Appellate Division in 38 DLR (AD) 172 held that the District Judge acting as an election appellate Tribunal is not a persona designata but a court subordinate to the High Court Division. 13. It had been held in a number of decisions that the Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary civil Court but a special forum of limited jurisdiction. The question, therefore, arises whether an order passed by a court of special jurisdiction is revisable by this Court under section 115 CPC. We can resolve this question easily if we can find an answer to the question, is the Artha Rin Adalat a Court subordinate to the High Court Division. In deciding this issue with regard to special statutes the superior Courts of this subcontinent have formulated certain principles. If appeal lies from a special tribunal to the High Court then that special tribunal is subordinate to the High Court. Similarly, if the special Court is under the administrative control of the High Court, it is also subordinate to the High Court. It we examine the provisions of the Act we find that section 7 provides that an appeal shall lie against a judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat to the High Court Division. Section 4(2) of the Act provides that the judges of the Artha Rin Adalat will be appointed from amongst the Subordinate Judges in consultation with the Supreme Court. Rule framed under the Act provides that the Artha Rin Adalat will be under the administrative control of the Supreme Court. It has been held in one case that if the Court is one from which an appeal lies to the High Court though in certain specified cases, then the Court is subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court and that is sufficient to attract the power of superintendency conferred on the High Court Besides Article 109 of the Constitution provides that High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all Courts subordinate to it and Article 114 provides: "There shall be in addition to the Supreme Court such courts subordinate thereto as may be established by law." 14. So, it is crystal clear that Artha Rin Adalat, though a special Court, is nevertheless a Court subordinate to the High Court Division and is, therefore, amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. So, we find that this revisional application filed by the petitioner is maintainable. 15. We have already held earlier that the Civil Procedure Code is not applicable in its entirety in a proceeding before the Artha Rin Adalat. Mr. Arif submitted that since the application of Order 8 of the Civil Procedure Code has not been barred by the Act, the Artha Rin Adalat is competent to entertain a counter claim under the provision of Order 8, role 6 (1) of the Civil Procedure Code. If we examine the scheme and the other provisions of the Act we find that it is only the financial institutions as defined in section 2 (Ka) which are entitled to institute a case in the Artha Rin Adalat for recovery of loan as defined in section 2(Ka) of the Act and no other person or institution is authouised to file a case before the Artha Rin Adalat So, if a defendant in a Artha Rin Adalat case is allowed to set up counter claim or set off he will be allowed to do a thing indirectly which he cannot do directly and this will run counter to the intent and purpose of the Act. Moreover, the right to set up a plea of counter claim is a substantive right and not a matter of mere procedure. We have examined the provisions of the Act and there is no provision for making counter claim by a defendant. The learned Artha Rin Adalat by entertaining the counter claim of the defendants opposite parties has acted in excess of its jurisdiction. 16. There is yet another aspect of the case. Even if it were held that Civil Procedure Code is applicable in the instant case then also the trial Court acted illegally and without jurisdiction in as much as the counter claim raised by the defendant does not come within the purview of rule 6 of Order 8 as the sum claimed by way of damages is not an ascertained amount. 17. Mr. Hasan Arif, the learned Advocate, previously took adjournments to place before us a decision of the Appellate Division. Today he has placed before us the Judgment and Order dated 13.6.94 of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Appeal No. 7 of 1994. This decision does not help the learned Advocate, rather it goes against him as it has been held therein that an Artha Rin Adalat cannot entertain any set off or counter claim in a suit tried by it. After a review of the aforesaid decisions and the provisions of the Act we find that the submissions of Mr. Khairul Haque have got substance and accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order dated 12.11.91, so far it relates to the rejection of the application dated 19.10.91 is set aside and the application dated 19.10.91 filed by the plaintiff is allowed and the counter claim is rejected. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost. End.

lawyer:
MA Aziz, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Badruddin Ahmed with Raquib Ahmed, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party No.1
parties:
Sultan Alam @ SA Badal ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Rupali Bank ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J.: This matter arises out of the following facts:

The opposite party Rupali Bank instituted Title Suit No. 12 of 1988 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 3, Khulna, for realisation of loan advanced to the defendant- petitioner and the amount due stood at Taka 3,30,183.00 with interest on 31.8.1987. Subsequently the suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.1 of 1991 on transfer to the Artha Rin Adalat No. 1 of Khulna. The said suit was decreed on contest as prayed for. Thereafter the defendant- petitioner filed an application under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for reviewing the judgment on the ground that several amounts on different heads were required to be deducted from the decretal amount By the impugned judgment and order dated 27.7.1991, the trial Court rejected all the grounds of review except one, which is that an amount of Taka 27,830.00 which was received by the plaintiff from Sadharan Bima Corporation on account of the defendant -petitioner was required to be deducted from the decretal amount. In the present Rule the defendant petitioner challenges the said order of the trial Court rejecting his other grounds of review.

2. Before we take up the matter on merit it would be pertinent to consider the basic questions involved in the matter, namely, whether the Artha Rin Adalat is a civil Court so as to be competent to entertain an application for review under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>3. Artha Rin Adalat has been constituted under section 3 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, for certain specific purpose, namely, for speedy recovery of dues of banks and some other specified financial institutions only. Section 5(4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, stipulates that the Artha Rin Adalat shall be "deemed" to be a civil Court and shall have all the powers and authority as are vested in a civil Court. In enacting special statutes legislature employs "deeming" clause. "Deeming" clauses of different statutes have been interpreted by the superior courts of the Sub-continent including the Privy Council. In the case of Radha Kissen Chamria and others Vs. Durga Prasad Chamria, AIR 1940 PC 167, it has been held that "As the analogy only arises by legal fiction, it must be limited to the purposes enacted by the context and cannot be given larger effect." Similarly in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax Vs Vadilal Lallu Bhat, AIR 1973 (SC) 1016 it has been held by the Indian Supreme Court that "legal fictions are only for definite purposes and they are limited to the purpose for which they are created and should not be extended beyond their legitimate field." In the case of Pubali Bank Vs. Chairman, First Labour Court Dhaka and another reported in 44 DLR (AD) 40, our Appellate Division in interpreting a "deeming" clause observed as follows:</u>

<u>"When the legislature enacts a "deeming" clause, the correct way to interpret the same is to find out for what purpose and upto what extent the legal fiction has been created. It is the function of the Court to find out the limitation of the legal fiction, to delimit its boundaries and not to extend the frontier of legal fiction beyond what has been provided in the statute".</u>

4. We have carefully scrutinised the relevant provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, and we find that Artha Rin Adalat has been brought into existence for some specific purposes. By section 5 (4) of the Act, the Artha Rin Adalat has been "deemed" to be a civil Court and it has been vested with all the powers of a civil Court as are vested to a Court under the provision of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908). Section 5(5) of the Act provides that the Artha Rin Adalat will follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure for regulating the procedure in respect of such proceedings if it is not contrary to the provisions of the Act. The nature and function of the Artha Rin Adalat coupled with its power and authority clearly indicate that it is a special forum of limited jurisdiction and not an ordinary civil Court. The view we are taking gets support from the observations made in the unreported case of Agrani Bank Vs. Sultana Jute Mills Ltd. (Writ Petition No. 1070 of 1991) decided by a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 1.12.93. It is observed:

"From the nature and function of the Artha Rin Adalat as provided under Artha Rin Adalat Act and from the facts that the Artha Rin Adalat is presided over by a subordinate judge we are of the view that Artha Rin Adalat though designated as a civil Court under the special Act is not a civil Court established under the Civil Court Act, 1887, having jurisdiction of general nature".

5. The Appellate Division have finally decided the legal status of the Artha Rin Adalat in the case of Md. Zahirul Islam Vs. National Bank Ltd. & others in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 251 and 318 of 1993 reported in 1994 (11) BLT SC (AD) 23 wherein their Lordships observed, "The Artha Rin Adalat is a special forum created by a special law for adjudication of suits which can be filed by a bank or a financial institution for recovery of its dues" and further held that in an appeal a defendant-respondent cannot file a cross-objection under Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>6. This being the legal status of Artha Rin Adalat we are to look into the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, to see whether the said Ain has empowered the Artha Rin Adalat to review its own judgment because it is well-settled proposition of law that right to review like the right of appeal is a substantive right and not a mere matter of procedure. It is also well-settled that the power to review is not an inherent power. It must be conferred by law either specifically or by necessary implication. There is a long line of decisions of the superior Courts of this subcontinent where it has been consistently held that canon of interpretation suggests that a right has to be conferred specifically. In the Artha Rin Adalat Ain it has been provided that an appeal shall lie against a judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat but we do not find any provision for review. From the other provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain it cannot be said that the power of review has been conferred on the Artha Rin Adalat by implication. We, therefore, hold that no application for review under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure lies in the Artha Rin Adalat. The review application filed by the defendant-petitioner was not entertainable by the Artha Rin Adalat and, as such, was incompetent In view of our above observations we are of the view that this revisional application is also incompetent and not maintainable. However, we maintain the impugned order on the ground, that by the order the trial Court has obviously corrected a clerical mistake by deducting Taka 27,830.00 from the decretal amount as the said amount was admittedly received by the plaintiff Bank on account of the petitioner from the Sadharan Bima Corporation.</u>

The Rule is accordingly discharged, however, without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Aftab Hossain ------ For the Petitioner
No one ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Chairman, Chittagong Port Authority, Chittagong ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Kalipada Dey & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Amin-Ur-Rahman Khan, J. ---This Rule is directed against the order dated 29-10-85 passed by the respondent No. 8 namely, The Chairman, Labour Court, Chittagong in I.R.O Case No. 79 of 1985 restraining the petitioner from selecting any Traffic Inspector through selection committee or by any other body on 6.11.85 or any other dates on the basis of the resolution 2.10.85 till disposal of the case.

2. The respondents 1-7 brought the I.R.O. Case No. 79 of 1985 under section 34 of I.R.O. 1969 with a prayer to direct the present petitioner to select Traffic Inspectors from only the existing Assistant Traffic Inspectors and not to deprive the present respondent Nos. 1-7 from their right to be selected, they being seniors as Assistant Traffic Inspectors.

3. The case of the respondent Nos. 1-7 who were the petitioners in the I.R.O. case was that they were corkers under the present petitioner and were selected in order of merit for appointment to the post of Assistant Traffic Inspector by letter dated 5.6.83 and their joining reports were accepted. Subsequently on 21.4.84 an order was passed by the Secretary, Chittagong Port Authority promoting 52 departmental staffs as Assistant Traffic Inspector about one year after the appointment of the respondent Nos. 1-7 who were the petitioners. The said Secretary by his order dated 21.4.84 and 23.4.83 gave seniority to those subsequently appointed Assistant Traffic Inspectors superseding the seniority of the present respondent Nos. 1-7 who were the petitioners. On the protest made by them the second party deputed them to other posts and thereafter the second party namely, the present petitioner formed a selection committee for promoting the senior Assistant Traffic Inspectors to the post of Traffic Inspector fixing 8.6.85 for such selection superseding the present respondent who were the petitioners. Being aggrieved thereby they brought the I.R.O. Case No. 79 of 1985. Upon filing the said case the respondents 1-7 who were petitioners in the case applied for a temporary injunction and obtained the impugned order. The present petitioner namely, the Chairman, Chittagong Port Authority challenged the impugned order by this writ petition.

4. The petitioner submitted that the Chittagong Port Authority is a statutory body and that the promotion of employees are made according to the Rules and the Traffic Inspectors are promoted from amongst the senior staffs of different categories through proper selection in consideration of the requisite eligibility and qualification, The respondents 1-7 had no basis for their claim and their application under I.R.O. was misconceived. They obtained the impugned order of temporary injunction which was passed without giving the petitioner any opportunity to show cause or to have a hearing. In the I.R.O. case no industrial dispute being present the labour court could not be deemed to be a Civil Court or to have any power of Civil Court for ordering temporary injunction. The said order was illegal and without jurisdiction and was liable to be quashed.

5. At the hearing before us none appeared on behalf of the respondents. Since the point involved was of general interest we gave an elaborate hearing to the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

6. Mr. Aftab Hossain the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that since the I.R.O. case was brought by the seven respondents under section 34 of the I.R.O. to represent their individual grievances such dispute could not be considered as an industrial dispute. Under section 36(2) of the I.R.O. the labour court is deemed to be a Civil Court and can exercise such powers as are vested in the Civil Court only and solely for the purpose of adjudicating and determining an industrial dispute. The case before the Labour Court that was brought by the respondent Nos. 1-7 in the capacity of individual workers not being an industrial dispute for adjudicating and determining that case the Labour Court could not be deemed to be a Civil Court and consequently it was not vested with the powers of Civil Court and for that the Labour Court could have no jurisdiction or authority to pass the impugned order of temporary injunction according to the provision of Order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Section 34 of the I.R.O. provides as follows:-

"Any collective bargaining agent or any employer or workman may apply to the Labour Court for the enforcement of any right guaranteed or secured to it or him by or under any law or any 'award or settlement."

7. In this case the seven respondents namely, respondents 1-7 in their capacity of individual workers brought the I.R.O. Case No. 79 of 1985 under the said section 34 of the I.R.O. seeking enforce dent of their right for being considered for selection to the higher post of Traffic Inspector. So, whether the dispute as raised by these seven respondents can be regarded as an industrial dispute is the foremost question to he considered and decided.

<u>8. In section 2 (XIII) industrial dispute has been defined in the following language :-</u>

<u>"Industrial Dispute" means any dispute or difference between employers and employees or between employers and workmen or between workmen and workmen, which is connected with the employment or non-employment or the terms of employment or the conditions of work of any person."</u>

<u>Section 43 of I.R.O. qualified the said definition and rather explains the said definition in the following language:</u>

<u>"No industrial dispute shall be deemed to exist unless it has been raised in the' prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or any employer."</u>

<u>8A. In this case it is evident that the present dispute in the I.R.O. Case No. 79 of 1985 was brought by an application under section 34 of the LRO by the seven respondents in their individual capacity as workers and certainly the dispute was not raised by a collective bargaining agent or by any employer in the prescribed manner. This being so according to section 43 the dispute in the LRO. Case No. 79 of 1985 can not be regarded in law as ail industrial dispute in view of the plain language of section 43. Though section 2 (XIII) gave a general definition of industrial dispute but that was clearly qualified and explained by the subsequent provision of section 43 of the I.R.O. In view of the provision of section 43 there remains no scope to hold that the dispute raised in I.R.O. Case No. 79 of 1985 was an industrial dispute because from the clear language of section 43 no industrial dispute can be deemed to exist unless it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or by an employer.</u>

9. In this connection several decisions were cited from the side of the petitioner. The earliest cited decision is a decision of the Division Bench of this Court in the case of Bangladesh Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. Vs. The Chairman, Labour Court, Chittagong reported in 27 DLR (1975) at page 367 wherein it has been held that section 43 of the Ordinance has very clearly laid down that no industrial dispute shall be decided to exist unless it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or an employer. In the said decision it has further been held that the Labour Court is to be deemed a Civil Court for specified purpose i.e. for the purpose of adjudicating and determining an industrial dispute and that the Labour Court trying a complaint of an individual worker was not a Labour Court adjudicating and determining a labour dispute and as such could not be deemed to be a civil court under section 12 (2) of the Labour Disputes Act, 1965 (which corresponds to section 36(2) of I.R.O.)

10. The next decision is in the case of Khulna Tobacco Industries Limited Vs Chairman, Labour Court, Khulna and another decided by a Division Bench of this Court reported in 29 DLR (1977) at page 148. In this decision it has been held, "Expression "shall be deemed to be a Civil Court" in section 36(2) shows that the Labour Court is a Civil Court for the purpose of adjudicating and determining a labour dispute (which is now termed as industrial dispute), The expression clearly indicates the intention of the legislator that the Labour Court is intended to be converted into a Civil Court. In sub-section (2) of section 36 the Labour Court has been clothed with only such powers as are available under the Code of Civil Procedure and are necessary for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute."

11. In the decision in the case of Manager Sonali Jute Mills Ltd. Vs. Secretary, Sonali Jute Mills Workers Union & decided by a Division Bench of this Court reported in 30 DLR (1978) page 141 it has been held as follows:-

"The law does not recognize the existence of industrial dispute unless it is raised by a collective bargaining agent in the prescribed manner, namely, by negotiation (section 26) conciliation (section 29), arbitration (section 31), and adjudication by Labour Court (section 35) Exercise of the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under section 36 was unwarranted inasmuch as it was not exercising the jurisdiction for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute. Labour Court is a Civil Court for limited purpose and since the power of injunction has not been conferred on it the canons of interpretation suggests that such power is not available because the power must be conferred expressly."

<u>12. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has held in the case of M/s. Railway Men  Stores Ltd. and others Vs. Chairman, Labour Court, Chittagong and another reported in 30 DLR (SC) (1978) page 251 that "an industrial dispute shall not be deemed to be in existence unless as has been provided in section 43 of the Ordinance, it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or employer." All the aforesaid decisions have uniformly guided and held that there cannot be any recognition of industrial dispute under the law i.e. under section 43 of the I.R.O. unless the dispute has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent. So in the present case, as we have already found the dispute was raised by several individual workers in their capacity as such in order to have their right enforced under section 34 of I.R.O. in the matter of their selection for promotion to the higher post of Traffic Inspector. So, it goes without saying that it was not raised in the prescribed manner by collective-bargaining agent or employer. This being so according to the provision of section 43 of the I.R.O., in is cannot be held or regarded to be an industrial dispute according to the provision of I.R.O.</u>

<u>13. Section 36 provides the powers and procedure of Labour Court. The provisions is as follows :- "Section 36 (1)- Subject to the provisions of this Ordinance, a Labour Court shall follow as nearly as possible summary procedure as prescribed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.</u>

<u>(2) A Labour Court shall, for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute, be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have the same powers as are vested in such Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) including the powers of-</u>

<u>(a) enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath,</u>

<u>(b) compelling the production of documents and material objects, and</u>

<u>(c) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents.</u>

<u>(3) A Labour Court shall, for the propose of trying an offence under the Ordinance have same powers as are vested in the Court of a Magistrate of the first class under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Act V of 1898) and shall, for the purpose of appeal from a sentence passed by it, be deemed to be a Court of Sessions under that Cede.</u>

<u>(4) No Court fee shall be payable for filing, exhibiting or recording any document in, or obtaining any document from, a Labour Court."</u>

<u>14. This section 36 is the only provision in the entire I.R.O. which lays down the procedure and powers of Labour Court in the matter of dispute of cases of civil and criminal nature. For the purpose of trying offences under the I.R.O. the Labour Court shall have the same power as are vested in the court of a Magistrate of the 1st class and as regards the procedure for the purpose of trying offences he shall follow as nearly as possible summary procedure as prescribed in the Code of Criminal Procedure vide section 36(1) and section 36(3) of the I.R.O. For the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute the Labour Court shall be deemed to be a civil court and he shall have the same powers as are vested in such court under the Code of Civil Procedure i.e. he shall follow all the procedures of the Code of Civil Procedure vide section 36(2) of the I.R.O. So, the position of the Labour Court is that only for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute it shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have the same powers as are vested in in such court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Neither the section 36 of the I.R.O. nor in any other section of the I R.O. the Labour Court has been vested with any power of Civil Court or any power to follow the procedure provided under the Code of Civil Procedure while adjudicating and determining individual dispute.</u>

<u>15. In the present case, it was an individual dispute which was raised by the seven respondents in their capacity of individual workers, and it not being an industrial dispute the Labour Court while adjudicating and determining the dispute raised in I. R.O. case No. 79 of 1985 could not be deemed to be a civil court or to have the powers vested in such court under the Code of Civil Procedure. The passing of an order of temporary injunction as provided in section 39(1)(c) is the power of a Civil Court and such power can be exercised only according to the procedure as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure. As we have already observed, in the present case no adjudication or determination of industrial dispute being involved the Labour Court dealing with such case cannot be deemed to be a civil court to have the power to follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure within the provisions of I.R.O. including section 36.</u>

16. In this connection we should also refer to some decisions in which it has been contrarily held that even in deciding such cases the Labour Court shall be deemed to be a civil court and shall be deemed to have power to grant injunction and to pass or set aside the ex parte decree by following the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure.

17. The earliest decision is in the case of M/S. M. M. Ispahani Ltd. vs. Chairman, 2nd Labour Court, Chittagong and another reported in 19 DLR (1967) page 612 in which a Division Bench of this Court held as follows :-

"The Labour Court mentioned in section 25 (i)(b) of the Standing Orders Act, 1965 is now the Labour Court as constituted under the Labour Disputes Act 1965 accompanied with all the trappings and powers of that Court under the latter Act. It is definitely implied in section 25 of the Standing Orders Act, 1965 that the Labour Court mentioned therein will function with all powers of that Court conferred on it under the Labour Disputes Act, 1965."

On a reading of this decision we find that it was not at all considered in the said decision whether the dispute raised in that case was an industrial dispute or not and for want of such consideration the decision given therein cannot be applied correctly and properly the point that has arisen in the present case.

18. The next decision is in the case of Raj Textile Mills Ltd. vs. Chairman, Labour Court, Khulna & another reported in 33 DLR (1981) page 376. In (his decision it has been held that in a case under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act the Labour Court can set aside an ex-parte order under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this decision no reasoning’s has been given except saying that the court relied upon the decision reported in 19 DLR 612. Thus as in the case of 19 DLR 612 so also in this case the moot question, namely whether the cases related to an industrial dispute or not were not considered or looked into and so those decisions cannot be suitably applied in the present case. This more so because we have already referred to the series of decisions where this moot point namely, whether there is any industrial dispute within the meaning of section 43 of I.R.O. was considered and the decision was that unless a dispute is raised in the prescribed manner by the collective bargaining agent or by an employer that cannot be regarded as an industrial dispute and consequently a Labour Court while deciding a case which is not concerned with any industrial dispute cannot be regarded as a civil court or to have the powers of civil court under section 36 of the I.R.O.

19. The last and rather latest decision that has come to our notice is a decision of a Division Bench of this Court given in the cases of Publi Bank Ltd. Vs. The Chairman, First Labour Court, Dhaka & another reported in B.C.R. 1986 page 129. In this case the court after considering the decision reported in 11 DLR, 19 DLR, 29 DLR, 30 DLR (HC) and 33 DLR preferred to agree to the decision reported in 19 DLR and 33 DLR and not to agree to the decisions reported in 29 DLR and 10 DLR (HC). In this decision it has been held-

Form a reading of the definition of the word "industrial dispute" in section 2 (XVIII). in our view an application under section 34 of the I.R.O. though not arising out of an industrial dispute as contemplated under section 43 of the I R.O. or which may be raised under sections 26 to 31 of the I.R.O. it is an industrial dispute as contemplated under section 36(1) (presumably 36(2) If we accept the proposition advanced by the learned Advocate for the opposite- party petitioner (hat the word 'industrial dispute as has been referred to in section 36(1), is an industrial dispute as may be raised under sections 26 to 31 and section 43, then the Labour Court would be devoid of any power and jurisdiction or a procedure to hear an application' under section 34 or the I.R.O. which in our view cannot be accepted."

<u>20. It appears that in giving this decision the Court held that in section 36(2) the word 'industrial dispute' was referable to industrial dispute as defined in section 2 of I.R.O. and not in section 43 of I.R.O. This interpretation was given only out of the anxiety that in the absence of such interpretation the labour court while deciding the cases of individual disputes will have no power and no procedure creating an absurd and unworkable situation. But whatever be the consequence provisions of the law in its plain language shall have to be followed. In this case we have already referred that the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has already interpreted the definition of 'industrial dispute' in the case reported in 30 DLR (SC) at page 251 by holding as follows :-</u>

<u>"Such an industrial dispute shall not be deemed to be in existence unless, as has been provided in section 43 of the Ordinance it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or employer."</u>

<u>21. The same meaning and interpretation of ' industrial dispute' 'was followed if another decision of the Appellate Division in the case of James Finlay Vs. Chairman. Second Labour Court, Dhaka reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 21. These interpretations given by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court did not come to the notice of the Court for which a different and contrary interpretation was given regarding the term industrial dispute’s contained in section 36(2) of I.R.O. We may note here that the definition of. Industrial dispute" as contained in section 43 of I.R.O. 1909 existed in the same language in the Labour Dispute Act, 1965 which was substituted by I.R.O. 1969. It is also to be noted that according to section 34 of I.R.O. before its amendment Con 17.10.70 existence of industrial dispute was a must without which no application could be made under section 34 of I.R.O. and even dispute of individual worker could be raised in the Labour Court under section 34 of I.R.O. only by the collective bargaining agent and no application under section 34 I.R.O. could be made by individual workers. It was only by amendment of section 34 LR.O. on 17.10.70 that individual workman was for the first time allowed to apply under section 34 I.R.O. besides the collective Bargaining Agent and employer. So reading sections 34 and 43 of 1 R.O. which existed before amendment of Section 34 on 17.10.70 it is found clear that Industrial dispute was always meant to be only the dispute that is raised by the Collective Bargaining Agent or by employer and Dot by individual worker or workers. It is also significant to note that section 36(2) of I.R.O. has not been amended though section 34 of IRO was amended on 17.10.70 which means that the Labour Court continues to be deemed to be a Civil Court only for adjudicating and determining industrial disputes and not for determining individual disputes. The Legislators while amending section 34 I.R.O. by allowing individual workers to apply under section 34 IRO did not amend section 36(2) of I.R.O. by providing that Labour Court shall also be deemed to be Civil Court while adjudicating and determining individual disputes. Thus we find that according to the plain language of section 36(2) read with section 43 of I.R.O. as also according to the background of the original section 34 of I.R.O. and its subsequent amendment a Labour Court while it does not adjudicate or determine any industrial dispute cannot he deemed to be a Civil Court. In other words, when a Labour Court adjudicates and determines an individual dispute it will remain a Labour Court pure and simple without having any power at Civil Court.</u>

<u>Then a pertinent question arises as to whether the Labour Court in such a situation will be powerless because of no power or procedure having been prescribed in the I.R.O.</u>

<u>22. The entire I.R.O. did not provide any where chat the Labour Court while adjudicating and determining individual disputes shall be deemed to be Civil Court or have power of civil court perhaps to simplify or ensure quicker disposal of individual disputes. At the same time the I.R.O. did not also provide any procedure to be followed by the Labour Court in respect of such cases. In that position it must be held that in the absence of any procedure being provided the Labour Court was left with its discretion to follow the procedure which it finds expedient for maintaining and seeming the rules of natural justice. A Labour Court has to decide an application under section 34 of I.R.O. submitted by individual workers judicially and not arbitrarily; so for that purpose it will have to adopt and follow some judicial procedure and in the absence of the procedure being provided in the I.R.O. it must be presumed the Legislators intended that Labour Court may follow its own procedure on the principle of natural justice, and can pass any appropriate order for that and unless such order is barred by any law. A similar decision has been taken by the Full Bench of Lahore High Court reported in P.L.D. (1972) Lahore at page 603.</u>

<u>For the aforesaid reasons we are unable to apply the decision in the case reported in B.C.R. 1986 page 129 to toe present case.</u>

<u>23. From our foregoing discussion of the factual and the legal aspect of the present case we find that in the I.R.O. case No. 79 of 1985 no industrial dispute being involved and contrarily individual dispute being involved the labour court while adjudicating or determining the dispute of the said case could not be deemed to be a civil court or to have any power vested in the civil court according to section 36 of the I.R.O., We have already held that throughout the I.R.O. there is no other provisions made vesting the power of civil court on the labour court or the power to follow the procedures of the Code of Civil Procedure in the matter of adjudicating and determining individual dispute. i.e, the disputes other than the industrial dispute So the question that now arise; is whether the labour court without being deemed to be a civil court and without having any power of civil court can grant a temporary injunction according to the provisions of Order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the series of decisions that we have already quoted carrier it has been held that the labour court cannot exercise such power of the civil court. If we refer to section 35(5)(d) of I.R.O. we may note that the labour court shall exercise and perform such other powers and functions as are or may be conferred upon or assigned to it by order under this Ordinance or under any other law. As we have already found that the labour court in the present ease had no power of Civil court and no other Jaw has come to our knowledge which empowers the labour court while adjudicating disputes other than industrial dispute to grant temporary injunctions. In this connection we may also refer to the provisions of Specific Relief Act. Section 52 of the Specific Relief Act provides as follows:-</u>

<u>"preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the Court by injunction, temporary or perpetual,"</u>

<u>Section 53 of the Spe9ific Relief Act provides ;-</u>

<u>"Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specified time or until the further order of the Court. They may be granted at any period of a suit and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure."</u>

<u>24. These two provisions show that the right of temporary or permanent injunction is created by the Specific Relief Act which enjoins that it can be granted only in a suit and the procedure in the matter of granting the temporary injunction is regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>This means that temporary injunction can only be granted in a suit and by a civil court by following the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure The power and procedure of civil court and of the Code of Civil Procedure being absent with the labour court while it adjudicates and determines individual dispute and not industrial dispute there is no scope for a labour court in such a situation to grant temporary injunction.</u>

In view of the above the impugned order of the labour court is found to be without any lawful authority.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned order is set aside.

Mohammed Abdur Rouf, J.--J agree.

End.
