Md. Jilani  ------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Md. Wahed Uddin Sarder ------- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule issued at the instance of the defendant petitioner in an application under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10.9.80 passed by Mr. Hassan Amin, Subordinate Judge and SCC Judge, Pabna in Small Cause Court Suit No. 1 of 1977.

2. The short facts giving rise to the Rule may be stated as follows:

The opposite party as plaintiff filed SCC Suit No. 1 of 1977 in the Court of the Small Cause Court Judge (Sub-Judge) at Pabna against the defendant-petitioner for evicting him from the suit-holding. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that he acquired the 'Ka' schedule property including the building thereon from one Bhabani Prasad Saha by way of exchange in the year 1965 and he has been possessing the same by residing in some part of the holding and realising rents from the tenants in other parts; that the defendant-petitioner was one of the bharatias of the 'Kha' schedule quater out of the 'Ka' schedule 4-storied building i.e. old Municipal Holding No. 72 and Hal No. 480. He was a tenant at-will and used to pay rent at a rental of Rs. 30/- per month, but defaulted in paying rents since January, 1968 and as such be became a habitual defaulter; that the defendant was not paying any rent in spite of repeated to kids. The plaintiff by issuing a notice under section 106 of the TP Act, terminated his tenancy right after the expiry of September, 1975. The notice was duly received by the defendant petitioner on 12.8.75, but he did not vacate the suit premises; that the defendant petitioner being a habitual defaulter and after termination of his tenancy right, he being a trespasser in the suit premises is liable to be evicted therefrom; that the plaintiff bonafide requires the suit premises and he is entitled to get possession of the same. Hence the suit.

3. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia that the plaintiff has no cause of action to file the suit and the same is barred by limitation. His case, inter alia is that he was inducted as tenant in the suit holding by landlord Bhabani Prasad Saha at a rental of Taka 20'00 and Taka 10'00 for supply of water, in all Taka 30'00 per month, from December. 1958; that he has been possessing the same since then and paying rents regularly; that he paid rents up to December, 1967, but the landlord Bhabani Prasad Saha could not realise rent from him for the case holding from January, 1968; that the said landlord died in the month of February or March, 1968 at Pabna Town and his sons were residing in India from the time of Partition and as such his properties including the suit holding were declared as enemy property in EP Misc. Case No. 35 (Pab)/1967-68 and the authority concerned took possession of the same. The disputed holding thereafter was leased out to him at a rental of Tk. 20'00 from 16.3.68. His further case is that the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property by this time intimated him about stay of further proceedings of the said Miscellaneous case by a letter dated 23.11.68 and as such he could not pay rents of the suit holding in the absence of the heirs of late Bhabani Prassad Saba; that he paid Tk. 2,272'55 paisa as Municipal tax, Sweeper tax, Water Supply tax, etc. from 1968 to February, 1977 in the absence of the landlord, Bhabani Prasad Saha. It is further alleged that the plaintiff never gave him any notice about the acquisition of the said property nor made any takid for the rents as alleged; that he is, however, ready to pay rents to the plaintiff, if he is declared owner of the suit holding; that Bhabani Prasad Saha was all along a resident of this country and he was never a resident of India; that the plaintiff never got the suit property by way of exchange and that the papers including the power of attorney in respect of the alleged exchange are forged; that the plaintiff has got no right, title and interest over the suit property and he has no bonafide requirement as alleged. Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. The plaintiff examined in all two witnesses including the postal peon and filed a number of documents including the registered deed of transfer of the suit property in his favour. The defendant- petitioner examined himself only as DW 1 and also filed a number of documents including the returned money order form and some chalans of the alleged payment of rents to the Rent Controller for the suit holding. The learned Small Cause Court Judge on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record came to the following findings that:

(1) the plaintiff has a prima facie title in the suit holding;

(2) there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant; (3) the defendant is a habitual defaulter;

(4) the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is a valid one and the same has been duly served upon the defendant and (5) the plaintiff requires the suit holding for his own necessity and upon such findings. the learned Small Cause Court Judge decreed the suit with costs and directed the defendant-petitioner to hand over vacant possession of the holding to plaintiff within 60 days by his judgment and decree dated 10.9.80. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant-petitioner filed the instant application and obtained the present Rule. A counter affidavit has been filed on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite-party. Thereafter an affidavit-in-reply and also a supplementary affidavit on behalf of the defendant- petitioner have been filed in this case.

5. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner firstly submits that the suit as framed is not maintainable and the plaint of the same ought to have been returned to the plaintiff under section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act as it involves the determination of the question of title but the learned Small Causes Court's Judge committed serious error of law in determining the said question of title in favour of the plaintiff in this SCC Suit and as a result there has been an error in the decision occasioning complete failure of justice.

6. Mr. Md. Abdul Majid the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite-party on the other hand submits that the suit is quite maintainable and the Small Cause Court judge has not committed any error of law in coming to a finding as to the question of prima-facie title of the plaintiff over the suit holding and also the relationship of the landlord and the tenant between the parties. He further submits that to return or not to return the plaint in a suit involving any question of title is the discretion of the Court concerned under section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act. The SCC Judge is perfectly within his competence and jurisdiction to incidentally go into the question of title involved in the suit and decide the same. In support of his contention.he cited some decisions reported in 26 DLR 314 and 22 DLR 841. To appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates on this point, let me refer to section 23 of the Small Causes Courts Act which reads as follows:

"notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this Act. when the right of a plaintiff and relief claimed by him in a Court of Small Causes depends upon the proof or disproof of a title to immoveable property or other title which such a Court cannot finally determine the Court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a Court having jurisdiction to determine the title."

<u>7. From a plain reading of the section it appears that the word 'may' shows that the power or authority under section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act is discretionary and not obligatory or mandatory. In the case of Mohammad Salim Vs. Mohammad Siddick Jamal & ors reported in 22 DLR 841, it has been held that:</u>

<u>"Ordinarily in deciding a case for evicting the tenant of a suit premises the SCC Judge has got no business to go into the question of title but in case of absolute necessity for the purpose of deciding the question raised in the suit the SCC Judge is competent to go into the question of title incidentally."</u>

8. Again in the case of Merajuddin Ahmed Vs. Md. Anwarul Islam & another reported in 26 DLR 314, it has been held:

"From a reading of section 23 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act it is clear that when the determination of any right before the Small Cause Court is dependent upon proof or disproof of a title to immovable property he may return the plaint to be filed in the Court having jurisdiction to determine title for a proper determination of the said question. This power is. however discretionary and it clearly indicates that Small Cause Court has the power to decide an incidental question of title in a suit which is essentially of Small Cause nature in case it chooses not to return the plaint. Its decision on the question of title will not of course, be final and, therefore, will not be res judicata in a suit brought before a Civil Court.

The provision of section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act does not lay down that an issue as to title renders a SCC Suit non-maintainable as such but enacts that the authority of a SCC Judge to hear such a suit is discretionary. "

<u>9. So, from the aforesaid provisions of section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act and the decisions referred to, it is sufficiently clear that the learned SCC Judge was wholly within his competence to decide the question of title of the plaintiff in the suit-holding incidentally and that is not the final determination of title which can be barred by res judicata. As such the learned sec Judge has not committed any illegality in coming to a finding as to the question of title over the suit-holding in favour of the plaintiff.</u>

10. Now, with regard to the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that in deciding the relationship of the landlord and the tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant, the learned Subordinate Judge has committed error of law by mis-appreciation and misconstruing the evidence particularly Ext. E, deed of transfer, the learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that the learned Subordinate Judge on proper consideration of the materials on record has determined the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant as landlord and tenant and there has been no mis-appreciation or misconstruction of any evidence either oral or documentary by the learned SCC Judge.

11. I have been taken through the impugned judgment, the oral evidence on record and also the Exhibits 1-16 filed on behalf of the plaintiff and the Exhibits A-E filed on behalf of the defendant- petitioner. All these exhibits, namely, Exhibits 1-16 and Ext. C series mainly have been taken into consideration by the trial Court in deciding the question of title of the plaintiff in the suit holding Exhibit. 3 is the Deed of Transfer dated 21.6.74 which was finally executed and registered in favour of the plaintiff-opposite-party by the Government for and on behalf of the landlord of the suit holding Bhabani Prasad Saha in exchange in accordance with law. The contents of the said deed appear to be very clear and distinct to show that it is a deed of transfer in favour of the plaintiff by way of exchange in respect of the suit-holding and other properties with the said Bhabani Prasad Saha. I do not find any mis-appreciation of the evidence or misconstruction of Ext. 3 or any Exhibits in the suit by the learned SCC Judge. The learned SCC Judge has rightly taken into consideration the other documents also, namely, the rent receipts, khatians, OCR etc. which are Exhibits in this case and correctly held that the plaintiff has prima facie title to the suit-holding. To determine the relationship of the landlord and the tenant between the parties, the learned SCC Judge has referred to some documents filed by the plaintiff as well as to some other documents of the defendant, namely, Ext. C Series, Ext. C is a money order receipt and Ext. C(I) is the postal Money Order Form sent to the plaintiff-opposite-party for an amount of Taka 300'00 in which the defendant- petitioner himself remitted the said amount of the rents for the suit-holding for several years starting from 1.1.68 with deductions of some amount allegedly spent by him on different heads in connection with the maintenance of the suit holding. From the Ext. D series also, it appears that the defendant-petitioner allegedly deposited rents by chalan showing the name of the plaintiff-opposite-party No. 1 as recipient of the rents for the years 1974-1980. In Exhibit D-14, it appears that the rents in lump for the period from January, 1974 to April, 1979, were sent by a chalan. Apart from the said Exhibits, the deposition of DW 1 is very relevant and important for consideration of the relationship of the plaintiff and the defendant. The DW 1 in cross-examination stated as follows:

"50 1/2 tenants of the suit buildings are paying rent to the plaintiff to his knowledge. The plaintiff preferred an appeal against the order of declaration of the suit buildings as enemy property and the order was passed in the year 1968. He is ready to continue as tenant for the suit holding under plaintiff if the rent be Tk. 75'00 per month. In 1975, the bharatias of the ground floor of the suit buildings began to pay rent to the plaintiff."

12. So, in consideration of all these materials and the evidence on record, it appears to be abundantly clear that the defendant-petitioner acknowledged by his own acts and utterances that the plaintiff-opposite-party is his landlord and this appears to have been done quite consciously and therefore it may be treated as attornment of the plaintiff-opposite-party to the previous admitted landlord of the suit holding i.e. Bhabani Prasad Saha. Accordingly, I find that the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties has been fully established in this case, and the learned SCC Judge has not committed any error of law in coming to the finding with regard to the question of title of the plaintiff-opposite-party and the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties.

13. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, next submits that the defendant-petitioner is not a defaulter, as he paid rents to the previous landlord Bhabani Prasad Saha upto 31st December, 1967 and thereafter he could not pay the rents for the holding, as the previous landlord died and his heirs were not here but living in India and their exact whereabouts were not known to the defendant-petitioner and further the suit-holding was declared as enemy property and he himself took lease of the same from the authorities concerned and paid rents to them. But on scrutiny of the records, nothing was found to show that he paid any rent to the Enemy Property authority at any time for the holding. It is further submitted on behalf of the defendant-petitioner that he also deposited rents on the suit holding to the House Rent Controller but there is nothing in the record to show such payment. The chalans i.e. Ext. D series show some payment of rents for the years 1974 to 1980 to the credit of the Subordinate Judge, Pabna Court in case No.1 (s)/1977 and in one of the chalans in Ext. D-14, it appears that the rents for several years were sent by one chalan in a lump.

14. The relevant provision under sub-section 5 of section 18 of the Rent Control Ordinance, 1963, as amended up to date, provides the circumstances under which the tenant can secure protection of his tenancy under sub-section 1 of section 18 of the Ordinance. Sub-section 5 of the said section reads as follows:

"No tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of this section in respect of any premises unless he pays the rent due by him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance within the time fixed in the contract with his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, or in the cases provided for in section 19 unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of such premises as provided in that section together with, in the case mentioned in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of that section, the cost of transmission referred to in that clause within time specified in that section.

"In the instant cause, it appears that there has been alleged payment of rents for the suit holding by the defendant-petitioner to the land lord or to the House Rent Controller since January, 1968. Even when the Enemy Property Authorities alleged to have recognized him as a lessee in the suit holding he failed to make any payment of rents to them. From Ext. C(1), it appears that he remitted a sum of Taka 300'00 to the plaintiff-opposite-party by a Postal Rent Money Order for the period from 1.1.68 to 31.10.77 deducting a quite substantial amount alleged to have been spent by him on different heads for the maintenance of the suit holding. The plaintiff-opposite-party of course refused to accept the same. Thereafter he deposited the rents for the years 1974 to 1980 by the alleged chalans Ext. D series sometimes in a lump. This shows that the defendant-petitioner was not at all regular in his payment of rents of the suit holding. It is well-settled that no protection can be given to a tenant under law, once the tenant is found to be a defaulter and payment of rents in lump for several months cannot save the tenant from the mischief of his eviction and that is why a tenant has to take all care to see that he does not become a defaulter. In this connection the following decisions reported in 33 DLR (AD) 55 and 29 DLR (SC) 13 and also 29 DLR 314 may be profitably cited. In the light of the above decisions when this case is considered, it cannot but be held that the defendant-petitioner grossly defaulted in making payments of monthly rents for the suit holding and as such he has been rightly found a defaulter by the learned SCC Judge. As such there is no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner on this point.

15. The next submission on behalf of the petitioner is that notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is not a valid one and the same was not duly served upon the defendant-petitioner. To prove the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the plaintiff has filed a copy of the notice and the postal receipt of the same as Exhibits 1-2. In this connection, the postal peon has also been examined by the plaintiff-opposite -party as PW 2 who has categorically stated that he served the notice upon the defendant-petitioner who received the same by putting his signature Ext. 2(a). It has been alleged on behalf of the defendant-petitioner that notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is vague and indefinite and that is not a valid notice, it is no doubt true that a valid notice is to be served under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the tenant before institution of a suit for eviction. In the instant case such notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was issued and the same appears to have been duly served by the plaintiff and received by the defendant. The plaintiff-opposite party in his deposition as PW 1, of course, admitted that Khatian number and plot number were not mentioned in the said notice, but the suit holding number was specifically given in the same.

<u>16. Now, let me see whether non-mentioning of the khatian number or plot number has in any way misled the defendant-petitioner and for that the notice should be held as bad and invalid. From the facts and circumstances of the case and also some documents, namely, Ext. C(1) and some other documents, it appears that even the defendant-petitioner himself did not mention any khatian number or plot number but the holding number only in those documents. So, it cannot be said that for non-mentioning of the said khatian or plot number, the defendant-petitioner has been misled or prejudiced in any way. Rather it appears that he has perfectly understood the suit premises by the holding number as given in the notice in question. It has been held in a number of decisions of our Court that a liberal consideration should be given to a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and minor inaccuracy or omission will not invalidate the service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this connection, the following decisions reported in 17 DLR 677, 19 DLR 905 and 19 DLR 324 may be cited. So, the learned SCC Judge has rightly held that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act in this case is a valid one and the same has been duly served upon the defendant-petitioner. Therefore, I find no substance in this contention also of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Now, the last submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the plaintiff- opposite party has not been able to prove bonafide requirement as alleged by him and the finding of the learned SCC Judge on this point is bad and illegal. It is true that so many facts and circumstances have not been stated or proved by the plaintiff-opposite- party to show his bonafide requirement, but PW 1 the plaintiff-opposite-party though briefly has categorically stated in his plaint and also in his deposition that he bonafide requires the case holding for his personal necessity and on this point there is no cross-examination by the defendant-petitioner also and in that view of the matter the learned SCC Judge has rightly held that the plaintiff-opposite- party has bonafide requirement of the case holding. I, therefore, find no substance in this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record both oral and documentary and my discussion above, I find no illegality in the impugned judgment and decree of the learned SCC Judge which have been passed in accordance with law and as such the same do not warrant any interference by this Court.</u>

17. In the result, the Rule is, therefore, discharged without any order as to costs.

18. The order of stay granted by this Court is vacated.

Let the records be sent down at once.

End.

lawyer:
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Md. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Shamsul Huq Chowdhury with Abdur Rahman, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Jahangir Nagar University Co-operative Housing Society ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Mujibur Rahman (Md) & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was earlier issued under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order dated 15-11-1989 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 372 of 1984. The learned Assistant Judge by the said order allowed the amendment of the plaint in respect of schedule attached to the plaint.

2. The petitioner's case in short is that the plaintiff-opposite-parties instituted Title Suit No. 288 of 1976 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Dhaka which was subsequently transferred to the Assistant judge, Savar, Dhaka and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 372 of 1984 for a declaration of title in the suit properties wherein the defendant petitioner was added subsequently. The further case of the petitioner is that the plaintiff instituted the suit alleging that 4.48 acres of land of plot No. 148 of Touzi No. 8173 of mouza Salia under Police Station Savar, District Dhaka originally belonged to the Dhaka Nowab Estate out of which 3.79 acres of land was given in settlement by the Manager of the said Estate under his memo. No. 591 DG 15-8-51 to one Abdur Rashid Bepari son of Abdul Jabbar Fakir of Miton and on receipt of Salami granted receipt on 6-3-58. Said Abdur Rashid Bepari possessed and enjoyed the said land and paid rent to the Nowab Estate upto 1361 BS and during the settlement operation the land was recorded in the name of said Abdur Rashid Bepari at PRR stage. But it was omitted in the copy prepared under section 46 of Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such objection raised in case No. 73 of 1964 and subsequently the land was recorded in the name of Abdur Rashid Bepari by opening khatian No. 38 who duly paid rent and got DCR. It is also the case, of the plaintiff that the name of said Abdur Rashid Bepari was recorded in the present RS khatian. Thereafter Abdur Rashid Bepari sold the suit properties to different persons including plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2. Plaintiff No. 2 transferred 76 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 3 out of his purchased 95 decimals and plaintiff No. 4 purchased 1.89 decimals of land from other transferee of Abdur Rashid Bepari. Thereafter when the plaintiffs applied for mutation of their names in the RS khatian they found the name of Saidur Rahman already mutated in the khatian. The plaintiffs then filed Misc. Case No. 34 of 1975 before the defendant No. 1 who found that the Circle Officer (Rev) was not the competent authority to record the name of predecessor of Abdur Rashid Bepari and mutation of Saidur Rahman's name was also found illegal and order passed for cancellation of the name of Abdur Rashid Bepari and treated the suit properties as government khas land and that compelled the plaintiffs to file the present suit for declaration that the orders of the defendant No. 1 dated 6-8-1987 are illegal, null and void and the plaintiffs are the lawful owners of the suit property.

3. Defendant-opposite party No. 5 and the present defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement. It is the case of the present petitioner that the land comprising an area of 12.18 acres in plot No. 148 khatian 31/35, 93/31 (ka) Mouza Chalia JL No. 626 in Upazila Savar belonged to Dhaka Nawab Estabe and the land was given in settlement by the then Manager of the said Estate on 15-8-51 in favour of Abdus Samad, Abdur Rahman, Abdur Rashid who paid rent to the Nowab Estate Dhaka and they were recognized tenants and while Abdur Rahman and Abdur Rashid were possessing the land they sold 5.72 acres of land in plot No. 148 to Shahidur Rahman who mutated his name in the SA khatian in Misc. Case No. 5(b) of 73-74 for 5.72 acres. The name of Shahidur Rahman was also recorded in the RS Khatian. Thereafter Saidur Rahman sold 4.09 acres to the present petitioner by different registered kabalas and handed over the transferred land to the petitioner who thereafter mutated their names in the relevant SA Record of Right in Misc. Case No. 674(B)P-1/75-76 and paid rent and they developed the entire land and allotted the same to the members of the society. It is also the case of the present petitioner that during RS operation the plaintiff opposite parties filed Misc. Case No. 34.75 before the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka praying for mutation of their name in place of Sahidur Rahman which was ultimately rejected. The plaintiff opposite parties have no right title, and possession in the suit property and their kabalas were created with ulterior motive.

4. It is also the case of the petitioner that after filing of their written statement the plaintiff opposite parties filed an application on 17-11-87 under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of the Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint. That petition for amendment was allowed by the court below by order dated 17-11-87. The present petitioner then filed additional written statement which was accepted by the Court. The plaintiff opposite parties then again on 4.9.89 filed another application under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for further amendment of the plaint for addition of a new prayer in respect of cause of action of the suit. In spite of objection from the side of the present petitioner the amendment was allowed by the Court's order dated 4.9.1989. Thereafter the suit appeared in the peremptory hearing list and evidence of PW I was recorded on 15-10-1989. Then the plaintiff opposite party on 15-11-1989 filed another application under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for amendment of the Schedule attached to the plaint. The present petitioner raised objection against this prayer for amendment for the plaint but the learned Assistant Judge by his order dated 15-11-1989 allowed the prayer for amendment of the plaint.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order dated 15-11-1989 the defendant petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

<u>6. Mr. Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, pressed this petition only on one point. He submits that the amendment in the plaint by order dated 15-11-1989 has changed the nature and character of the plaint. He argued that the amendment of the plaint may be made at any stage but by way of amendment the character of the plaint cannot be changed. He further submits that this order dated 15-11-1989 was passed after examination of the plaintiff and the plaintiff opposite party by way of amendment has introduced some thing new in the plaint which has totally changed the character of the plaint. Mr. Khandaker while pressing his point placed reliance on a decision reported in 13 DLR 871 (Alokeshi Bank Vs. Aftabuddin). The learned Advocate submits that this decision has enunciated a principle of law on the amendment of the plaint made under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the effect that amendment of the plaint can not be allowed if such amendment changed the character of the plaint.</u>

7. Mr. Shamsul Huq Choudhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that the Trial Court has not committed any illegality in allowing the amendment by order dated 15-11-1989 as amendment may be made at any stage of the proceedings even upto appellate stage and the present amendment has not in any way changed the character and nature of the suit as well as of the plaint. Relying on a decision reported in 29 DLR (SC) 311 (Golam Hafiz Mia Vs. Khadem Ali Meah) the learned Advocate submits that amendment of the pleading can be made at any stage of the suit provided such amendment does not prejudice the interest of the other party which it has got by lapse of time nor it would change the nature of suit. He argued that during the pendency of the suit the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land for which previously an amendment petition was filed praying for inserting a prayer for recovery of khas possession of the suit land and the present amendment was found necessary for specifying the boundary of the suit land. This amendment has not in any way changed the character and nature of the suit as well as of the plaint.

<u>8. The learned Advocate for the opposite party relying on another decision reported in 28 DLR 131 (Sultan Ahmed Vs. Purna Chandra Karmaker and others) submits that amendment of the plaint can be allowed when it does not alter the averment of the plaint. According to the learned Advocate, the amendment which is in question now has not altered the averment of the plaint which remained as it was and only for getting an effective decree in the suit the schedule of the plaint has been amended by incorporation of certain boundaries which has not altered the averment made in the plaint in any manner whatsoever. Relying on another decision reported in 12 DLR 626 (Daguram Mandal Vs. Omela Shundari Bewa) the learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that the amendment made in the plaint has not changed the character and nature of the suit and of the plaint but the amendment indicated a full and correct description of the properties in suit which is necessary for passing an effective decree. This amendment provided a right and correct description of the land in suit. The learned Advocate submits that after previous amendment the suit became a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the last amendment is nothing but incorporation of correct description of the suit land and it has not prejudiced the defendants in any way and it only removed the mis-description of the property for getting an effective decree.</u>

9. From the perusal of the papers filed it appears that the plaintiff filed the suit praying for a declaration that the plaintiffs are the rightful owners of the schedule property and that the orders passed by the defendant No. 1 on 6-8-76 is null and void and that the name of the plaintiff should be recorded in the present RS khatian in respect of the schedule of land showing 0.95 decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff No. 1, 0.18 in favour of plaintiff No. 2, 0.76 in favour of plaintiff No. 3 and 1.90 in favour of plaintiff No. 4 after releasing it from the khas khatian of the government. The plaintiff at the time of filing the plaint described the suit property as follows :

"All that pieces and parcel of 3.79 three acres and seventy nine decimals of land in plot No. 148 khatian No. 88 mouza No. 8673 and mouza No. 626 Salia under PS Savar Dist. Dhaka."

10. The plaintiffs then filed a petition for amendment of the plaint by adding words "out of 14.15 acres of land" in the schedule after the words 0.79 decimals of land. Admittedly the plaintiffs subsequently filed another amendment petition wherein they prayed for recovery of khas possession of the suit land. These amendments were not challenged before any higher Court by any of the defendants. The plaintiff opposite parties again filed another petition for amendment of the plaint and in that petition the plaintiffs prayed for inserting specific boundary in the schedule, as according to them there will be difficulty in getting a decree for khas possession if the land is not specifically described.

11. The learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties allowed the amendment of the plaint and also permitted the defendant to file additional written statement, if they so desire.

<u>12. Now the question is whether this amendment has changed the character of the plaint. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties has not controverted the principle of law set-forth in the decision reported in 13 DLR 871 that by way of amendment the character of the plaint cannot be changed but he submitted that amendment has not changed the character of the plaint and he further argued that as the suit ultimately turned into a suit for recovery of khas possession such an amendment became necessary for getting an effective decree.</u>

13. When the suit was filed plaintiffs had not prayed for recovery of possession. Their only prayer was for a decree that they arc the rightful owner of the suit land and they also prayed for a declaration that certain orders passed by the ADC (Rev.) are null and void.

<u>14. At the time of filing the suit their case was that they were in possession of the suit land. But subsequently they came with the plea that during the pendency of the suit they have been dispossessed from the suit land and at their instance the prayer portion was amended by adding recovery of khas possession. When such an amendment is made the plaintiffs at the same-time ought to have prayed for amendment of the schedule of the land so that it may clearly indicate for which land they want recovery of khas possession. Subsequently the plaintiff filed a petition giving specific boundary from where they wanted to eject the defendants or, to say, recover their possession. In the case reported in 12 DLR page 626 the fact was that the application was for pre-emption by a co-sharer of the property transferred by kabala and what happened was that by some unfortunate error the property was described with reference to the Charcha Survey and not with reference to the CS Khatian. The court found that the Trial Court rightly allowed the amendment and decided the real question in dispute between the parties. The principle of law enunciated in that decision is that amendment may be allowed for giving specific description of the land for which the suit has been filed. In the present suit before us amendment was made describing clearly the land for which the plaintiff prayed for recovery of khas possession. In the case reported in 28 DLR 130 it has been held that where an amendment of the plaint in a suit does not alter the averment of the plaint but is sought in view of the subsequent happenings after the filing of the suit, such prayer for amendment can be allowed. Here in the present suit after filing of the suit the plaintiff made a prayer for recovery of possession alleging that during the pendency of the suit they have been dispossessed from the suit land. But while amending the plaint they failed to properly describe the land for which they prayed for recovery of khas possession. The present amendment in question has not changed the character and nature of the suit as the plaint has been amended making the present suit a suit for recovery of possession and also for declaration.</u>

<u>15. The learned Advocate for the petitioner while pressing the petition relied on the decision reported in 13 DLR 871 wherein it has been held that an amendment which if allowed would change the character of the plaint though not the character of the suit cannot be allowed as that will prejudice the defendant in his defence. In the said suit the plaintiffs case as stated in the plaint originally was that he had paid to defendant and the latter had received certain amount of money. When it was proved that the defendant could not and did not receive the money from the plaintiff, the latter wanted to say that somebody else on behalf of the defendant received the money and wanted to amend the plaint to that effect; but it was held that could not be done as it would change the character of the plaint. The present suit as it stands now after all previous amendments is a suit for declaration with prayer for recovery of khas possession. But in the present amendment certain specific boundary has only been incorporated in keeping the other averments intact. This amendment, therefore, has not changed the character of the plaint. It is therefore found that the facts leading to the case reported in 13 DLR 871 and facts and circumstances of the present case before us are different. In that view of the matter I hold that the case reported in 13 DLR 871 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case before us. The latest amendment has practically removed the mis-description in the schedule which has not in any way prejudiced the defendant petitioner. Further also it appears that after allowing the amendment the Trial Court has already allowed the defendant to file additional written statement if they so desire. Thus after considering the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides I hold that the amendment made by order dated 15.11.1989 has not changed the character of the plaint and the Trial Court has not committed any illegality which may call for any interference by this court at this stage.</u>

16. There is, therefore, no merit in this application. The rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.

17. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman, J.: By this application under section 160(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 read with section 66 of the Income-Tax Act, 1922 the applicant preferred the following question of law for our decision:

"Whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal is justified in holding that the appeals are time barred counting the period of limitation of 60 days from 15.1.86, when the order of the Appellate Joint Commissioner was served on the Deputy Commissioner of taxes, inasmuch as under section 33(2) of the Income-Tax Act and section 158(4) of Ordinance XXXVI of 1984 the Commissioner of Taxes is entitled to file an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within 60 days from the communication of order to him (Commissioner of Taxes)."

At the outset before deciding the application we must observe that as the order of the Tribunal was passed on April 26, 1987 the application was to be filed U/S 160(1) of the Ordinance and not U/S 160(1) read with s.66 of the Income-Tax Act, 1922 as has been done by the applicant inasmuch as the Tribunal passed the order when the Ordinance already came into force. Tagging of s. 66 of the IT Act, 1922, therefore, in our opinion is redundant.

2. The aforesaid question arises out of the order of the Tribunal passed on April 26, 1987 in ITA No. 2131 of 1985-86 rejecting the appeal of the revenue on the ground of limitation. Therefore, we shall confine ourselves on the question of limitation.

3. The assessee M/s. MA Hossain and Co. filed return showing net loss at Tk. 2,41,802.00 for the assessment year 1984-85. The Assistant Commissioner of Taxes on 29.9.85 completed assessment computing taxable income at Tk. 5,84,249.00 after disallowing expenses claimed by the assessee. Against the order of assessment the assessee preferred Income Tax Appeal No. 31/Cont. II/85-86 before the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes, (North) Zone, Dhaka who by his order dated 1.12.85 allowed the appeal in part reducing the addition of Tk. 3,00,000.00 to Tk. 1,00,000.00.

4. Against the aforesaid order of the Joint Appellate Commissioner of Taxes the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Contractors, Circle-Il, Dhaka preferred the aforesaid appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Bangladesh, Dhaka Division, Bench. The Tribunal by its order dated April 26, 1987 rejected the appeal on the ground of limitation holding that as the order of the AJCT was communicated to the DCT on 15.1.86 the appeal was to be filed by 18.3.86 and the appeal having been filed on 5.4.86 was time-barred. The Tribunal further held that the last date for filing the appeal on 4.4.1986 as stated in the Memorandum of the OCT was not correct and in absence of any application for condonation of delay the delay in filing the appeal could not be condoned.

<u>5. On reference to the Order of the Tribunal we are of the opinion that the question as formulated referred to above arises out of the Order of the Tribunal. Under section 158 of the Income-Tax Ordinance, 1984 appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal from an order passed under s. 128 or under section 156 by the Appellate Joint Commissioner of, Taxes and from the order of Inspecting Joint Commissioner exercising the powers of a Deputy Commissioner of Taxes under section 10 or from the order of Inspecting Joint Commissioner under section 120 of the Ordinance. Under sub-section (3) of s. 158 the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes may appeal 10 the Appellate Tribunal against the order of Appellate Joint Commissioner if the Commissioner directs him to prefer appeal against the order of the AJCT. Sub-section (5) of s. 156 enjoins the Appellate Joint Commissioner to communicate the order passed by him to the appellant, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and the Commissioner. Sub-section (4) of section 158 enjoins that every appeal under sub-section (1) or sub-section (3) shall be filed within 60 days of the date on which the order sought 10 be appealed against is communicated to the assessee or to the Commissioner, as the case may be Proviso to sub-section (4) authorises Appellate Tribunal to admit a time-barred appeal if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not presenting the appeal within the period prescribed in sub-section (4) of section 158 of the Ordinance. Our reading of sub-section (3) of section 158 read with sub-section (5) of section 156 of the Ordinance is that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not entitled to prefer an appeal against the order of the Appellate Joint Commissioner unless he is directed to me the appeal by the Commissioner of Taxes to whom the Appellate Joint Commissioner is bound to communicate its order on appeal. In this case it appears that the Appellate Tribunal took the view that as the order of the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes was communicated to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes on 15.1.86 the appeal filed before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal on 5.4.86 was barred by Limitation. Mere communication of the order passed by the AJCT to the OCT is not enough. The order is also to be communicated to the Commissioner under sub-section (5) of s. 156 which is mandatory. Therefore, the expression "is communicated to the assessee or to the Commissioner," in our opinion, means communication by the AJCT of its order and not by the DCT. Thus, our reading of section 158(4) is that time runs for filing appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal not from the date of communication of the order of AJCT to the OCT as has been held by the Tribunal but from date of communication of the order of AJC to the Commissioner.</u>

6. From the statement made in paragraph 4 of this reference application it appears that the order of the Tribunal was communicated to the Commissioner on 4.2.86. Mr. Maksudur Rahman relying upon S. 12 of the Limitation Act contends that the day on which the order was communicated shall be excluded in reckoning the period of limitation. He submits that as the order of the Appellate Joint Commissioner was communicated on 4.2.86 the appeal filed on 5.4.86 was within time in view of the provision of s.12 of the Limitation Act and the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the appeal was barred by limitation. Mr. Maksudur Rahman further contends that as the appeal was filed within time the question of ruing an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act does not arise and the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there being no application for condonation of delay the delay could not be condoned. We find force in this contention of the Revenue. As we arc of the opinion that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was not justified in rejecting the appeal on the ground of limitation we answer the question in the negative.

The parties are to bear their own costs.

End.
