full_judgment:
This Rule obtained by the petitioner under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree passed by learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 45 of 1980 reversing those of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Patuakhali passed in Title Suit No. 137 of 1970.

2. The plaintiff opposite-party No. 1 instituted the aforesaid suit in the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Patuakhali for specific performance of contract against the defendant No 1 the petitioner and for permanent injunction against the defendant-opposite-party Nos. 1-4 on the allegations, inter alia, that the petitioner was owner of the laud in suit described In schedule 'ka' to the plaint and he executed a bainapatra in favour of plaintiff-opposite-party No. 1 on 25th Bhadra, 1370 BS corresponding to 11-9-063 for sale of the land together with the huts standing here on fully described in schedule 'ka'. According to the term of the said bainapatra, a kabala in favour of the opposite-party No 1 was to be executed and registered within the month of Magh, 1374 BS; that the petitioner after receiving Tk. 800 as earnest money delivered possession of the property in suit to the opposite-party No. 1; that subsequently 0.11 acres of land out of 0.14 acres appertaining to the suit plot No. 683 was acquired by the WAPDA in LA Case No. (W) 39/1965 66 and compensation for the said land at Tk 6,957, for cost of removal of 4 huts at Tk 840 and for loss of business at Tk. 400 was assessed. The opposite-party No. 1 withdrew a sum of Tk. 400 out of the said compensation money. Thereafter, the petitioner in collusion with staff of the local Land Acquisition Department was trying to withdraw compensation money and refused the demand for execution and registration of the kabala for the property under the bainapatra.

3. The defendant No. 1 petitioner through his constituted Attorney Subal contested the suit by filing written statement. He denied the execution of the bainapatra and delivery of possession of the disputed property to the opposite-party No. 1. His case was that the bainapatra was a forged and fraudulent document and he did never enter into any contract with the opposite party No. 1 for sale of the suit property. He also denied receipt of the alleged earnest money amounting to Tk. 800. The petitioner's further case was that he previously had entered into a contract with one Kala Chand Dutta in 1962 for sale of the property in suit at Tk. 8,000: The opposite-party No. 1 was a trespasser into the suit but and he had no right to claim and withdraw the compensation money from the Land Acquisition Department and that the suit was liable to be dismissed.

On the pleadings of the parties the learned Sub-ordinate Judge framed the following issues"

"1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form and has it been properly valued and stamped?

2. Is the alleged Bainapatra dated 11-9- 63 executed by the defendant 1 legal, valid with consideration and is the plaintiff entitled to specific performance of contract entered therein particularly after acquisition of the subject matter of contract?

3. Can the defendant Nos. 2-4 be remained from paying to defendant No. 1 the alleged compensation money as prayed for?"

4. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge dismissed the suit on contest holding that the bainapatra dated 11-9-1963 Exhibit 1 was false, forged and a created document. The appeal taken by the opposite party No. 1 against the judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge to the learned District Judge on transfer was allowed by the learned Additional District Judge who set-aside the Judgment of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge and allowed the appeal decreeing the suit ex parte.

<u>5. Mr. PC Guha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner assailed the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge on several ground, Firstly, he argued that the learned. Addl District Judge fell into a serious error in expunging the written statement filed by the constituted attorney of the petitioner and expunging the evidence of petitioner from record. He submitted that learned Additional District Judge was not right in taking the view that the power-of-attorney not being authenticated by a notary public as required under section 85 of the Evidence Act could not be accepted as valid document and on the strength of the said power-of-attorney, written statement and Vokalatnama filled by the attorney could not be accepted. He referred to me section 33 of the Registration Act in aid of his submission that the power-of-attorney being preserved by the petitioner before the sub-registrar and duly registered by was a valid document and we learned Addl. District Judge committed an error of law in expunging the written statement and evidence of the petitioner. Section 33 of the Registration Act provides that a power-of-attorney which is executed by a person who resides in Bangladesh at the relevant time and registered by a Sub-registrar shall be only recognized for the purpose of presentation and registration of a document before the Sub-registrar. Sub-section 4 of section 333 provides that such power-of-attorney will be proved by its production alone without further proof The learned Advocate contends that, when a power-of-attorney can be recognised under section 33 of the Act for purpose of registration of a document by the Sub-Registrar the same can also be recognized by the court for the purpose of presentation of a written statement by the Attorney. The learned advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention also cited the case of Nurunnesa & others vs Babur Alim Bepari reported in 33 DLR 124 but that case is not directly on the point. In that case the question fell for consideration before their Lordships was whether a power-of-attorney authenticated before a Magistrate at Alipore in India was admissible in Bangladesh as a valid power-of-attorney. But considering the provisions of different enactments the learned Judges, of the Appellate Division answered the question in the affirmative. It was further held by their Lordships that a power-of-attorney executed in terms of Registration Act or under other provisions of law confers a valid power on the attorney to act as an agent for the principal.</u>

6. On the other hand, the learned Advocate appearing opposite-party No. 1 very strenuously argued that the expungement of the written statement and evidence of the petitioner was based on the view taken by the learned Additional District Judge that the power-of-attorney was violative of the provisions of section 85 of the Evidence Act. It was submitted that for becoming a valid document it must be authenticated by the notary public. He went on that the power-of-attorney was not authenticated by the authorities described in section 85 of the Evidence Act and, as such, the power-of-attorney was not a valid document. He, therefore, contended that the attorney of the defendant No. 1 acting on the strength of the said power-of-attorney in filing written statement in the court acted in a manner not authorized by law and, as such, the learned Additional District Judge rightly expunged the written statement and evidences from the record.

<u>7. Now let us examine the contentions of the learned Advocates. Section 33 is not directly on the point as under this section a power-of-attorney is recognized for the purpose of presentation of a document before Sub-Registrar for registration. In the present case the power-of-attorney in question was executed in Bangladesh and at the relevant time the principal was a resident of Bangladesh and it was also registered in Bangladesh. There is no denial by opposite-party No. 1 of this fact. That being the position the power-of-attorney is a duly executed and. authenticated document being registered by Sub-Registered. Now the question is whether the said power-of-attorney can be said to be non-existent for the purpose of presentation of written statement as the same was not authenticated by a notary public as provided in section 85 of the Evidence Act. Let us conveniently quote section 85:</u>

<u>'85. The Court shall presume that every document purporting to be a power-of-attorney, and to have been executed before, and authenticated by, a rotary public, or any court, Judge, Magistrate, Bangladesh Counsel or Vice-Counsel, or representative of the Government, was so executed and authenticated."</u>

<u>From a close reading of section 85 of the Evidence Act it appears that the said section only raises a presumption as to execution and authentication of a power-of-attorney executed and authenticated by the executants and the authority described in the section itself. Nowhere from the language of section 85 of the Evidence Act it could be read that a power-of-attorney executed by a person resident in Bangladesh like the present defendant No.1 and duly registered by a Sub-Registrar is not a legally valid document. In this case, it was not the case of the plaintiff that the defendant No. 1 did not execute the power-of-attorney and the same was not duly registered. Although registration of a power-of-attorney is not compulsory the power-of-attorney having been duly registered, under the provision of Registration Act and there being no challenge as to its genuineness of its execution by the petitioner I do not find any force in the contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite-party that the power-of-attorney cannot be accepted as a valid document. In my opinion although the power-of-attorney was not authenticated by a notary public as required under section 85 of the Evidence Act the same being executed by the petitioner and duly registered under the provisions of Registration Act is a valid document. In that view of the matter the written statement filed by the attorney of the defendant the petitioner on the strength of the said power-of-attorney was duly presented. Section 85 only raised a presumption regarding execution and authentication of power-of-attorney which is executed and authenticated outside the territory of Bangladesh but it does not say that a duly executed and registered power-of-attorney in Bangladesh unacceptable and invalid document for the reason of non-authentication. The learned advocate for the opposite-party also could not show from the record that the learned Additional District Judge expunged the written statement on any other ground or under Order II, rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>8. Order II, rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that a court can strike out the defence for non-compliance by the defendant with an order of the court on an application by a party to the proceeding. In that view of the matter, I hold that the Additional District Judge was wrong in expunging the written statement and evidences from the record and decreeing the suit ex-parte It also appears from the judgment of the trial court that although the trial court expunged the written statement yet allowed the defendant No. 1 to adopt the same on his prayer and dismissed the suit on contest. But the learned Additional District Judge held that written statement filed by Subodh Chandra Kar could not be adopted by defendant No. i as the same was filed on the strength of power-of-attorney which was not in existence in the eye of law. The learned Advocate for opposite-party also argued that the power-of-attorney not having been cancelled or rescinded the defendant No. 1 cannot be allowed to adopt the written statement filed by his constituted attorney Subodh Chandra Kar as the act of the principal may give rise to inconsistent and contradictory acts between the agent and principal. The defendant No. 1 in this case having adopted and adopted the written statement filed by his attorney nothing inconsistent and contradictory to the acts of the agent rather he ratified the acts of the agent. For adopting a written statement already filed by the agent on the basis of a power-of-attorney in a suit instituted against the principal, the principal need not cancel or rescind and revoke the power-of-attorney executed in favour of the agent in that adoption of the written statement by the principal is rather ratification of the acts of the agent. Therefore, in this case the defendant No. 1 (principal) having ratified the act of his agent by adopting the written statement this contention of the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1 has got also no substance.</u>

9. So far as the finding on execution of the bainapatra, Exhibit 1 is concerned both learned advocates very strenuously at length argued in support of their respective contentions. The learned advocate for the petitioner seriously urged before me that the finding of the learned Additional District Judge to the effect that the bainapatra is not false, forged or created document is not at all based on consideration of material evidence on record end did not advert to the reasoning of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge while reversing the finding regarding bainapatra. According to him, therefore, the judgment of the lower appellate court was not a proper judgment of reversal and the finding is not binding on the High Court Division.

<u>10. The learned advocate for opposite-party No. 1 relying on the case of Pathona vs Mst. Wasai reported in (1965) 17 DLR (SC) 47 submitted that erroneous finding of fact is binding in the High Court Division. In the said case it was held :</u>

<u>"That an erroneous finding of fact is a different thing from an error or defect in the procedure and that there is no Jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground of such erroneous finding, however gross or inexcusable the error may seem to be "</u>

<u>But the facts of the case were different from the facts of the present case and in that case their Lordships gave decision on the extent of the power of High Court to reassess evidence for its own finding on a question of fact on interpretation of section 100(C) of the Code of Civil Procedure, But in the instant case before me it is not the question of re-assessment of the evidence by the High Court Division for having a different finding on fact of its own from that of the Lower Appellate Court rather the point is how far the Lower Appellate Court considered the evidences upon which the trial court based its decision and to see whether non-consideration of these evidences and failure on the part of the Lower Appellate Court to advert to the reasoning of trial court resulted in an error in the decision for arriving at such finding by the Lower Appellate Court. In the facts and circumstances of the present case, High Court Division is quite competent to examine this aspect under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure in view of the amendment. So, the said case does not help the learned Advocate which was decided altogether on a different footing. The learned Advocate also placed reliance on the case reported in (1978) 30 DLR 81 (SC), This is not also applicable in the present case as the facts of that case are quite different. In that case the decision was also given on the extent of jurisdiction of High Court to interfere with a finding of facts of the lower appellate court under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. At page 86 of the report it was held in that in the absence of any error of law or error of procedure affecting the merits of the case the High Court Division is bound by any finding of a fact; however erroneous it may appear to the High Court Division. In respect however gross or inexcusable the error of the appreciation of the evidence on which the said finding is based." But the power of High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure after amendment is not circumscribed by such limitation. The High Court Division certainly in a proper and a fit case can set-aside the finding of fact arrived at by the court of appeal below more so when the said finding is contrary to the finding of the trial court and arrived at without adverting to reasoning that weighed with the trial court.</u>

11. As the defendant challenged the execution of bainapatra Exhibit 1 dated 11-9-1963 it was sent to the Hand Writing Expert along with the kabala dated 9-6-56 Exhibit 3 executed by the petitioner, a petition dated 28-10-69 Exhibit 4 purported to be signed by the petitioner filed in MR Case No. 50 of 1963 was also sent and specimen signature of the petitioner dated 2-4-73. The hand writing expert submitted his report with the opinion that signature on bainapatra Exhibit 1 was the signature of the petitioner. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge did not place any reliance upon the opinion of the Hand Writing Expert and after comparing the signature of the petitioner appearing on Exhibit 1, Exhibit 3, Exhibit 4, etc, empowered under section 73 of the Evidence Act came to his own finding that signature on bainapatra Exhibit 1 and on the petition Exhibit 4. do not tally with the specimen signature of the petitioner, the signature of the petitioner on the kabala dated 5-9-56 and his signature on deposition, The trial court observed;

"On careful examination of specimen signature of Manindra Nath Kar 1 find that these 'C' series i.e. specimen signature tally with the signature on kabala, Exhibit 2 and signature on deposition in this suit and seems to be true that these are products of same hand and the signature on Bainapatra and petition dated 28-6-63 are products of same hand."

12. The trial court while coming to the aforesaid finding also took into consideration the reference regarding the bainapatra in the said petition Exhibit 4 which was executed on 9-11-1963, a date subsequent to the date of the petition Exhibit 4 which was written on 28-6-1963. The petition Exhibit 4 contains a statement regarding talk of sale of the property in dispute. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge found that the bainapatra being executed on 11-9-1963 after a few months of the said petition dated 28-6-63 Exhibit4 reference of that bainapatra in the said petition is important material for holding that the bainapatra was created. The trial court observed it is false and forged in view of reference made in petition dated 28-6-63. But the reasoning of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge did not receive due consideration of the learned Additional District Judge. It appears from the judgment that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge also himself perused the bainapatra and noticed overwriting of 'O' in the figure in the Bengali expression “ইতিমন ১৩৭০/২৫ মে ভাদ্র” and in figure 2 of Bhadra 25th and found that 25th Bhadra should be written in Bengalias “২৫ শে” not “২৫শে” as contained in the bainapatra. He also found that number of attesting witnesses was changed from '3' to '5' and names of the attesting witness to the bainapatra were written in different ink and in an unusual place on the bainapatra. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge; also noticed the name of the village of witness Ratan Majumder given in the bainapatra was different from the name given in the Plaint and he also found that the defendant No. 1 at the time of execution of the alleged bainapatra used to live in village Angaria but his address was shown at village Gaida although the defendant No. 1 left Gaida after disposing of all his land. He also noticed the statement made in para No. 2 of the petition to the effect that the defendant No. 1 had delivered possession of the disputed property to the plaintiff before the date of the petition. Taking into consideration of all these facts the learned Sub-ordinate Judge found the bainapatra to be false forged and created one. The learned Additional District Judge on perusal of the bainapatra observed that the date “২৫ ই ভাদ্র” is an good as “২৫ ই ভাদ্র” that change of figures from 3 to 5 relating to the member of attesting witnesses was a bona6de mistake although that was not the case of the defendant opposite party No. 1.

13. I was also taken through records. A cursory view into the disputed signature of the petitioner appearing on the said bainapatra as well as the place of writing of the names of 2 attesting witnesses appearing on the body of the said bainapatra, the petition dated 28-6-63 and the date appearing in the contents of the said bainapatra which, inter alia, records, “তদানুসারে অদ্যাপি সে কথিত সম্প্রত্তি ভোগদখল করিতেছে” the expression "অদ্যাপি " which has got reference to 28-6-63 i.e. to say the date of the petition makes it clear enough to belie the story of the agreement for sale of the property to the plaintiff. This is an absurd proposition that a reference could be made to a transaction which never saw the light of the day as because the bainapatra was executed on 11-9-63 while the said petition is dated 28-6-53. In view of the above discussion, it appears that the learned Advocate District Judge reversed the decision of the Ordinate Judge without at all adverting to the reasoning of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge and without considering the evidence of the defendant No 1 which were expunged erroneously by him from the record.

<u>14. The learned advocate for the Petitioner also argued that as the suit was admittedly filed on 1-4-70 i. e more than 3 years after the date as the stipulated in the said bainapatra to execute the kabala within Magh 1374 B.S it was barred tinder Article 113 of the Limitation Act. A suit for specific performance of contract has to be tied before expiry of 3 years of the stipulated date for performance of the contract or before expiry of 3 years of the dale of notice of refusal as provided in article 113 of the Limitation Act. Article 113 of the Limitation Act may conveniently be quoted as under:</u>

<u>113. For specific performance Three years of contract</u>

<u>The date fixed for the performance, or if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.</u>

<u>In this case the plaintiff also did not disclose the date when he bad tendered the balance money and demanded execution of which petitioner refused to execute and register. In that view of the matter limitation will run from the date fixed for the performance. The present suit being instituted more than three years after the date as stipulated in the bainapatra is barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act as it falls within the first clause of the third column of this Article.</u>

<u>15. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also argued that relief sought for in a suit for specific performance of contract is a discretionary relief and the plaintiff must come before the court to have a declaration for such relief with a clean hand. He contends that the reference of bainapatra dated 9-11-63 containing in the petition dated 28-6-63, addresses of the defendant No. 1 given in the bainapatra coupled with the fact that the plaintiff did not disclose in the plaint the date when he tendered balance money and demanded execution of kabala sufficiently betray that the plaintiff was not clean in his conduct and on this count also he is not entitled to a decree for specific performance of contract. The learned Additional District Judge did not consider this aspect of the case which was taken into consideration by the trial court. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-party vehemently raised objection to the ground on limitation contending that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge himself found that the suit was not barred by limit at on and no cross appeal being preferred by the defendant No. 1 before the Lower Appellate Court against such finding this question of limitation cannot he looked into at this stage in the High Court Division, The contention of the learned advocate is not tenable. Firstly the defendant can urge a point in the appeal preferred by the plaintiff without preferring cross objection under Order XLI, rule 22 which was decided against. Secondly the question of limitation is a question of law and this can be gone into even at the last resort. In that view of the matter, I hold that the relief being discretionary one the opposite party No. 1 is not entitled to a decree for specific performance of contract and the suit having been instituted more than three years after the date fixed in the Bainapatra for execution on of kabala is also barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above the judgment and order of the learned Additional District Judge is hereby set-aside and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, is restored and the suit is dismissed.</u>

In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Abdus Salam Khan, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
GH Afrin with Syed AB Mahmudul Hoque, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Samarendra Nath Roy Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
Vs
Abdul Jabbar and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani, J.: This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the trial Court's order rejecting an application for amendment of the plaint on a major ground which is that the said application consisting of wide typed pages is itself a new plaint, and on two minor grounds, one is that the suit is at the stage of final hearing and the other is that previously another such application was allowed and so again an application obstructs normal rule of disposal.

2. The petitioner has instituted a suit for declaration of his title to the suit properties described in twelve schedules and for permanent injunction. There are six defendants. Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 are contesting the suit by filing a joint written statement setting up their own title to the suit properties. It appears that by this application the plaintiff sought to delete his entire pleadings and to substitute them by new pleadings as to acquisition of his title to the suit properties. It is an extreme case of its kind and needs careful treatment.

3. Order 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure has the heading "Pleadings Generally". Its rule 1 defines "pleading" which means plaint or written statement. Rule 2 directs that pleading shall contain material facts, but not the evidence. Rule 17 contains the provisions for amendment of pleadings as hereunder—

"The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties."

4. This rule 17 has got two distinct parts. The first part may be called discretionary provision, gives discretion to the court (by using the word "may") to allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as the court considers just.

5. The second part, may be called mandatory provision, directs the court (by using the word "shall") to allow all such amendments which may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties.

6. Thus rule 17 contemplates not only one sort of amendments of the pleadings which are necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions of controversy between the parties, but also other sorts of alterations or amendments which the parties may desire.

7. Mark the use of the words "alter or amend" in the first part and only the word "amendment" in similar position in the second part of rule 17. Also mark the expression "at any stage" in the rule.

<u>8. In case the court finds that the proposed amendment is necessary for determining the real questions in controversy between the parties, such amendment must be granted and there is no discretion for the court in this regard. In 54 CWN 445, the plaintiff brought suit for a declaration of his title in certain plots of land. On one reading of the plaint it would appear that he claimed an undivided six annas in those plots. But in the body of the plaint he claimed that he was in exclusive possession of his share by cultivation. The plaintiff sought to amend the plaint so as to claim specific portions of the plots. The amendment was allowed so that the court could decide the real issue in the case, that is, whether or not the plaintiff was entitled to portions of the plots which he had alleged to have exclusive possession by cultivation. In AIR 1964 Cal 439, an eviction suit was filed against the tenant on the allegation that the plaintiff had purchased the suit premises from its previous owner Sarjubala. In the original written statement it was contended by the defendant that there was an agreement for sale between Sarjubala and himself and that plaintiff had purchased with notice of this agreement. By an application for amendment of the written statement the defendant sought to introduce a case that Sarjubala who claimed her title under a Will was only a residuary legatee and as the administration of that will was not then completed plaintiff could not acquire title to the property. The amendment was allowed as it was necessary for determining the real question between the parties, that is, the legal effect of the plaintiffs purchase from Sarjubala.</u>

9. In case of alteration or amendment or both of any other sorts in the pleadings, absolute discretion rests upon the court. This discretion, however, must not be arbitrary or vague or fanciful so as to cause injustice, but must be sound, legal and regular. Rule 17 itself directs that this discretion is to be exercised "in such manner and on such terms as may be just". In this respect there is a sea of decisions enough to puzzle a new swimmer. Rational views among them, therefore, are summarised as hereunder:

1. Ordinarily on payment of costs to the other side, a party is allowed to alter or amend his pleadings.

2. Truth or falsity of the case put in the amendment or the party will not be able to establish the facts necessary to prove the amendment is no ground for refusing amendment If it is false or not proved petitioner will fail in suit

3. Court should be liberal in allowing a party to alter or amend his pleadings except in the following cases.

(a) where the application is malafide or fraudulent or intends to overreach. In 13 DLR 871, plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of contract stated in his plaint that the defendant received the earnest money from him, but when it was found that the defendant could not receive the money from him as she was away from that place, the plaintiff sought to amend the plaint that somebody else received the money on behalf of the defendant. In 1994 BLT (AD) 4, defendants in a suit for their eviction from the suit premises stated in the Written statement that the defendant No. 1 as tenant started his business in the suit premises and paid rent to the original owner, but at a very late stage sought to amend their pleadings that the defendant No. 1 took settlement of the suit premises on permanent basis on payment of salami. In both these cases, the prayer for amendment of the pleadings was refused.

(b) Where it is made at a stage when it will require trial of action afresh.

(c) Where it seeks to remove an admission in the pleading.

(d) Where it will change the suit into a different kind of suit

(i) due to complete change in the subject matter of the action on a distinct cause of action. The expression "cause of action" in general term means "every fact which it is material to be proved to entitle a plaintiff to succeed." But in the present context this expression means "a new claim made on a new basis constituted by new facts." In AIR 1922 PC 249, the defendant in 1903 entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of two sites of oil wells. The first were six out of the twelve sites that she would obtain for 1902 and the second were three out of the twelve sites that she would obtain for 1903 from the Government. So far as the sites of 1902 were concerned the contract was duly satisfied. But with regard to the 1903 sites difficulties arose. Ultimately, according to the plaintiff`s pleadings, the defendant in 1912 verbally promised to give three sites out of those she obtained in 1912, but afterwards she did not give them. Then the plaintiff in 1913 sued for specific performance of the said verbal agreement. It is important to know here that none of these sites concerning the alleged verbal agreement related to any of the sites that were originally allotted in 1903. The plaintiff failed to establish the verbal agreement and then he sought to amend the plaint by claiming damages for breach of the contract of 1903. It was held that the amendment could not be granted as it would perm it a new case to be made out on a distinct cause of action. But conversion of a suit for specific performance of contract into one for damages for breach of contract or amendment in the alternative for refund of earnest money or in a suit for exclusive title, amendment for alternative relief of partition or like conversion or amendment on the basis of the same cause of action should be allowed.

(ii) due to change of the parties. In AIR 1964 (Cal) 57, a suit was filed against a Club which was neither an incorporated body nor a registered society and as such suit was not maintainable. Plaintiff then sought to amend the plaint by bringing some of the members of that Club in the representative capacity. The application for amendment was rejected as its effect would have been to convert the suit into a different suit against different parties.

(e) where it takes away from the other party a legal right accrued to him by lapse of time but court's power of allowing amendment is not circumscribed by the law of limitation in the following cases even on expiry of the period of limitation-

(i) to correct the name of a party in case of genuine mistake or to alter the capacity in which a party sues in case he might have sued at the time of filing the suit or of making counter-claim.

(ii) to add or substitute a new cause of action if it arises out of the same facts or substantially the same facts in respect of which relief has already been claimed,

(iii) to add extra relief which does not constitute addition of a new cause of action, but amounts to a different or additional approach to the same facts in the pleading.

(4) Where it does not come under the mischief of 3(d) above, then amendment is allowed.

(i) to modify or recast the original cause of action or to add new or alternative cause of action.

(ii) to extend or to alter the relief or to add relief including inconsistent relief flowing from same set of facts as in the original suit,

(iii) to add events occurring after institution of the suit.

(5) Generally all kinds of honest mistake or blunder are allowed to rectify by amendment if it can be done without causing prejudice to the other side. Prejudice here means detriment to one's claim.

10. In the instant case the effect of the proposed amendment will not change the fundamental character of the suit which will still remain a suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction based on the same cause of action though by the proposed amendment plaintiff seeks to introduce a new case of acquisition of his title to the suit property by altering his earlier pleadings. A plaintiff can set up as many roots of title as possible and they may be even conflicting and inconsistent.

<u>11. Thus the major ground as aforesaid of the trial Court for refusing the amendment is not tenable in law. So also the other two minor grounds as the amendment was proposed before the trial and its obstruction to normal rule of disposal can be compensated by costs to the other side.</u>

<u>This Rule is, therefore, made absolute without costs. The impugned order dated 16.8.92 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Narshingdi, in Title Suit No. 29 of 1990 is set aside. Plaintiffs application dated 2.8.92 seeking amendment of the plaint is allowed on condition that the plaintiff should pay a cost of Taka 2,000.00 to the contesting defendants within two months from the date of receipt of this order by the trial Court, in default the application shall stand rejected.</u>

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 123 of 1980.
lawyer:
Mr. A. K. Badrul Huq with Mr. P.C. Guha and Mr. Manahendra Batabal, Advocate ----- For the Appellants. 
Mr. Hemayetuddin Ahmed with Mr. Menhajuddin Ahmed Khan, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Chan Juri Talukder & anr ------Appellants
vs.
Chingneshay Magni & ors ------Respondents
full_judgment:
Nurul Huque Bhuiyan, J: - This appeal by defendants Nos. 1-2 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 29.4.80 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 90 of 1972 and arises out of a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of joint possession of schedule Ka property on partition of items 2-S thereof and for declaration of title and recovery of possession of schedules Kha and Ga property of the plaint.

2. The respondent No.1 as plaintiff instituted the suit on the allegations inter alia that her husband Thanchaneo Talukder was the owner of the suit properties and he died on 30.3.71 at Dhaka Medical College Hospital. Thanchanco was a Budhist by religion and his heir would be governed by Burmese Budhist Law of Inheritance, Mebuse Mogni, the first wife of Thanchaneo Talukder, died 6n years before the marriage of the plaintiff. According to the Burmese Budist Law of Inheritance the plaintiff is the only legal heir of Thanchaneo. Defendants Nos. 1, 2 and 4 are full brothers, defendant No. 3 is the sister and defendant Nos. 5-7 are brother's sons of the deceased Thanchanco. After the death of Thanchanco the defendants began to make conspiracy against the plaintiff to grab her property and forced her to live in the house of her father. She filed a petition before the Martial Law Administrator who sent the petition to Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed, Magistrate 1st Class, Barguna for enquiry. At the time of enquiry by the Magistrate the defendants claimed that Thanchaneo made a will in their favour. The Magistrate submitted a report on 10.6.71 on the finding that the said claim of the defendants is false and that the plaintiff is the only heir of Thanchaneo. In the night of 17.7.81 Bisudhananda Mahathero, the President of Budhya Kristi Prochar Sangha, called the plaintiffs father from his house by coercion and threat and gave him proposal for partition of the properties of the plaintiff between the plaintiff and the defendants and compelled the plaintiffs father to sign on a blank paper and after obtaining the signature from the plaintiffs father Bisudhananda Mahathcro kept the paper with the officer in charge of Amtali Police Station. The plaintiff never appointed Bisudhananda Mahathero or anybody else to effect partition of her husband's property. She did not empower Bisudhananda Mahathero or her father to do so. The plaintiff has been possessing the properties left by her husband. The defendants are demanding the land of her husband. They have no title or possession over the suit land. They have been threatening the plaintiff with dispossession since August, 1972 and hence the suit.

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending inter alia that the suit is not maintainable. It is bad for defect of parties, barred by limitation under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the suit is not properly valued and stamped. The land described in the schedule of the plaint is vague and unspecified as there is no mention of C.S. and R.S. Plots. The Budhist Tribes of Patuakhali District are not .guided by Burmese Budhist Law of Inheritance. They are governed by Customary Law and Succession Act and hence the award of Bisudhananda Mahathero shall apply. The defendants are also the legal heirs of Thanchaneo along with the plaintiff. In the report Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed stated that Thanchaneo Talukder made a will before his death. Bisudhananda Mahathero at the instance of the Martial Law Authority made a family arrangement according to the Burmese Budhist Law. The plaintiff is literate and after knowing fully weIl about the contents of the award she signed on it 8I1d she is bound by it. Bisudhananda Mahathero made the award only to restore peace between the plaintiff and the defendants. The award was submitted before the Martial Law Authority. So the question of threat or coercion in effecting the award does not arise. The defendants have been possessing the land and Bisudhananda Mahathero divided the movables between the parties with consent of the parties and that was done according to the will made by Thanchaneo. The defendant No.1 also filed an additional written statement contending that according to Burmese Budhist Law of Inheritance the plaintiff, anika married widow, is entitled to only 4 annas of the property left by Thanchanco and the remaining 12 annas of the property left by Thanchaneo shaIl devolve upon his blood relations. Mebuse Mogni, the first wife of Thanchanco, died in the year 1968 and she was of superior category and the plaintiff was married in the year 1968 and she was of inferior category and according to law she will get 4 annas and the remaining 12 annas shall go to the blood relation of Than chaneo. The movables are noted in schedule Kha and Ga. Thanchaneo had 30 buffaloes and 4 cows. In S.A. Khatian No. 188 the area of land is 26.12 decimals which was recorded in the name of Thanchaneo but by Mutation Case No. 56 of 1972-734 annas was recorded in the name of the plaintiff and 12 annas was recorded in the names of other blood relations of Thanchaneo. The land of S.A. Khatian No. 517 belonged to Maibu Mogni and after her death the entire land was recorded in the name of her daughter Mabuse Mogni (Vide Mutation Case No. 14/72-73). 4 annas share of Khatian 518 belonged to Maibu Mogni, mother of Thanchanco and defendants 1-4. It is recorded in the names of defendants Nos. 1-4 (Vide rv1utation Case No. 13/72-73). 8 annas of S.A. Khatian Nos. 76 and 77 belonged to Maibu Mogni and it was recorded in the names of defendant Nos. 1-4. Defendant No. 19, Monghase son of defendant No. l, purchased 3 acres of land from Thanchanco from S.A. Khatian 414 (Vide kabala dated 3.2.58 Ext. A(2). Maofu Mog, son of defendant No.4, purchased 3 acres of land from Thanchaneo Talukder by kabala Ext. A dated 18.l2.52 and he then sold the same to defendant No. 19 Monghase by kabala Ext. A(1) dated 29.7.57 and thereafter defendant No.19 mutated his name in Mutation Case No. 4214 of 1957 under section 54 of the State Acquisition Act. Defendant No.19 also got 1.33 decimals of land from S.A. Khatian No. 369 and mutated his name in Mutation Case No. 8537 of 1963-64. He also got 5.33 decimals by kabalas from Thanchaneo from S.A. Khatian No. 414. Thanchaneo also gifted his remaining land to his adopted daughter Eyema Mogni. The defendants have been possessing the land for more than 12 years and as such the suit is barred by limitation. The gold is mortgaged in Barisal Officers' Co-operative Bank and Mercantile Bank and this defendant paid the principal amount with interest amounting to Tk. 2,000/-. Besides this defendant has cleared up dues of Thanchanco. Before the learned Subordinate Judge following issues were framed:-

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

3. Is the suit time-barred both general and special?

4. Is the suit bad u/s. 42 of S.R. Act?

5. Is the plaint sufficiently stamped and valued?

6. Is the suit property correctly identified?

7. Has the plaintiff right, title, interest and possession over the suit land?

8. To what relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled?

4. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence adduced by the parties, the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in part declaring the plaintiffs title to Ka schedule land excepting 6 acres and confirming her possession therein, decreeing the suit in preliminary form introspect of 19.72 acres (wrongly stated as 46.23 acres) and declaring in part plaintiffs title in movable property described in schedules Kha and Ga of the plaint with direction that the plaintiff would get 30 buffaloes out of 41 and no cow and 34 togas 7 annas gold out of 41 togas 7 annas described in schedule Ga(2) of the plaint and confirming her possession therein.

5. Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has submitted by making reference to Order 1, Rule 3 and Order 2, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure that as the reliefs sought for in the plaint and the causes of action for the suit do not relate to common question of law or fact all the defendants could not be joined in the suit and as such the suit as framed is not maintainable.

6. Mr. Hemayetuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent No. 1, has in reply submitted by making reference to Order 1, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the reliefs prayed for in the plaint and the causes of action for the suit relate to common question of law or fact and as such any number of defendants could be joined as defendants in the suit and the suit was quite maintainable. It is found that the reliefs prayed for in the plaint and the causes of action for the suit relate to common question of law and fact and common question of law and fact would arise against the defendants jointly or severally and as such they are found to have been rightly joined as defendants in the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge has correctly found the suit to be maintainable on consideration of the reliefs prayed for in the plaint and the causes of action for the suit.

The learned Advocate for the appellants has next submitted that the suit properties are not identifiable and their description suffers from vagueness and indefiniteness and as such no decree can be passed.

7. On perusal of the schedules to the plaint it is found that the suit land has been specifically described in the schedule Ka(1) to Ka (9) and the cattle, buffaloes and gold also have been specifically described schedules' Kha' and 'Ga' and there is no vagueness or indefiniteness in the description of the land in schedule 'Ka' and of the cattle, buffaloes and gold in schedules "Kha' and 'Ga' to the plaint and that being the position it cannot be said that the suit properties are not identifiable and their description suffers from vagueness or indefiniteness and for that no decree can be passed as submitted on behalf of the appellants.

8. The learned Advocate for the appellants has further submitted that the suit suffers from defect of party as the recorded owners of S.A. Khatian No. 154 in respect of. 23 decimals and the recorded owners of S.A. Khatian No. 190 in respect of 72 decimals of S.A. Plot No. 699 have not been impleaded in the suit and that therefore a decree that may be passed for partition in the suit will be infructuous as the same may be set at naught at the instance of any left out party. In support of his submission he has relied upon the cases of Gopesh Chandra Ghosh and others Vs. Ashit Kumar Ghosh and others, 7 P.L.R. (AD) 619; Laksman Mondal Vs. Laksmi Dasi and another, 10 P.L.R. (DA) 27; Asadunnessa and others Vs. Qumaruzzaman and others, 26 DLR (H.C.) 363 and Abu Saber Aziz Mohammad and others V s. Govt. of Bangladesh and others, 31 DLR (AD) 218. In this connection it may be pointed out that an issue as to defect of party was raised before the learned Subordinate Judge and the learned Subordinate Judge decided the issue in favour of the plaintiff with the remark that the defendants did not file the S.A. Khatian No. 154 and S.A. Khatian 190 showing the entry of the remaining .35 decimals of land of the suit plot No. 699.

9. The appellants have filed the certified copies of S.A. Khatian Nos. 154 and 190 in this Court by way of additional evidence and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties we have accepted the certified copies of S.A. Khatians Nos. 154 and 190 as additional evidence on the ground that the Khatians are public documents. The learned Advocate for plaintiff respondent No.1 has submitted that the plaintiff having claimed the entire .12 decimals of land of S.A. Khatian No. 77 of plot No. 699 and he having not claimed the rest .35 decimals of land of plot No. 699 recorded in S.A. Khatians Nos. 154 and 190, the suit does not suffer from defect of party and in support of his submission he has relied upon the case of Mir Shariatullah Vs. Abdur Rahman Bapary and others, 8 DLR (DA) 645. In the case reported in 7 P.L.R. (DA) 619 it has been held that the suit for partition is incompetent if all the co- owners are not parties to the suit as no effective decree can be passed in the absence of anyone of them. In the case reported in 10. P.L.R. (DA) 27 it has been held that the suit for partition without bringing the rest of the land of the tenancy into the hotchpotch and without impleading the other parties interested in the land, is not maintainable. In the case reported in 26 DLR (H.C.) 363 arising out of a suit for recovery of possession on declaration of title it has been held that it is one of the established principles of judicial procedure that no Court shall pass a decree which is infructuous and can be set at naught at the will of a person who has not been made a party to the suit. In the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 218 it has been observed :- "All objections on the ground of non-Joinder or misjoinder of parties’ ought to have been taken at the earliest possible opportunity and any such objection not so taken be deemed to have been waived. Having regard to the law of procedure, it can pertinently be contended that the defendants cannot raise the question of non-joinder of parties for the first time in the court of first appeal. No Court should pass an infructuous decree. If it comes to the notice of the Court that for the absence of a party who was a necessary party in the suit, the decree which may be passed may run into jeopardy, the Court may not pass such a decree."

10. It has been further observed in this case that the plaintiffs having sought for a declaration of their exclusive title to schedule A land and for confirmation of possession therein it is extremely difficult to pass a decree in their favour in the absence of necessary parties who may be prejudicially affected by such a decree or the decree may be rendered infructuous by them and that in these circumstances it would not be proper to dispose of the suit in their absence and on the basis of an application filed on behalf of the plaintiffs before the Appellate Division for amendment of plaint for addition of certain persons as proforma defendants and for other amendments and the Appellate Division allowed the appeal, set side the judgments and decrees of High Court Division as well as of the trial Court and remanded the suit to the trial Court with direction to finally dispose of the suit after considering the application for amendment of plaint. In the case reported in 8 DLR (DA) 645 relied upon by the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 it has been observed :-

"A suit for partition of a portion of a joint estate is maintainable when such portion is the only property hid jointly by the plaintiffs and defendants, although the defendants may be jointly interested with persons other than the plaintiffs in the remaining portion of the estate. This is merely a recognition of the elementary principle that a suit for partition properly framed does not include within its scope a property in which some only of the parties arc interested as owners".

11. The proposition of law enunciated in the decisions of the above noted cases cried upon by the learned Advocate for the appellants support the view that no effective decree for partition can be passed in the absence of any necessary party and without bringing the rest of plot No. 699 in the hotchpotch that no court shall pass a decree which is infructuous and can be set at naught by a person who is a necessary party but has not been impleaded in the suit and that if it comes to the notice of the Court that for the absence of a necessary party the decree which may be passed may run into jeopardy the Court may not pass such a decree. In the instant case the recorded owners of S.A. Khatians Nos. 154 and 190 in respect of .35 decimals of land of S.A. Plot No. 699 are surely necessary parties but they have not been impleaded in the suit and any decree' for partition that may be passed in the suit may run into jeopardy and as it may be set at naught or rendered infructuous at the will of the said recorded owners and in that view we held that a decree for partition in the absence of the said recorded owners of S.A. Khatians Nos. 154 and 190 should not be passed' in the suit. In the present case defendant No.1 filed written statement on 22.4.74 and additional written statement on 7.8.76 but the plaint was amended on 25.8.76 incorporating a prayer for partition and as such the question of raising objection as to defect of party arose from the date of amendment of plaint on 25.8.76 after the written statement and additional written statement were filed by the defendant No.1 and so the defendant No.1 who contested the suit had no opportunity to raise objection as to defect of party and this being so the defendants can not be said to have waived the objection as to defect of party. It may be noted that the question of defect of party for non-joinder of the recorded owners of S.A. Khatians Nos. 154 and 190 in respect of .35 decimals of land was raised in the trial court but the plaintiff did not file any application in the trial nor has she filed any in this court for amendment of the plaint for the purpose of addition of the said recorded owners in the suit nor any oral prayer on her behalf is made for remand of the case for the said purpose. The facts of the case reported in 8 DLR (DA) 645 relied upon by the learned Advocate for respondent No.1 are distinguishable from the facts of the present case. In that case a portion of a joint estate was the only property held jointly by the plaintiffs and the defendants although the defendants might be jointly interested with person other than the plaintiffs in the remaining portion of the estate but in the present case the plaintiff holds .12 decimals of land in S.A. Khatian No. 77 in plot No. 699 along with other persons who also hold .35 decimals of land in S.A. Khatians Nos. 154 and 190 in the same p IN namely 699 and yet they are not impleaded in the suit. In the light of the principles laid down in 9 P.L.R. (DA) 619, 10 P.L.R. (DA) 27, 26 DLR (H.C.) 363 and 31 D.L.R. (DA) 218 it can be held that the law laid down in 8 DLR (AD) 645 is no longer a good law.

<u>12. The learned Advocate for the appellants has also submitted that in view of the alleged family arrangement between the plaintiff and the defendants in pursuance of the alleged arrangement Ext. B by the original owner of the land namely Thanchaneo, the husband of the plaintiff, the plaintiff can claim only 1/4 share in the property left behind by her husband Thanchaneo. In considering this submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants first of all we have to see what the legal position of the alleged arrangements is. The learned Advocate for the rডspondent No.1 has submitted that the arrangement Ext. B made by Thanchanco is characterized as a will in paragraph 14 of the written statement filed by defendant No. 1. It was also found to be a will by Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed, Magistrate, 1st Class, Barguna in his enquiry report submitted as per direction of the Martial Law Authority. So in view of the pleading of defendant No.1 and the report of the learned Magistrate the arrangement Ext. B, made by Thanchanco the original owner of the property, is a will. Under the Burmese Budhist law of inheritance a Burmese Budhist cannot make a will and it is conceded before us by the learned Advocate for the appellants that the par- ties in the suit are Burmese Budhists and they are governed by Burmese Budhist Law of Inheritance. That being the position the will is not admissible in evidence. The learned Advocate for the appellants has sought to argue that Ext. B is not a will but it is a family arrangement. The learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 has argued that Ext. B cannot be a family arrangement because it is not an arrangement among the heirs and because it is unilateral. In this connection he has relied upon the decision in the case of Ramjan Ali Mistri Vs. Shamsul Huq and others, 17 DLR (Dhaka) 649 wherein it has been held :-</u>

<u>"Amongst Burmah Budhists the father fore-seeing that the heirs may quarrel about the division of property on his death, not infrequently arranges a special contract before his death among those heirs, whereby they bind themselves to accept a certain method of partition, but such an arrangement will not usually give them a right to recover the property from their father during his lifetime and such arrangements are not binding until the parent dies and the heirs act upon it and are thereby estopped from challenging its validity."</u>

<u>From the principle enunciated in this case it is apparent that by such family arrangement there cannot be transfer of interest but there can only be arrangement for possession of the joint property amongst the heirs. In the instant case the arrangement Ext. B was made by Thanchanco for the defendants and the plaintiff was not a party to it. The plaintiff was the sale heir of the property left behind by her husband Thanchaneo under the Burmese Budhists Law of Inheritance and the defendants for whom the arrangement Ext. B was made are outsiders and not heirs and as such this arrangement is no arrangement in the eye of law and as such not admissible in evidence. It is Suited in paragraph 13 of the written statement filed by defendant No.1 that Bisudhananda Mahathero, the President of Budhya Kristi Prochar Sangha, made an award on the has is of family sculcment according to Budhist Law at the request of the District Martial Law Administrator. Defendant No. 1 Chan Juri Talukder as D.W. 1. has stated in his cross-examination that there was an award at the instance of Bisudhananda Mahathero in which the plaintiffs had consent. Thus from the pleading of defendant No. 1 and from his evidence it is clear that allegedly there was an award in respect of the property of the plaintiff at the instance of Bisudhananda Mahathero Neither the original of the alleged award nor the certified copy thereof has been filed in Court by the defendants. A true copy of the alleged award has only been filed. Mr. Hemayetuddin Ahmed the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 has submitted that the original of the alleged award having not been filed in Court the question of consideration of the allegged award does not arise. It is perfectly corrects say that the original of the alleged award having no been filed in Court the alleged award cannot be can sidered. The alleged award is again a non-testamentary instrument which purports or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest of the value of Tk. 100/- or upwards to or in immovable property as mentioned in section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act and as such it is compulsorily registrable and the alleged award having not been registered it is not enforceable in law under section 49 of the Registration Act. Finding difficulty the learned Advocate for the appellant has sought to argue that it is not an award but it is a family arrangement and that the plaintiff through her father gave consent to it and so it is binding on her. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 in reply has argued that in view of his pleading and evidence that there was an award as noted above the defendant No. 1 cannot now turn round and say that it is not an award but is a family arrangement. He has further argued that even assuming for the sake of argument that it is a family arrangement then also it can be said without any fear of contradiction that it is not a family arrangement in the eye of law as plaintiff was not a consenting party to the alleged family arrangement. That the plaintiff was not a consenting party to the alleged family arrangement has been proved by D.W. 3 who has stated in his cross-examination that “বাদিনীকে কিছুই জিজ্ঞাসা করে নাই। সে সেখানে ছিল না।”</u>

<u>and D.W. 3 was not declared hostile by the defendants. Thus the plaintiff not being a consenting party to the alleged family arrangement the alleged arrangement is not admissible in evidence and it can neither he binding on her nor it can deprive her of her property.</u>

13. The appellants have filed an application in this Court for considering the alleged family arrangement i.e. the true copy of the family arrangement as additional evidence. But as the defendants have not filed in Court the original of the alleged family arrangement the question of its consideration does not arise and the application is, therefore, rejected. During the hearing of this appeal the appellants have filed another application for passing order for translation in Bengali or English of the contents of the alleged family arrangement Ext. B executed by Thanchaneo, husband of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 has vehemently opposed the application contending that at this belated stage of the case the application can not be considered. The alleged will or family arrangement Ext. B having been found to be inadmissible in evidence the question of its translation in Bengali or English language does not at all arise. It may be pointed out that although the suit was pending before the trial Court for more than 8 years from its institution on 30.2.72 to its disposal on 29.4.80 and the appeal has been pending in this Court from 7.7.80 for more than 8 years the defendants took no step to get the translation of Ext. B in Bengali or English language and file the same in the trial Court or in this Court although they had sufficient opportunity to do so during the last 16 years. The pleading and evidence in the case are sufficient for the purpose of decision on Ext. B and the learned Subordinate Judge has correctly decided the legal position of Ext. B within the frame-work of the pleading and evidence in the case and there is therefore no necessity to go for the translation of Ext. B and furthermore to allow the prayer of the defendants for translation of Ext. B at this belated stage will be putting a premium on the laches of the defendants. The application for translation of Ext. B is accordingly rejected.

14. The last submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants is that in view of the provisions of President's Order No. 98 of 1972)Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Order, 1972) the Court cannot pass a decree declaring the title of the plaintiff for land in excess of 100 standard bighas. In this connection the relevant provisions of P.O. 98 of 1972 are discussed below :-

" 3. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law for the time being in force,

(a) no family shall be entitled to retain any land held by it in excess of one hundred standard bighas in the aggregate and all lands held by it in excess of that quantity shall be surrendered to the Government ; and

(b)

Article 5 provides that for the purpose of clause (a) of Article 3, a family shall be deemed to be holding  land in excess of the hundred standard big has, if the aggregate of the total quantity of land held by the members of the family on the date of submission of the statement under Article 7 together with the total quantity of land, if any, transferred by them after the 16th day of December, 1971, and before the date of submission of such statement exceeds one hundred standard big has and the limitation imposed by that clause shall be applied to such family on the basis of such aggregate.

15. Article 6 provides that a family holding a total quantity of land in excess of one hundred standard bighas in the aggregate within the meaning of Article 5 shall have the option to select, out of the land actually held by it, the lands to be surrendered to the Government being in excess of one hundred standard bighas.

16. Article 7 provides that within sixty days from the date of commencement of this Order, the head of every family holding land in excess of one hundred standard bighas within the meaning of Article 5 shall submit to the Revenue Officer, within whose jurisdiction he resides, a statement, in such form and manner as may be prescribed, showing the particulars of all lands.

17. Article 8 provides that if any head of a family fails, without any reasonable cause to submit the statement required under Article 7 within the time mentioned therein or willfully makes any omission from, or incorrect declaration in, the statement submitted by him under that Article, he shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten thousand taka or with both and the land for which no statement has been submitted or which has been omitted from the statement or in respect of which the incorrect declaration has been made shall stand forfeited to the Government.

Under Article 9 any person may furnish to the Revenue Officer the name and address of any head of a family which according to his information and belief, holds land in excess of one hundred standard bighas.

18. Article 10 runs as follows:-

"10(1) on receipt of a statement under Article 7 or of information under Article 9, the Revenue-Officer shall have such statement or information verified by necessary enquiries and shall, after giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, pass an order accepting the excess lands surrendered by a family or forfeiting any land under Article 8, as the case may be ;

Provided that where a family does not exercise its option to select the land to be surrendered to the Government or the option so exercised docs not conform to the provisions of Article 6, the Revienue Officer shall make such selection himself in the prescribed manner.

(2) An order of the Revenue Officer under clause (1) accepting any excess land or forfeiting any land shall contain the full particulars of such land and upon the passing of such order, such land shall, subject to the provision of Article 11, vest in the Government free from all encumbrances."

19. Under the proviso to Article 10 in case a family does not exercise its option to select land to be surrendered to the Government or option so exercised docs not conform to the provisions of Article 6 the Revenue Officer is required to make such selection himself and under Article 10(2) he is required to pass an order accepting any excess land or forfeiting any land and that upon such selection or passing of order for acceptance of any excess land or forfeiture of any land, such land shall vest in the Government subject to appeal under Article 11 of P.O. 98 of 1972. Thus it is apparent that the Revenue Officer himself selects the land to be surrendered to the Government. In the present case there has been no selection of excess land by the Revenue Officer nor has he passed any order accepting any excess land or forfeiting any land and in the absence of such selection or order by the Revenue Officer the excess land, if any, held by the plaintiff cannot vest in the Government. There is, therefore, no bar in passing a decree in respect of plaintiffs claim in excess of 100 standard bighas. After the disposal of the case if it is named that the plaintiff has title and possession in and in excess of 100 standard bighas then the Gunmen which is a party in this case will be at liberty to take step to recover it.

<u>20. In the above circumstances, it is held that টবe plaintiff has been able to prove her 16 anna title the suit land and the learned Subordinate Judge, on correct appreciation of the facts and circumstances the case and evidence on record and on a correct principle of law, has correctly decreed the plaintiffs 5 annas title in the suit land. It appears from scheme Ka(3) that the plaintiff claims 1.75 acres out of 5.35 acres in her 1/12th share but on calculation it found that the area given as her claim at 1.75 acres a mistake and it should be 1.36 acres and as such e total claim of the plaintiff in schedule Ka(1) to a(8) will be 51.84 acres instead of 52.23 acres and her claim is 45.84 acres after deduction of 6 acres lid away by her late husband as it appears from the kabalas Ext. A-A(2). On a correct appreciation of e facts and circumstances of the case and pleadings the parties and the submissions of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 the learned subordinate Judge has correctly found that the plaintiff is entitled to get 30 buffaloes out of 41 buffaloes id no cow and 34 togas 7 annas gold out of 41tolas annas gold and we fully agree with him.</u>

21. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part without any order as to costs. The decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is upheld with the codification that the plaintiffs title in Ka schedule and to the extent of 45.84 acres excepting 6 acres of land of Ext. A-A(2) is declared and her joint possession therein confirmed and the decree declaring in part re plaintiffs title to the movable properties derived in schedules 'Kha' and 'Ga' to the plaint directs the plaintiff to get 30 buffaloes out of 41 buffers and no cow and 34 tolas 7 annas of gold out of 41 tolas 7 annas of gold and her possession therein is firmed but the preliminary decree for partition of schedule Ka(2) to Ka (8) of the plaint is set aside.

End.
