full_judgment:
This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 2-3-74 passed by Mr. Hafizuddin Ahmed, Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Jessore in Title Appeal No. 115 of 1973 reversing those dated 8-6-73 passed by Mr. J.A. Akhand, Munsif, Second Court, Jessore in Title Suit No. 170 of 1970 for permanent injunction.

2. The plaintiffs are the appellants in this Second Appeal. Their case in short is that Suit Dag Nos. 1402 and 1405 as shown in the plaint-schedule originally belonged to Upendra Nath Ghose and Dhirendra Nath Ghose in equal shares. The Ghose brothers jama settled .50 acre of land from Dag No. 1403 to Aswini Kumar Biswas, father of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and husband of plaintiff No. 3 by registered kabala dated 4.11.42 A. D. at a jama of Tk. 4/50 on receipt of Tk. 100/- as selami. This Aswini Kumar also took jama settlement of the remaining .67 acre as stated in the plaint from Dag No. 1402 and .27 acre from Dag No. 1405 in the benami of his mother Sadhana Bala Biswas by a registered lease deed Ext 1 dated 23.1.45 A. D. at a jama of Tk. 13/00 and as selami of Tk. 1000/- only. Aswini Kumar had possessed the above lands taken by bandabasta since the time of jama settlement. Sadhana died in 1950 A. D. in Jessore Town. Then Aswini Kumar also died in May, 1951 A. D. Further case of the plaintiffs is that the plaintiffs and their predecessors are members of the Christian Community living in Jessore for a long period. The rent-roll relating to the plaintIand has been prepared showing plaintiff  Nos. 1 and 2 having 8 annas share and Jnanendra Biswas, the youngest brother of Aswini Kumar, having 8/- annas share. The said entry in the record of right is wrong and that Jnanendra has never possessed the suit-land as he has been living in India as an Indian national since 1932.

3. The defendant Government served a notice upon the plaintiffs to surrender possession of the suit land which has been declared as enemy property. Plaintiff No. 1 being a poor employee of the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Jessore became perplexed on receipt of the said notice and sought advice of the Superintendent of the Local Enemy Property Office arid then filed an application for taking lease of the suit land, Meanwhile the plaintiffs learnt that defendant No. 4 in the benami of the defendant No. 3 and other defendants Nos. 5 to 10 have taken lease of the suit-land on the basis of which they have been threatening the plaintiffs with dispossession there from since 21.3.70. Hence the suit for permanent injunction.

4. The suit was contested by defendant No. 2, the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property who is Respondent No. 1 in this Second Appeal by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and the same was not properly valued and stamped. The substantive defence case was that 16 annas share of the suit property covered by the lease deed Ext. 1 belonged equally to Aswini Kumar and Jnanendra, the two brothers as their ancestral property. Jnanendra possessed his portion by demarcation and in specific share and that the khatian in the last rent-roll operation was correctly prepared and published under E. B. S. A. & T Act showing Aswini Kumar being dead his sons in 8 annas share and Jnanendra Kumar in 8 annas share in the lands convered by Ext. 1. The plaintiffs did neither protest against the above record of right nor file any case for correction of the same. Since Jnanendra left for India long before the IndoPak War in September, 1965 in connection with his employment there, his property (i.e. the suit land) was treated as Enemy Property vide E.P.C. No. 57KW/69 and accordingly notice directing the unauthorised occupiers namely, the plaintiffs to surrender possession thereof was issued. Plaintiff No. 1 Bimal Kanti Biswas received the notice on 21.5.69. There-after the suit land was demarcated and .42 acre thereof was leased out to defendant Nos. 3 to 10 and the remaining .30 acre was finalised in the record to grant lease in favour of the plaintiffs. Defendant Nos. 3 to 10 have already entered into possession in some portion of the suit-land. Hence there was no question of any threat of dispossession. The false suit filed by the plaintiffs was therefore liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. The learned Munsiff framed the following issues for consideration:-namely, 1) Is the suit non-maintainable? 2) Have the plaintiffs possession in the suit land? 3) Have they prima facie tide thereto?

6. The plaintiffs examined only two witnesses including plaintiff No. 1 as P. W. 1 and the contesting defendant examined only one D. W. in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif now Assistant Judge, on consideration of the materials on record was pleased to decree the suit for permanent injunction on contest against the contesting defendant No. 2 and ex parte against the rest by his judgment and decree as stated above, holding, inter alia, that the suit is maintainable and the plaintiffs have possession and also prima facie title in the suit land.

7. On appeal by the contesting defendant No. 2, the learned Subordinate Judge reversed the findings and decision of the learned Munsiff and dismissed the suit and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court by his judgment and decree as stated above holding, inter alia that the plaintiffs cannot get relief in the manner as prayed for and that "even plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration of their title to the suit land without making further prayer for declaration that Ext. 1 is a benami document, I doubt very much whether the plaintiffs could escape the liability of section 42 of the S.R. Act."

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court, the plaintiffs have preferred this Second Appeal.

9. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellants, firstly submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed grave error of law in holding that "This suit being a suit for permanent injunction I cannot legally adjudicate as to whether the transaction by Ext. 1 is a benami one. Unless there is any declaration by a competent court that the transaction by Ext. 1 was in essence jama settlement by Aswini Kumar Biswas in the benami of his mother Sadhana Bala Biswas, the plain-tiffs cannot say that Aswini Kumar Biswas had acquired title by Ext. 1" and also in holding that "In a suit for permanent injunction, the plaintiffs' title to the suit land must be unclouded. In the instant suit plaintiffs title to the suit-land is clouded because Ext. 1 stands not in the name of Aswini Kumar but in the name of Sadhana Bala Biswas. Therefore, the plaintiffs can not get relief in the manner as prayed for by them."

10. Elucidating his submission, the learned Advocate for the appellants argues that in a suit for permanent injunction, the question of title can be gone into, if necessary and that there is no bar in deciding incidentally the question of title in such a suit. In the instant case, the learned Subordinate Judge, on the one hand, observes that, "this being a suit for permanent injunction I cannot legally adjudicate as to whether the transaction by Ext. 1 is a benami one." but, at the same time, he observes that "the oral evidence coming out from the statement of P.W. 1 Bimal Kanti Biswas that he knew that his grand mother was his father's benamder because his father was a petty Government servant cannot suffice for a declaration that Ext. 1 is a benami document." From this, the learned Advocate for the appellants wants to submit that the learned Subordinate Judge was in confusion as to whether in a suit for permanent injunction simpliciter, he was incompetent to adjudicate as to whether the transaction by Ext. 1 was a benami one. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that a suit for permanent injunction is quite maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title and as such the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law in holding that the plain-tiffs cannot get any relief in the manner as prayed for. In support of his contention, he has cited a decision reported in A.I.R. 1936 (Madras) 936 wherein it has been held that;

"Where the allegation of the plaintiff is that he is in lawful possession of the properties and that his possession is threatened to be interfered with by the defendants, he is entitled to sue for a mere injunction without adding prayer for declaration of his rights." So far competency of the Court to incidentally decide a question of title in a suit for permanent injunction, he has cited another decision reported in 31 DLR at page 217.

11. Mr. Syed Mokaddes Ali, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the contesting defendant-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly held that the plaintiffs cannot get relief in the manner as prayed for and the question of benami transaction by Ext. 1 cannot be adjudicated upon, unless there is a declaration by a competent court to the effect that the transaction Ext. 1 was actually a jama settlement in favour of Aswini in the benami of Sadhana Bala Biswas, In elaborating his argument, the learned Advocate for the respondent submits that in a case for seeking relief by way of permanent injunction, the plaintiffs must establish his legal right and actual laWful possession in the suit property. In this connection he has referred to sections 54 and 56 of the Specific Relief Act which relate to perpetual injunction matters. He further submits that permanent in-junction is an equitable relief as such the maxim that "he who seeks equity, must also do equity and come with clean hands." should be followed. In this connection he has referred to two decisions reported in AJ R. 1958 (Andhra Pradesh) 43 and A.I.R. 1958 (Punjab) 190. In the case of Ilyderabad Stock Exchange Ltd. Vs. Rangnath Rathi and Co. reported in A.I.R. 1958(Andhra Pradesh) 43, it has been held by a Division Bench that "sections 54 and 56 must be read together as supplementary to each other. The former defines the circumstances under which perpetual injunction may be granted; the latter enumerates the cases where an injunction must not be granted." It has been further held that "mere prospect or apprehension of injury or the belief that the act complained of may or will be done is not sufficient. A man seeking an injunction must show that the act complained of is in fact a violation of his right and which if carried into effect will necessarily result in violation of his right." It has further been held that "As the relief by way of a perpetual injunction is purely of equitable ammeter the plaintiff must satisfy the Court that his own conduct and dealings in the matter had been fair and honest". In this very decision it has been further held that "The expression 'obligation' has been defined in section 3 of the Act as including every duty enforceable by law. The word 'obligation' in section 54 of the Act may be taken to be a tie or bond which constrains a person to do or suffer something. It implies a right in another person to which it is co-related and it restricts the freedom of the obligee with respect to definite acts and forbearances, but in order that it may be enforced by a Court, it must be legal obligation and not merely moral, social or religious". In the decision reported in A.I.R. 1985 (Punjab) 190 in the case of Kamal Distillery Co. Ltd. & others, Vs Ladli Parshad Jaiswal & another, it has been held that "plaintiffs right to obtain relief by way of a permanent injunction depends upon the provisions contained in section 54 and 56 of the Specific Relief Act.

The question of Court's jurisdiction to entertain a suit is distinct from the question, whether having jurisdiction, it should exercise it in view of the circumstances of the particular case. The granting or refusing of injunctive relief rests within the Court's judicial discretion, guided by law and in harmony with the well-established principles of equity after exercise of due care and caution.

The claimant for such a relief must show that he has a superior equity in his favour entitling him to the injunction asked as against the defendants. He has also to show, that he has been acting towards the defendants in a fair and equitable manner, free from any taint or fraud, sharp practice, undue influence or illegality. It is a cardinal principle of broad applicability that he who seeks equity must do equity.

The other maxim, that he who comes in equity must come with clean hands, also embodies a principle of wide amplitude and expresses the basic concept of equity jurisprudence. According to this rule, equity declines to lend its aid to a person whose conduct has been inequitable in relation to the subject matter of the suit. The principle is, that he who has done inequity shall not have equity."

12. In the instant case the learned Advocate for the respondent referring to some facts of this suit and the documents Exts. B and B1 wants to submit that the plaintiffs, particularly plaintiff No. 1, filed an application before the Enemy Property authority praying for taking lease of the suit property knowing and admitting that it was declared enemy property and stating that half of the disputed property belonged to them only. Further the suit property was recorded in the S.A. Khatian in the names of two sons of Aswini Kumar and his brother Jnanendra Kumar in 8 annas share each and the share of Jnanendra i.e. the suit property was declared as enemy property, but the plaintiffs did not institute any suit or proceeding for correction of the record or for bringing the suit property out from the list of the enemy property, but in-stead filed the present suit for permanent injunction only. So, referring to this conduct of the plaintiffs, the learned Advocate for the respondent submits that the plaintiffs have not come with clean hands and before establishment of their legal and lawful possession in the suit property, they are not at all entitled to get any relief by way of permanent injunction and as such their simple suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable. He has also cited a decision reported in 30 DLR page 161 to show that when right, title of the plaintiff is disputed, a simple suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable without a prayer for declaration of that right or title.

13. Now, on this point of maintainability, the trial Court observed as follows. "Firstly, the suit as it is not improper so as to give the plaintiffs the required relief. Secondly, were not the suit-land treated as enemy property, the plaintiffs would certainly have filed a case u/s 143 A of the & T Act for correction of the Khatian or of a suit for declaration of their exclusive title to the suit land."

14. On the face of it, there appears that the learned Munsif was under a serious misconception of law. There was no bar in filing a suit for declaration of plaintiffs' exclusive title to the suit land or for correction of the record under section 143A of the E.B.A. & T Act though the property was declared as Enemy Property. So the finding of the learned Munsif on the point of maintainability of the suit is palpably illegal. As to the finding of the lower Appellate Court on this point, it does not appear from the impugned judgment that the question of maintainability has been properly decided in its true perspective. The learned Subordinate Judge, on the one hand, says that he cannot illegally adjudicate as to whether the transaction Ext. 1 is a benami one and, on the other hand, in a slip-shod manner, he has dis-cussed the question of benami without proper application of judicial mind.

15. I have carefully gone through the impugned judgments of both the Courts below and considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides. There is no denial of the fact that Ext. 1 by which Aswini Kumar Biswas claimed to have acquired title by way of benami transaction is the sheet-anchor of the plaintiff's claim for the suit property. If the plaintiffs being successors in interest of the said Aswini Kumar Biswas fail to prove that Ext. 1 is a benami document in favour of the alleged real purchaser Aswini Kumar Biswas, then the plaintiffs would have no legal right and lawful possession to the suit property which has been admittedly recorded in the name of Jnanendra Biswas in his 8 annas share as one of the sons of late Sadhana Bala Biswas, the recipient of the lease-deed Ext. l. In that event when Jnancndra Kumar Biswas being admittedly an Indian national permanently residing in India since 1932, his share to the extent of 8 annas as appearing in the S.A. Khatian could not but be declared as Enemy Property by operation of law. So, the most pertinent question will be whether Aswini Kumar Biswas, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, acquired title over the suit property by virtue of Ext. 1 in the benami of Sadhana Bala Biswas. If it is found on evidence that Ext.1 is not actually a benami document and that the suit land has been rightly declared as enemy property, then in that case it will be difficult for the plaintiffs to establish their legal possession in the suit property as well as any legal obligation in their favour, for the prevention of the breach of which they can come with a prayer for permanent injunction. So, from the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears that a very complicated question of title requires to be determined in this case on proper evidence, and without a declaration of which by a competent court, a mere suit for permanent injunction is not at all maintainable and as such the decision reported in A.I.R. 1936 (Madras) 936 has no application in the facts and circumstances of this case and so far the decision reported in 31 DLR page 217 to the effect that in a partition suit the question of title can be incidentally determined is not also helpful for the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellants as a complicated question of title is involved in this case and unless that is decided first on sufficient evidence, the plaintiffs are not entitled to the equitable relief for permanent injunction. In view of the above I am in full agreement with the views expressed in the decisions reported in A.I.R. 1958 (Punjab) 190 and also A.I.R. 1958 (Andhra Pradesh) 43 as regards the requirements for granting permanent injunction as enjoined in sections 54 and 56 of the Specific Relief Act. So, on the first point urged before me by the learned Advocate for the appellants I hold that the findings of both the Courts below on the same suffer from serious legal infirmities and are liable to be set aside.

16. The next point urged on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant by Mr. M.A. Rahim, the learned Advocate, is that the lower appellate Court committed error of law in holding that Ext. 4, an alleged declaration made by the said Jnaneddra Kumar Biswas before a Notary Public in India, cannot be accepted in the eye of law and in wrongly excluding the same from consideration in the determination of the question of plaintiffs title or the alleged enemy nature of the suit-property. I have seen the document Ext. 4 in this suit. It appears that it is a document of declaration allegedly executed on 28th August, 1970 by one Jnanendra Nath Biswas, son of late Panchu & Panchanon by birth Christian group leader Baptist Mission 41, Lower Circular Road, Calcuta-16, resident of Beni Pukur Lane, Calcuta-14 disclaiming, inter alia, his interest in the disputed land measuring 1.44 acres in the name of Sadhana Bala, his mother and solemnly affirmed and declared on the same date before one Karati Sanker Mitra, Notary Public of 57, Hans Mukherjee Road, Calcutta-25. On the second page of the document, a photograph has been impressed without any signature or attestation of any authority or person. Of course, some special adhesive stamps worth Rs. 15/25 annas in all have been pressed on the first page of the said document Ext. 4 with seals of Treasury Officer, Jessore without any signature or date. Admittedly, it is a foreign document executed by a foreigner in a foreign country and that document had been exhibited here as Ext A in the present suit on behalf of the plaintiffs. Law requires that a foreign document should be presented to the Collector within 3 months of the receipt of the same in Bangladesh under section 18(2) of the Stamp Act who shall stamp the same in such a manner as the Government may by rule prescribe, with a stamp of such value as the person so taking such instrument may require and pay for. Section 12 of the Stamp Act has prescribed the method for affixing the adhesive stamps to any instrument chargeable with duty and it runs as follows:-

12(1)(a) Whoever affixes any adhesive stamp to any instrument chargeable with duty which has been executed by any person shall, when affixing such stamp, cancel the same so that it cannot be used again; and

(b) Whoever executes any instrument on any paper bearing an adhesive stamp shall, at the time of execution, unless such stamp has been already cancelled in manner aforesaid cancel the same so that it cannot be used again.

(2) Any instrument bearing an adhesive stamp which has not been cancelled so that it cannot be used again, shall, so far as such stamp is concerned, be deemed to be unstamped.

(3) The person required by sub-section (1) to cancel an adhesive stamp may cancel it by writing on or across the stamp his name or initials or the name or initials of his firm with the true date of his so writing or in any other effectual manner."

Thus it appears that the instant document has not been duly stamped in accordance with law. As regards admissibility of a document not duly stamped, section 35 of the Stamp Act provides as follows,

"35. Instruments not duly stamped inadmissible in evidence, etc. No instrument charge- able with duty shall be admitted in evidence for any purpose by any person having by law or consent of parties authority to receive evidence or shall be acted upon, registered or authenticated by any such person or by any public officer, unless such instrument is duly stamped;

Provided that:

A) any such instrument not being an instrument chargeable with a duty of (ten poisha or five poisha) only, or a bill of exchange or promissory note, shall, subject to all just exceptions be admitted in evidence on payment of the duty with which the same is chargeable, or, in the case of an instrument insufficiently stamped, of the amount required to make up such duty, together with a penalty of five (Taka), or, when ten times the amount of the proper duty or deficient portion thereof exceeds five (Taka) or a sum equal to ten times such duty or portion ".

17. Now, when it is found the document was not duly stamped, it ought not to have been admitted into the evidence before the payment of sufficient stamp-duty and the penalty thereof and the same ought to have been impounded by the Court under section 33 of the Stamp Act. But strangely enough, that the document in question has been marked as Ext. 4 on 6.6.73 and enlisted in the list of documents of the plaintiffs, with a different ink, though there was no witness on behalf of the plaintiffs to prove the same which is admittedly a private document. Nothing appears from the record as to how this document was submitted in Court and admitted into evidence. The trial Court has mainly relied on this document to decide issue No.3 as to prima facie title of the plaintiffs to the suit land.

18. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that even if the document Ext. 4 has not been duly stamped in accordance with law, still as it was already admitted into evidence and marked as Ext. 4, the question of its admissibility at this stage cannot be raised in view of section 36 of the Stamp Act which provides as follows:-

"36. Admission of instrument where not to be questioned: Where an instrument has been admitted in evidence, such admission shall not except as provided in section 61, be called in question at any stage of the same suit or proceeding on the ground that the instrument has not been duly stamped."

<u>19. Admittedly this document has somehow' been marked as Ext. 4 and considered by the trial Court as evidence, in spite of the fact that it was not duly stamped. But, question is whether there is any a absolute bar in view of the aforesaid provisions of section 36 of the Stamp Act, in disputing the admissibility of the document. I think the answer is 'No'.</u>

<u>In such circumstances, the admissibility of document may be questioned and the same may be impounded under section 61 of the Stamp Act which reads as follows:-</u>

<u>"61 (1) When any Court in the exercise of its civil or revenue jurisdiction or any criminal Court in a proceeding under Chapter XVI or Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, makes any order admitting any instrument in evidence as duly stamped or as not requiring a stamp, or upon payment of duty and a penalty under section 35, the Court to which appeals lie from, or references are made by, such first-mentioned Court may, of its motion -or on the application of the Collector, take such order into consideration.</u>

<u>(2) If such Court, after such consideration, is of opinion that such instrument should not have been admitted in evidence without the payment of duty and penalty under section 35, or without the payment of a higher duty and penalty than those paid, it may record a declaration to that effect and determine the amount of duty with which such instrument is chargeable, and may require any person in whose possession or power such instrument then is, to produce the same, and may impound the same when produced "</u>

20. In this connection a decision reported in 28 DLR at page 313 may be referred to. It has been held therein that:

"Where an instrument has been admitted in evidence such admission shall not be questioned at any stage of the proceeding on the ground that the instrument of transfer has been duly admitted in evidence without objection and in the affidavit-in-opposition also no such objection was taken that the instrument of transfer was not duly stamped for being not cancelled.

The legal consequence of a stamp remaining un cancelled is that the instrument shall be deemed to be unstamped instrument, that it shall be impounded and it might be again duly stamped with due cancellation thereof."

<u>21. So, in view of the above position of law, Ext. 4, the foreign private document being not duly stamped ought to have been impounded and the same could be used in evidence only after being duly stamped with cancellation thereof according to the provisions of law. Therefore, I hold that both the Courts below committed error of law in dealing with the said foreign document, Ext. 4, while deciding the question of prima-facie title in the suit property. The learned Advocate for the respondent referring to section 14 of the Notaries Ordinance, 1961 (Ordinance XIX of 1961) further submits that Ext. 4 is not admissible in evidence as the same is a mere declaration made by a foreigner Jnanendra Nath Biswas before a Notary Public of Calcutta. It is submitted on behalf of the respondent that before admitting this document, it is to be seen whether such kind of notarial act has any reciprocal arrangement between Bangladesh and India. In this connection he has cited a decision reported in 1981 B.L.D.(AD) 86 to show that at least upto 1980 there was no such reciprocal arrangement. In any view of the matter, if there was any, that has to be proved on evidence by the plaintiffs.</u>

22. Now, in the midst of the hearing of this appeal, an application has been filed in this court on behalf of the plaintiffs-appellants praying for allowing an amendment of the plaint of the Title Suit No. 170 of 1970 out of which the second appeal has aris-en, by adding a prayer in the plaint to the following effect:-"

“(ক) নালিশী জমি ইং ২৩/১/৪৫ তারিখেক বন্দোবস্তী দলিলমূলে বাদীগণের পূর্ববর্তী অশ্বিনী কুমার বিশ্বাস তদ্বীয় মাতা সাধনা বালা বিশ্বাসের বেনামে অর্জন করা এবং নালিশী জমিতে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব দখল থাকা প্রচারের ডিক্রি দিতে মর্জি হয়”।

23. It has been stated in the application that all the necessary facts have already been narrated in respect of the claim of benami and other things in the plaint of the suit for permanent injunction and no new facts or cause of action require to be incorporated in the plaint. It has been submitted that the prayer for declaration on the point of benami was not included in the pleading through sheer inadvertance and bonafide mistake of the learned lawyer concerned and not for any laches or negligence on the part of the plaintiffs and that the plaintiffs would be seriously prejudiced if the amendment sought for is not allowed. The application is presumably under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows:-

"The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy, between the parties."

24. The learned Advocate for the appellant has cited a number of decisions reported in 29 DLR(SC) 311, 31 DLR (AD) 133, 36 DLR (AD) 252. B.L.D. 1987(AD) 55 to show that the amendment of the pleadings can be allowed at any stage of the proceeding for the purpose of determination of the real question of controversy between the parties and in the interest of justice. The learned Advocate for the respondent has been served with a copy of the application. His only submission is that at such a belated stage the amendment should not be allowed and if at all allowed the defendant may be permitted to file additional written statement, and also to raise the question of limitation. It has been held in the case of Sufia Khanam Chowdhury Vs. Faizun Nessa Chowdhur reported in B.L.D. 1987(AD) 55 that

"Even if the prayer for further relief was not included in the plaint the Court got power to direct amendment of the plaint, so as to include such prayer at any stage of the proceedings if it is considered necessary in the interest of justice. The only condition for amendment of the plaint is that it will not take the defendant by surprise by introducing any new case or any new cause of action altogether or it will not change the character of the suit.

As to limitation, though the law of Limitation is to be followed in the matter of amendment, but in appropriate cases the rigidity may be relaxed and amendment may be allowed even after the expiry of the period of limitation."

25. In the case of Managing Committee N.M.C. Model High School and ors. Vs. Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury reported in 31 DLR (AD) 133, it has been held that;

"amendment of the pleadings could be allowed at any stage of the proceedings for the purpose of determining the real question of controversy between the parties, but it could not be allowed, if it changed the nature and character of the suit, or if the prayer for amendment had be-come barred by lapse of time and a right had accrued to the other side.

But the latter principle can be departed from, if there are circumstances which outweigh the hardship and cause a prejudice to the appellant.

One of the fundamental principles governing the amendment of the pleadings is that all the controversies between the parties as far as possible should be included and multiplicity of the proceedings avoided."

26. In the case of Golam Hafez Mia Vs. Khadem Ali Meah reported in 29 DLR(SC) 311, it has been held that "

It has been the consistent view of judicial authorities, that amendment of the pleadings are allowed, even when a legal right had accrued to the other party, if special circumstances of the case outweigh such consideration. In exercising this power, the Court would, no doubt, be reluctant to allow such an amendment, which would have the effect of totally altering the nature of the suit, or take away a valuable right accrued by lapse of time, but where in the circumstances of a particular case, it would be plainly inequitable to refuse such a relief, the court will not hesitate to act. "This view has been followed in the decision reported in 36 DLR (AD) 253.

<u>27. So, in view of the provisions of Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the uniform decisions of the highest Court as cited above, there is no bar in allowing amendment of a pleading even at this stage in second appeal in the interest of justice and for determination of the real controversy between the parties in the suit and for avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. Only thing that has to be seen is whether by amendment absolutely a new cause of action is introduced and the nature and character of the suit is altogether changed. Here in this case by the proposed amendment, it appears that no new facts or cause of action have been sought to be introduced in the plaint to change the nature and character of the suit. I have perused the plaint of the suit for permanent injunction and I find that all the relevant facts regarding acquisition of title by way of benami and also facts relating to enemy property have been described, therein. It appears that application has been made only to amend the prayer portion of the pleading and nothing else. So, I am of the view that in the interest of justice and equity and to avoid multiplicity of the proceedings, the prayer for amendment of the plaint should be allowed.</u>

28. Accordingly, the prayer is allowed. Now in view of my above findings and observations. I hold that the suit for permanent injunction in the facts and circumstances of the case without a prayer for declaration of title is not maintainable and as such the impugned judgments and decrees of the Courts below can not be sustained in law which are accordingly set aside. But in view of the prayer for amendment of the plaint by the plaintiffs which I have al-lowed in the interest of justice, let the suit be sent back on remand to the trial Court with a direction that the plaintiffs be allowed to amend their plaint as prayed for, subject to the payment of proper court-fees within 3(three) weeks from the date of arrival of the records and notice thereof to the parties concerned. The defendants will be at liberty to file additional written statement, if any. The trial Court is directed to try the suit afresh in the light of the observations made above on the evidence on record; of course, if the parties desire to adduce additional evidence and the Court thinks proper, the parties may be allowed to adduce such evidence.

The appeal is thus allowed but without any order as to costs. Let the lower Courts' records along with a copy of this judgment be sent down expeditiously.

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dated 17.6.1980 passed by the High Court Division in F.A. No. 431 of 1968.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division passed in F.A No 431 of 1968 affirming the judgment of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka with modification.

2. The plaintiff respondent instituted the suit for declaration that the order of compulsory retirement of the plaintiff vide Notification No. 1417- PH dated 5.6.59 are illegal, ultravires, void and further the plaintiff is still in service under the Government.

3. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court the view was taken that the Screening Committee had acted without jurisdiction inasmuch as the committee did not comply with the provision of Public Conduct (Screening Ordinance III of 1959). In this view of the matter the suit Wall decreed.

4. The Government preferred an appeal being F.A. No. 431 of 1968. A Division Bench of the High Court Division came to the conclusion that the suit was rightly decreed inasmuch as the enquiry by the Screening Committee was not in accordance with law and therefore:

“It’s finding and recommendations are bad in law and any order of the Authority based on such findings and recommendations is also bad in law and cannot be sustained". Reliance was placed on the decision in Amir Hossain's case P.L.D. 1963 (SC) 185. The learned Judge took pain to consider the report of the Screening Committee and the adverse remark in the annual confidential report of the plaintiff and then concluded that such adverse remarks had not been sub-satiated by any specific instances nor such remarks were ever communicated to him and he had no opportunity to represent against them. The learned Judges then came to the conclusion that under section 10 of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance. 1959, though the order of finding by an appointing authority or Screening Committee cannot be called in Question but the ruling in Zafrul Ahmed's case. 12 DLR (SC) 9 will be attracted and such finding by such authority is therefore not immune from challenge. The learned Judges distinguished the decision in 21 DLR (SC) 16 and 25 DLR (SC) 94 on the ground .that those are the decisions which-rest on the charge of "inefficiency" but in the present case the charge was for 'misconduct'. In this view of the matter the appeal was dismissed.

5. Leave was granted to consider the question whether the Learned Judges of the High Court Division were well founded in applying the case of Amir Hossain and whether the principle of Muzuqullah's case and Nasiruddin Ahmed's case are attracted and whether under Article 6(5) (b) of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order. 1959 the impugned order is immune from challenge.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney General in painstaking manner presented the factual aspects of the case and the relevant law. The learned Additional Attorney General submitted that the High Court Division had fallen into an error of taking notice of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, (1959) (Ordinance III of 1959) and have failed to notice the ratio laid down in two cases (1969) 21 DLR(SC) and (1973) 25 DLR (SC).

7. It is unfortunate that the High Court Division considered the provision of the Ordinance III of 1959. That Ordinance was provided for the constitution, power and procedure of the Committee appointed to scrutinise the conduct of certain persons, That Ordinance has given the power to appoint Committee and for recording finding and the procedure of that Committee and then section 10 bars the jurisdiction of the Court. That Ordinance was promulgated on 21st January, 1959 Action was taken in this case under Article 6(51 (b) of the Laws (Continuance in Force Order, 1959. President's Order No. 1 of 1959 dated 9th March, 1959 was promulgated adding new clauses 3 and 4 and clause 5 was subsequently amended by President's Order No. 5 of 1959 promulgated on 23rd April. 1959. The two sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause 5 of Article 6 as amended are reproduced below:

Article 6

Clause (5)

"Nothing in this Article or in any rule or instrument having the force of law shall prevent a person mentioned in clause (1) from being:-

(a) suspended reduced in rank, removed or dismissed for being corrupt or for misconduct or for inefficiency after such enquiry as may be held under the orders of the Central Government; or

(b) retired for any cause mentioned in the preceding sub-clause, or for having the reputation of being corrupt, on suspension (if any) as may be admissible to him proportionate or otherwise, by an order of the authority mentioned in clause (3) made before the 1st of July, 1959 and no appeal shall lie against such order nor shall such order, be called in question in any court".

<u>8. It will be noticed that sub-clause (b) by reference to clause (a) includes "misconduct" as a ground for compulsory retirement of a person in the service, if the order of termination is made before the 1st July, 1959. This provision is a part of a supra constitutional law (Continuance in Force) Order, 1959. It is independent of any other law and has an overriding effect as its says: "nothing in this article or in any law, rule or instrument having force of law shall prevent" a person mentioned in clause (1) from being compulsorily retired under sub-clause (b) and no appeal has been provided for. Since the action against the plaintiff was taken under this provision we fail to understand the reasoning’s of the High Court Division as to how provisions of Ordinance III of 1959 are attracted. As has been noticed in the case Murzuqullah, (1969) 21 DLR (SC) 16, even if any enquiry was made that was merely gratuitous because clause (a) speaks of "after such enquiry as may be held", clause (b) which stands on a different footing' provides for compulsory retirement "for any cause mentioned in (a)" but no enquiry has been provided for taking any action under clause (b). The compulsory retirement order was passed on 3.6.59 and the requirement of Article 6 is that such order must be passed before 1st of July, 1959 and since the Order was passed within the period, i.e. fell within the ambit of the statute and protected by the preclusion clause "no appeal shall lie against such order nor shall such order be called in question in any court". The learned Judges relied on the case of Amir Hossain reported in P.L.D. 1963 (SC)185. In that case enquiry was initiated under the provisions of Ordinance No. III of 1959 and the Screening Committee in a cryptic order recommended removal which reads as under:</u>

<u>"Seen explanation Heard in person His prosecution under section 193/468 B.P.C. has been sanctioned by the D.I.I. May be removed for misconduct".</u>

9. Mere initiation of a criminal case had weighed with the Screening Committee notwithstanding that the petitioner in that case was tried and acquitted by the Special Judge the Supreme Court considered that in the absence of any finding of guilt, the appointing authority is not in a position to come to such conclusion, since the enquiry on which the screening Committee found the officer guilty is insufficient to sustain it. The bar under section 10 of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 could not be raised because the Supreme Court found "the finding in this case is no finding for which protection against judicial examination can be claimed and the order which proceeded thereon is equally liable to interference". This decision has no manner of application in the present case and the reliance by the High Court Division on this decision was totally irrelevant. In the case of Nazlruddin Ahmed reported in 25 DLR (SC) 94 it was held that there was no bar for the Governor to refer the case of a public servant to the Screening Committee for the assessment of public servant's conduct and for recommendation with reference to any independent enquiry under any particular law and hence the Governor was within his province in ordering retirement of the appellant under sub-clause (b) of Clause (5). It was observed:

"The Screening Committee held the enquiry in this case at the request of the Governor; who could indisputably get himself informed as to the truth or otherwise of the allegation against the plaintiff through any agency he must choose in the absence of a provision to the contrary. With respect, we are of the opinion that no question of lack of jurisdiction is invoked in the instant case, either of the Screening Committee to enquire into the allegation against the plaintiff-or the Governor in passing the impugned order of retirement."

Further the court noticed the provision of Article 6 (5) and concluded:

"We are precluded from challenging the validity of the said order which was made within the period specified in clause (5) of the Article 6 of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958".

<u>10. The learned Judges of the High Court Division proceeded on the assumption that the Screening Committee had jurisdiction to hold enquiry into .a charge of misconduct under the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 and concluded that "it was therefore a statutory enquiry. Being a statutory enquiry the Screening Committee was bound to hold enquiry in accordance with law". Herein liesthe error. In the present proceeding no enquiry was necessary by any Committee since the Governor could "indisputably get himself informed as to the truth or otherwise of the allegation against the plaintiff' through any agency he might choose in the absence of a provision to the contrary" (Vide 25 D.L.R. S.C. 94). That was the error committed by the trial court and the High Court in 21 D.L.R. (S.C.) 16. The Supreme Court observed:</u>

<u>"We regret to say that both the trial Judge and the High Court have gone off the mark in seeking guidance from the provisions of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 and the rules made thereunder, as they were wholly irrelevant in the decision of this case. The High Court in particular had itself pertinently posed the questions whether the officer could be retired compulsorily on the ground of inefficiency under the powers quoted in the impugned order. Yet, while reaching its conclusion it totally lost sight of the nature and extent of that power. The source of the power for retiring the respondent compulsorily, as quoted in the Governor's order, cited above is sub-clause (b) of clause (5) of Article 6 of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1959".</u>

<u>This was the error in the present case also. The decision of Amir Hossain which was decided under Public Conduct Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 has no manner of application. The contention of the plaintiff is therefore devoid of any substance and is covered by the two decisions referred to above. The High Court had fallen into error and therefore the order and judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside.</u>

In the result therefore this appeal is allowed and the judgment and order of the Courts below are set aside and the plaintiff's suit is dismissed No costs.

End.

parties:

Trading Corporation of Bangladesh ------ Respondent in all the Writ Petitions
case_source: In the matter of: Applications under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J :- These five Rules Nisi were obtained at various times by these seven Petitioners under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh challenging either the second show cause notices provisionally removing them from the service of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh or the order of removal from service itself. As they involve common question of law, they have been heard together and will be disposed of by the same judgment 

2. The petitioners are not Government servants. They are employees of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, a body corporate established under the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 68 of 1972). Under Articles 24 and 25 thereof the Government and the Board of Directors of the Corporation are authorised to make rules and regulations respectively to give effect 10 the provisions of the said Presidential Order. It is admitted that no rules or regulations have been framed by the Government or the Corporation to determine the terms and conditions of service including the disciplinary proceedings against the officers and other employees of the Corporation. It is, however, alleged by the petitioners and freely admitted by the respondent-Corporation that for purposes of regulating the disciplinary proceedings against its officers and other employees, the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh has been following the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976, hereinafter referred to as the Rules of 1976. It is also alleged by the petitioners and conceded by the Corporation that upon the repeal of the Rules of 1976, the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1984, hereinafter referred to as the Rules of 1984 are being followed by the Corporation from 21.7.84. 

3. In the Rules of 1976, the authority could prescribe a time-limit within which the inquiry should be completed by the Inquiry Officer. No consequence was provided for if the time-limit could not be adhered to. In the Rules of 1984, however, effective from 21.7.84, sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 provided as follows:- 

In case of failure of the authority to take decision within one hundred and twenty working days from the date of communicating the charges under these rules or within one hundred and fifty working days from the date the Government servant is placed under suspension, whichever is earlier, the accused shall stand discharged of the charges brought against him and in such event the persons responsible for such failure shall be proceeded against under these rules." 

4. It is the contention of the petitioners in all these writ petitions that after sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984 came into operation on 21.7.84, 120 or 150 working days, as the case may be, had elapsed in each of these Rules when the impugned orders were passed. It is their contention that they stand discharged of the charges brought against them for continuation of the proceedings beyond the period of limitation and, therefore, the impugned orders passed were illegal and without jurisdiction. 

5. From the side of the respondent-Corporation the argument is two-fold. First, the Rules of 1984 have no statutory or automatic application to the cases of the officers and other employees of the Corporation. Secondly, sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984 have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of each case. 

6. Such being the bone of contention between the parties, relevant facts of each case may now be summarised as follows. 

7. In Writ Petition No. 83 of 1985 the petitioner was a Senior Executive-in-Charge of the Corporation at the relevant time. He received a charge-sheet (Annexure-A) dated 10.2.83 admittedly under Rule 3(a) (b) and (c) of the Rules of 1976 for inefficiency, misconduct and corruption. He replied to the charge sheet on 2.3.83. An Inquiry Officer inquired into the charges from the first week of May, 1983 upto the 1st June, 1983. The inquiry report was submitted on 11.10.84. The impugned order i.e. the second show cause notice (Annexure-D) was served on the petitioner on 4.4.85. By the impugned order the petitioner was provisionally removed from the service of the Corporation and he was asked to show cause why the said order shall not be confirmed, The petitioner has challenged the second show cause notice on the ground that 188 working days have elapsed between the coming into force of the Rules of 1984 and the passing of the impugned order on 4.4.85. The petitioner, therefore, stands discharged of the charges brought against him. The impugned order (Annexure-D) is illegal and void. 

8. In Writ Petition No.137 of 1985 the petitioner was an Assistant Stores Officer of the Corporation at the relevant time. He was suspended by an order dated 18.1.83. Certain charges under Rule 3 of the Rules of 1976 were served on him on 31.5.83. The petitioner replied to the charges on 27.6.83. The inquiry against him commenced from 14.8.83 and was completed by the last week of March, 1984. The inquiry report was submitted on 15.8.84. The impugned order i.e. the second show cause notice (Annexure-F) was served on the petitioner on 29.5.85. By the impugned order he was asked to show cause why he shall not be removed from the service of the Corporation. The petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi against the second show cause notice (Annexure-F) on the ground that between the coming into force of the Rules of 1984 on 21.7.84 and the issuance of the impugned order on 29.5.85. 250 working days have elapsed and. therefore undersubrule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984 the petitioner stands discharged from the charges brought against him. 

9. In Writ Petition No. 355 of 1985 there are two petitioners. Petitioner No. 1 Md. Ishaque Khan was a Store Assistant and the petitioner No. 2 Akbar Ali Mallick was a Security Assistant of the Corporation at the relevant time at Khulna. They were placed under suspension on 12.11.81 and 26.12.81 respectively. Both the petitioners were served with charge-sheets dated 28.4.82 under Rule 3(b) and (c) of the Rules of 1976 for misconduct and corruption. The petitioner No. 1 submitted his reply on 22.6.82 and the petitioner No. 2 submitted his reply on 21.6.82. An Inquiry Officer was appointed to inquire into the charges against them. The inquiry was held from 9.8.82 to 16.8.82. The Inquiry Officer submitted his report on 5.10.82. Thereafter three years elapsed. By the impugned order (Annexure-F) both the petitioners were served with a common show cause notice on 12.9.85 provisionally removing them from the service of the Corporation and asking them to show cause why the provisional order of removal from service shall not be confirmed. It is the contention of the petitioners that after the coming into force of the Rules of 1984 on 21.7.84. 346 working days have elapsed when the impugned order was passed and. therefore, the accused-petitioners stand discharged of the charges brought against them under sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984. 

10. In Writ Petition No. 21 of 1986 the petitioner was a Jetty Supervisor of the Corporation at the relevant time. He received a charge-sheet dated 27.11.81 under Rule 3(b) and (c) of the Rules of 1976 for misconduct and corruption. He submitted his reply on 23.12.81. The inquiry was held on 20.5.82 and 24.5.82. The Inquiry Officer submitted the inquiry report on 13.8.82. A second show cause notice was served on the petitioner on 2.9.84. The petitioner submitted explanation on 4.10.84. By the impugned order (Annexure-G) the petitioner was removed from the service of the Corporation on 28.10.85. The petitioner submits that more than 120 working days have elapsed between 27.11.81 and 21.7.84 and. therefore, he stands discharged of the charges brought against him under sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984.

11. In Writ Petition No. 33 of 1986 there are two petitioners. The petitioner No. 1 Abul Kalam @ Abul Kalam (II) and the petitioner No. 2 Abdul Jabbar were both Security Guards of the Corporation's Regional Office at Khulna. Both of them were suspended by an Office Order dated 9.11.81. They were served with a charge-sheet dated 14.5.85 (AnnexuresD and D(1) under Rule 3(a), (b) and (d) of the Rules of 1984 for negligence, misconduct and corruption. They replied to the charge-sheet on 30.5.85. It is their case that no action has yet been taken by the respondent- Corporation ever since they filed their replies to the respective charge-sheets. As the petitioners were communicated the charges under the Rules of 1984, the respondent-Corporation had to take a decision within 150 working days from the date they were placed under suspension. As the Rules of 1984 came into force from 21.7.84 the date of suspension will be calculated from 21.7.84. More than 250 working days have elapsed between 21.7.84 and 30.5.85 and. therefore, the accused-petitioners stand discharged of the charges brought against them. 

12. Both M/s. Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Advocate for the petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 83 of 1985 and 137 of 1985 and Abdur Rab (I), learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition Nos. 355 of 1985, 21 of 1986 and 33 of 1986 have submitted that all the petitioners except the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 33 of 1986 were charged under Rule 3 of the Rules of 1976. The petitioners in Writ Petition No. 33 of 1986 have been charged under Rule 3 of the Rules of 1984. In all the charge-sheets in has been conceded that the said Rules of 1976 or 1984 are either being followed or adopted by the respondent-Corporation. In all the charge-sheets the petitioners were asked to show cause why they shall not be dismissed or removed from the services of the Corporation in terms of the relevant Rules of the Rules of 1976 or 1984. The learned Advocates submit that it does not lie in the mouth of the employer now to contend that the Writ petitions against the impugned orders are not maintainable, because the said orders were passed in pursuance of the recommendations of a domestic inquiry which was not held under any statutory Rules. The Rules of 1976, and later on the Rules of 1984, were adopted and followed consistently by the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh. The Corporation cannot now turn back and say that it followed or adopted those Rules only as a handmaid of convenience, as a working arrangement, but no legal right can be founded on those Rules. 


13. Both the learned. Advocates for the petitioners have relied on the case of M.A. Hai -Vs- Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, 32 D.L.R.(A.D.) 46 in support of their submission that the writ petitions are fully maintainable because the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh having adopted the Rules of 1976 and the Rules of 1984 the petitioners have acquired a legal right to enforce those Rules in the writ jurisdiction. 

14. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 83 of 1985 M.A. Hai was the appellant in the case reported in 32 DLR. (A.D)-46. Before the present proceedings were drawn up against him certain proceedings were drawn up against him earlier under Rule 3(b) and (c) of the Rules of 1976 on 6.4.77 and 25.4.77 when he was a store Officer in the Corporation. He showed cause, but the Inquiry Officer found him guilty of negligence and recommended that he be warned. The Corporation, however, removed him from service provisionally and asked him to show cause why the provisional order of removal shall not be confirmed. The petitioner submitted his reply but by order dated 13.4.78 he was removed from the service of the Corporation. The petitioner challenged the said order of removal by filing Writ Petition No. 438 of 1978. He complained that he was not given any personal hearing either by the Inquiry Officer or by the Chairman of the Corporation. Witnesses were examined by the Inquiry Officer in. his absence and he was not given any opportunity to cross-examine them. 

15. The High Court Division in its judgment, reported in 31 D.L.R. 326, held that the Corporation has been following the Rules of 1976 not by any statutory instrument or notification published in the Gazette but by way of a working arrangement. Those Rules cannot be enforced by a Court in case of violation of the terms and conditions of service of the Corporation's officers and employees. The Corporation has not yet made its own service rules in pursuance of the President's Order No. 68 of 1972. The position of the petitioner vis-a-vis his employer is not that of a master and servant. It will be guided by the principles of natural justice. The High Court Division further held that the petitioner need not be heard by the Inquiry Officer or by the Chairman of the Corporation and witnesses need not be examined in presence of the Inquiry Officer and no opportunity need be given to cross-examine the witnesses, because the principles of natural justice do not embrace those rights. 

16. The petitioner M.A. Hai appealed and in reversing the aforesaid decision of the High Court Division, the Appellate Division held in the said reported decision in 32 D.L.R.( AD) 46 that in view of the elaborate proceeding taken under the Rules of 1976, the contentions of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh ought not to have been accepted by the High Court Division.

17. It has not been clearly decided, in our opinion, in the case reported in 32 D.L.R. (A.D.) 46, that the Rules of 1976, followed and adopted by the Corporation, but not statutorily adopted by notification in the official Gazette, are nevertheless enforceable under the writ jurisdiction of this Court, if any Rules of 1976 are violated. The Appellate Division has gone to the extent of holding that a writ petition may be founded on the allegation that the petitioner was removed from service on the basis of a departmental proceeding taken in his absence and on the basis of examining witnesses and recording their statements in his absence and thereby violating the principles of natural justice. 

18. In these Rules, however, we are called upon to decide an issue of a larger dimension. We are called upon to decide, as to whether any violation of the Rules of 1976 or the Rules of 1984 which have not been statutorily adopted by the Corporation can be made the basis of a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

19. Before we answer this question we need to point out that in Writ Petition No 83 of 1985 the petitioner has annexed Annexure-F which is an office circular of the Corporation dated 4.12.84. The Corporation has taken note of sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984 and instructions have been issued in the said circular to complete the disciplinary proceedings within the period specified in the said sub-rule. We have also been given a photostat copy of an office order dated 22.10.86 passed by the Secretary of the Corporation imposing certain punishment against Mr. Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, Senior Executive of the Corporation for failing to complete a departmental proceeding within the time-limit prescribed by sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984. The learned Advocates for the petitioners have argued from Annexure-F and from the aforesaid order dated 22.10.86 that the Rules of 1984 have also been fully adopted by the Corporation including sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 with all its penal consequences. Mr.Kazi A.T. Monwaruddin, learned Advocate for the respondent-Corporation agrees that the Corporation has been following the Rules of 1976 and 1984, but the same is merely a working arrangement. The Corporation has not adopted the said Rules statutorily. 

20. In our view the Corporation was not obliged to follow the Rules of 1976 or 1984 or any Government Rules for that matter, because these Rules give to the Government servants much higher and better rights and remedies in respect of departmental proceedings than the Corporation employees are entitled to. But once the Corporation makes a conscious choice of these better Rules, it holds out a promise to its officers and other employees to the effect that in respect of disciplinary proceedings it means to provide its officers and other employees with some better and higher rights and remedies. Once the Corporation-proceeds against its officers and other employees invoking the said Rules, it is estopped from denying those rights and remedies which are contained in the said Rules at a subsequent stage on the ground that it was merely following a working arrangement. We are of the opinion that the principle of promissory estopped will come into play and the Corporation will be estopped from turning round and saying that its Rules were extra-legal and were founded upon mere convenience. 

21. When the Corporation proceeds against an employee under the Rules of 1976 and 1984 it makes a promise to the employee concerned that he or she will be governed by the said Rules. If the employee acts upon the said promise and submits his or her explanation to the charges then the employee acts in reliance of the promise and alters his or her position. The Corporation would be held bound by the promise and the promise would be entitled to enforce the promise against the Corporation. As Mr. Justice Frankfurter so lucidly enunciated in Vitarelli vs, Seaton (1959) 359 US 535: 3 L Ed 2d 1012: 

"An executive agency must be rigorously held to the stands by which it professes its action to 	be judged 	Accordingly, if dismissal from employment is based on a defined procedure, even though generous beyond the requirements that bind such agency, that procedure must be scrupulously observed 	This judicially evolved rule of administrative law is now firmly established and, if I may add, rightly so. He that takes the procedural sword shall perish with the swords." 

(Quoted in Ramana Dayaram Shetty Vs The International Airport Authority of India and others, A.I.R. 1979 (S.C) 1928). 22. We hold, therefore, that all the writ petitions are fully maintainable. 

23. It has been alternatively argued on behalf of the petitioners that if it is held that the Rules of 1976 and 1984 do not give the petitioners any right to maintain an application under Article 102 of the Constitution then the proceedings themselves are illegal and without jurisdiction because, admittedly, the Government and the Corporation have not framed any Rules or Regulations, and relying upon the cases of M. Noman -Vs- the Dhaka Improvement Trust, 16 D.L.R. (Dhaka) 536 and The District Council of Cornilla -Vs- Dr.M.Khalilur Rahman, 33 D.L.R. 438 it has been contended that when there is no rule there is no power and, therefore, the initiation of the disciplinary proceeding was without jurisdiction. 

24. We may note in passing that in the case of Azizul Mollah -Vs- Taher Ali, 32 D.L.R.(A.D) 65 the Appellate Division has held that it is not impossible to work a statute without rules framed under it, although statute prescribes its framing. In the cases reported in 16 D.L.R. (Dhaka) 536, 33 D.L.R. 438 and 32 D.L.R.(A.D) 65 the requirements of law were such that in the absence of rules a void was created which could only be filled up, in the absence of rules, by imaginative interpretation. In other words, the exercise of statutory power was made subject to rules. In such circumstances it was held in those cases that if there was no rule, there was no power. In the present case, the exercise of power in initiating disciplinary proceedings against its employees the corporation is not required to act subject to rules. Articles 24 and 25 of the President's Order No. 68 of 1972 merely authorised the Government and the Corporation to frame rules or regulations to give effect to the purposes of the said Presidential Order, but the said Articles nowhere say that the Government or the Corporation may execise their powers under the said Order only subject to the said rules arid regulations. Accordingly we hold that in the present cases the Corporation is fully competent to institute disciplinary proceedings against its officers and other employees even though no Rules and Regulations have been framed under Article 24 and 25 of the President's Order No.68 of 1972. 

25. We now proceed to examine whether sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 of the Rules of 1984 is at all applicable to the facts and circumstances of these 5 Rules. 

26. We have already seen that in all the writ petitions the petitioners were served with a charge-sheet or were suspended, either 120 days or 150 days, as the cases may be, before the Rules of 1984 came into force on 21.7.84. The present cases were therefore pending proceedings when the Rules of 1984 came into force. Pending proceedings will be governed by Rule 26(1) and (2) of the Rules of 1984 which are as follows :- 

"26. Repeal and savings.-(I) The Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976.are hereby repealed. 

(2) Such repeal shall not affect the previous operation of the said rules or anything done or any action taken thereunder, and any proceedings under the said rules pending at the commencement of these rules shall be continued, and disposed of as far as may be, in accordance with the provisions of these rules." 

27. The upshot of the provisions of sub-rule (2) of Rule 26 is that all pending proceedings shall be continued and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the Rules of 1984, not in to, but as far as may be. In other words, as many provisions of the Rules of 1984 shall be followed as is possible. 

28. Therefore, in continuing the pending proceedings and disposing them of all efforts should be made to follow the provisions of sub-rule (II) of Rule 7. But can the provisions of sub-rule (II) be followed at all in the present cases? 

29. It is clear that the time limit of 120 working days or 150 days are to be counted from the date of communicating the charges" under these rules" or from the date the employee is placed under suspension, whichever is earlier. All the charges in all the writ petitions were communicated to the petitioners long before the Rules of 1984 came into force. The charges were communicated under the Rules of 1984 in Writ Petition No. 33 of 1986, but the petitioner was suspended on 9.11.8l. The date of suspension is the earlier date. It has been submitted that as soon as the Rules of 1984 came into force on 21.7.84 the words within 120 working days from the date of communicating the charges under these rules "or " within 150 working days from the date the Government servant is placed under suspension" shall be deemed to be the date of coming into force of the Rules of 1984. We are franticly unable to accept this submission for this will amount to rule-making on our part. We cannot read into the Rules what is not there. A legal fiction can be created only.by a statute and it is not open to us to create a legal fiction by interpreting a Rule. If the pending proceedings were to be covered by sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 then clearer words ought to have been employed to bring their cases within the ambit of the said sub-rule either in the said sub-rule itself or in sub-rule (2) of Rule 26. As we read it sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 is only prospective in operation. The period of limitation will be counted only from the dale when the charges are communicated under these rules or within 150 working days from the date the employee is placed under suspension, whichever is earlier. In all the present cases the petitioners were either served with charge-sheets or suspended long before the expiry of 120 working days or 150 working days from the dale of coming into force of the Rules of 1984. Sub-rule (II) of Rule 7 is simply inapplicable in the facts and circumstances of these cases. 

30. In the result all the Rules are discharged but without any order as to costs. 

Mohammad Ismail Uddin Sarker, J - I agree.

End.
