parties:
Sonwar (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Kamal Kha ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued, on an application under section 25 of Small Causes Courts Act, 1887, calling upon the defendant opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 29.5.90 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court and SCC Judge, Sylhet in SCC Suit No. 47 of 1986 should not be set aside.

2. The petitioner instituted SCC Suit No. 3 of 1985 for a decree of eviction of the opposite party from the suit premises which on transfer to the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court and SCC Judge, was renumbered as SCC Suit No. 47 of 1986. The petitioner let out two shops as described in the schedule to the plaint (hereinafter referred to as "the suit premises") to the opposite party in 1966 at a monthly rental of Taka 50.00 and the rent was to be paid within 7 days of the next following month. The opposite party started business of workshop for repairing Baby Taxies, etc. in the suit premises. The opposite party is a habitual defaulter in payment of rent and through neglects and latches, he paid rent up to March, 1983 and thereafter defaulted. The opposite party caused damage to the suit premises by removing the partition wall in between the shop houses and opened a door and a window in the southern side by cutting the wall and by such act the whole structure had been damaged. The petitioner bonafide requires the suit premises for starting a business through his unemployed sons after reconstruction of the whole structure. The petitioner thereafter issued a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 16.8.1984 asking the opposite part to vacate the suit premises on the expiry of 30th September, 1984. The said notice was duly served upon the opposite party by registered post on 18.8.84. In spite of receipt of the notice, the opposite party did not vacate the suit premises and hence the petitioner filed the suit for the relief stated above.

3. The defendant-opposite party having duly appeared contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein he denied all the material allegations made in the plaint and contended, amongst others, that the suit was hit by principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence.

4. His case, in short, was that he made improvement and extension of the suit premises at a cost of Taka 7,500.00 which was to be adjusted from the monthly rent. After some years opposite party changed his business and started a tea stall in the suit premises within the" knowledge" of the petitioner. The opposite party was never a defaulter in payment of rent of the petitioner. The petitioner occasionally visited the suit premises and realised rent for two months, three months, six months and one year at a time and issued receipts in favour of the opposite party. He also incurred an expense of Taka 672.73 paisa for having electric connection in the suit premises. The petitioner relised rent up to March, 1983 and thereafter he did not approach the opposite party for realisation of monthly rent presumably because he owed a substantial sum of money to the opposite party. The opposite party requested the petitioner in the last week of October, 1983 to receive the rent for the period from April to October, 1983 but the petitioner gave evasive reply. Thereafter the opposite party remitted Taka 350.00 as rent for the said period to the petitioner by a money order dated 14.11.83 but the petitioner refused to accept the money order on 17.11.83. Thereafter the opposite party sent arrear rent to the petitioner by money order on three different occasions but the petitioner refused all those money orders and falsely filed the suit to avoid adjustment of Taka 8,177.73 paisa which the opposite party had incurred for making improvement and having electric connection in the suit premises.

5. The learned SCC Judge, on consideration of the evidence, dismissed the suit Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned SCC Judge, the petitioner invoked the revisional jurisdiction of this court and obtained the present Rule.

6. It is admitted that the petitioner let out to the opposite party the suit premises from December, 1966 at a monthly rental of Taka 50.00. It is also not disputed that the opposite party made certain alteration and extension in the suit premises at a certain cost. According to the opposite party, these were done with the consent of the petitioner who agreed to adjust the cost incurred from the monthly rent. But the petitioner denied it and alleged that these are done unauthorisedly without his permission and consent and, as such, there could be no assurance of adjustment of the cost incurred from the monthly rent. The petitioner sought eviction of the opposite party primarily on the ground of habitual default in payment of rent and his bonafide requirement of the suit premises for making provision for employment of his unemployed sons after reconstruction of the entire structure of the suit premises. The finding of fact of the court below that the petitioner does not require the suit premises for his unemployed sons has not been challenged presumably for lack of cogent evidence on this point on the side of the petitioner.

7. It is admitted that the petitioner issued a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 16.8.84 terminating the tenancy of the opposite party on the expiry of 30th September, 1984 and sent the same by registered post which was received by the opposite on 18.8.84. According to the opposite party, he offered the rent for the period from April to October, 1983 to the petitioner in the last part of October, 1983 and on refusal of the petitioner to accept the same he sent the arrear rent of the said period by a money order on 14.11.83 but this was refused by the petitioner on 17.11.83, In spite of refusal of the petitioner to accept the arrear rent sent by money order, the opposite party did not deposit the said rent with the House Rent Control within a fortnight after the refusal of the money order though he subsequently sent the arrear rent by 3 money orders which were all refused by the petitioner as before. Under the Transfer of Property Act, the landlord has a right to terminate the tenancy by giving a notice to quit on the tenant in the manner prescribed under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Premises Rent Control Ordinance has made substantial encorachment into the tenancy law of the country for the purpose of protecting the tenant from ejectment from the tenanted premises and has given the tenant certain safeguards notwithstanding the provision of the Transfer of Property Act or Contract Act.

8. Sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance reads thus:

"(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, 1872, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and perform the conditions of the tenancy."

Sub-section (5) of that section provides that the rent is to be paid within the time fixed in the contract or in the absence of such contract by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable. The opposite party has not remitted the arrear rent for the period from April to October, 1983 or for the subsequent period within 15 days of the next following month and as such he was not entitled to the protection of section 18. The rent receipts Exts. Ka to Ka(35) show payment of rent by the opposite party to the petitioner in lump for the period from December, 1966 to March, 1983 for several months together ranging from 2 to 28 months at a time and the rent was accepted by the petitioner. Mere acceptance of arrear rent is not sufficient to save the opposite party from being a defaulter in payment of rent.

<u>9. Mr. MA Mannan, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, submits that the evidence on record shows that there was an agreement between the landlord and the tenant that the landlord would collect the rent from the tenant at intervals at his convenience and that the said practice continued till March, 1983 and that though the opposite party defaulted in paying rent within the 15th day of the next following month, the landlord shall be deemed to have waived the default and consequently he cannot make it a ground for eviction of the opposite party. In this connection he has referred to the decision in the case of Md. Golam Hossain Vs. Mst. Asia Khatun reported in 40 DLR (AD) 1 where several previous decisions of the Appellate Division were also referred.</u>

10. Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, on the other hand, submits that the opposite party did not make out any case of waiver in the pleadings or in the evidence and in such circumstances the opposite party cannot escape from being defaulter in payment of rent. He has also referred to decisions of the Appellate Division in the case of Ramjan Ali Mistry Vs. Md. Hedayetulla reported in 31 DLR (AD) 183, the case of Profulla Kumar Chakraborty Vs. Anil Proshad Chowdhury & others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 55,' the case of Binning & Co. Bangladesh Ltd. Vs. MIs. Nasirabad Properties Ltd. reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89 and the case of M/s. A Haque and Co. & another Vs. Al-haj Zakir Hossain reported in 40 DLR (AD) 109 in support of his contention that the opposite party, in the facts and circumstances of the case, cannot invoke the plea of waiver.

<u>11. In the instant case there is no written agreement by which the tenancy was created. According to the landlord-petitioner, the opposite party was to pay the rent by the 7th of the following month, but he could not prove that by any cogent evidence. In the absence of any contract to the contrary as to the time of payment of monthly rent, I am of the view that the tenant was liable to pay the monthly rent by the 15th of the next following month as provided in section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. The opposite party has not paid the rent within the time for any month except on 1.11.81 when he paid the rent for 28 months at a time. A tenant is under as obligation to pay rent to the landlord after the same has become due and the landlord was not required to approach the tenant for payment. The non-payment of rent within the 15th of the next month disentitled the opposite party to the protection against eviction for default of payment of rent. The only exception that can take the tenant out of the mischief of the default is waiver. Mere acceptance of arrear rent is not however sufficient to constitute waiver. Whether there has been waiver by the landlord must be gathered from the facts of each case and no standard formula can be laid down. In the case of Ramjan Ali Mistry, 31 DLR (AD) 183 their Lordships observed as under:</u>

<u>"There may be a case of waiver or acquiescence or such supervening facts and circumstances as to make the compliance with the enactment beyond the control of the tenant. However, it will depend on the facts of a particular case to see whether there has been default in the payment of rent in terms of the statute but once the fact is established in terms of the Ordinance, legal consequence flowing therefrom cannot be averted."</u>

<u>In all the decisions of the Appellate Division referred to above except the case of Md. Golam Hossain 40 DLR (AD) 1 the plea of waiver was not accepted in view of the facts and the evidence in those cases. But in the case of Golam Hossain it was found that the evidence that had been led showed that there was an agreement or arrangement between the landlord and the tenant that the Karmachari of the landlord could come and collect the rent. In the instant case the opposite party did not even allege that there was such an agreement between him and the petitioner that the latter would collect the rent at certain intervad at his convenience. There is also no evidence of such agreement as to collection of rent; rather the evidence of opposite party as DW 1 negatived the alleged arrangement. He stated in his evidence that the petitioner used to collect rent in lump as he owed money to him which was incurred for improvement of the suit premises. Sufficient to say that there is absolutely no evidence on record to prove that the opposite party incurred the said expenses for improvement of the suit premises with the consent of the petitioner and that amount was to be adjusted from the monthly rent. The Dakhila Exts. Ka to Ka (35) do not show any adjustment of rent. If the story of improvement with consent of the plaintiff-petitioner would have been true, the opposite party would not have made payment of rent till March, 1983 without adjustment.</u>

12. The learned SCC Judge has not arrived at any definite finding that the opposite party was not a habitual defaulter in payment of rent but he only made some observations that the opposite party paid rent after accumulation of arrears of rent which was accepted by the landlord without objection. Mere acceptance of arrear rent is not sufficient to constitute waiver. The learned SCC Judge has not dealt with the question of waiver so as to bring out the opposite party from the category of habitual defaulter. In view of the pleadings and the evidence in this case, the principle laid down in the decision in the case of Md. Golam Hossain's case is not attracted. The opposite party, it is alleged, tendered rent for the period from April to October, 1983 in the last part of October, 1983, but the petitioner refused to accept the same and thereafter the opposite party remitted the said rent by money order on 14.11.83 which was refused by the petitioner on 17.11.83. Even after petitioner's refusal to accept the rent up to October, 1983, the opposite party did not deposit the rent with the House Rent Control as required by section 19(1) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and thereby made himself a defaulter in payment of rent. The tenant opposite party is not entitled to the protection of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and I, therefore, find that the opposite party is a habitual defaulter in payment of rent and he is liable to be evicted from the suit premises. The decision of the learned court below on the point is not in accordance with law.

13. Mr. MA Mannan further submits that this court in a revision under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act cannot disturb the finding of the fact arrived at by the learned SCC Judge and in support of his contention he has placed his reliance in the case of Abdus Sattar and others Vs. Suresh Chandra Das and others reported in 32 DLR(AD) 170. The learned SCC Judge, as I have already pointed out earlier, did not arrive as any definite finding that the opposite party was not a defaulter in payment of rent and, as such, no question of disturbing the finding of fact arises. The principle laid down in the case of Abdus Sattar referred above has no application in the case before me. In view of my finding that the opposite party was a habitual defaulter in payment of rent, I am of the view that the learned SCC Judge has not decided the case in accordance with law and, as such, the impugned judgment and order cannot be sustained in law.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The suit is decreed on contest against the defendant opposite parties without costs. The petitioner does get khas possession of the suit premises by evicting the opposite party there from.

End.
