case_source: From the judgment and order dated November 26, 1980 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978.
full_judgment:
K. Hossain. C.J:- I have gone through the Judgment written by Ruhul Islam J. in Civil Appeals No. 67 to 70 of 1981 and 88 of 1981, and also the dissenting judgment of Shahabuddin Ahmed J. only in Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981 and I concur with the decision of Ruhul Islam, J.

Fazle Munim J:- T have gone through the judgment of Ruhul Islam, J. with which the learned Chief Justice and Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. have concurred and also the judgment of Shahabuddin Ahmed J. So faras Civil Appeal Nos. 67, 68, 69 and 88 of 1981 are concerned I express my agreement with the views of Ruhul Islam, J. and also concur with his conclusions in this appeal. As regard s Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981. I agree with the conclusion of Shahabuddin Ahmed J. but do not agree with his views on the extent of the Government's discretion in view of the amendment of the Government's Servants Retirement Act, No.XII of 1974 in retiring a Government servant from his service on completion of 25 years of service. With the insertion of the expressions "in the public interest" in section 9(2) of the Act by the Government Servants (Retirement) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1981, the Government's discretion to retire a Government servant on completion of 25 years of service has become justifiable. Whether such order of retirement has been passed in the public interest can now, if challenged, be examined by the court. If after presentation of materials by the Government, the Court is of the opinion that the impugned order has not been passed in the public interest it can declare it to be so. This kind of restriction imposed by the amending Ordinance upon the Government's absolute power to retire a Government servant is commensurate with the need to maintain a sense of dignity and security in the mind of the Government servants. I have nothing more to add.

Ruhul Islam, J:-These five appeals by special leave arise in connection with Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 wherein respondent No.1 Shah Azharuddin Ahmed as the petitioner challenged the order compulsorily retiring hi from service under section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974. The writ petition has been allowed with the consequential declaration as prayed for. In course of the judgment the learned Judges made certain observation and findings and order relating to costs in the cause, which led to filing separate appeals by the persons aggrieved by the findings and the order. Civil Appeal Nos. 67 to fi9 of 1981 have been filed by Mr. Habibullah Khan; Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981 has been filed by the Government of Bangladesh and others; and Civil Appeal No. 88 of 1981 has been filed by Mr. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury.

4. Respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed by filing Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 challenged the legality of the order passed by the Director General of Radio Bangladesh dated October 4, 1978 retiring him from government service under section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 (Act XII of 1974). Respondent's case in short is that he joined the government service with the then All India Radio in March, 1947. After partition of India in 1947 he opted for Pakistan and continued to serve Radio Pakistan at Dacca up to December 1971. Since after independence he continued to serve with Radio Bangladesh.He was promoted to the rank of Superintendent with effect from 1-9-73 and subsequently he was promoted to the rank of an Administrative Officer, which is a Class If gazetted post, with effect from 3-2-77, He was posted in the Directorate of News (News Wing) Radio Bangladesh. While discharging his duties as the Administrative Officer he detected a number of irregularities in the functioning of the office involving huge financial loss to the organization. Some of the irregularities detected by him concerned the Director of News Anisuzzaman Chowdhury (Respondent No. 3). The respondent had to report about the irregularities detected by him to the Director General, Radio Bangladesh. In doing this the respondent incurred extreme displeasure of respondent No. 3 who in retaliation humiliated and harassed the petitioner on a number of occasions in front of his own subordinates. On the order of the Director General a preliminary enquiry was made by Mr. Kamaluddin Ahmed, the then Deputy Director General (N & M) and a report dated 20-578 was submitted by him. The allegations were found to be true. This enraged the Respondent No. 3 so much, that he had Shah Azharuddin Ahmed transferred to the Directorate of External services, Radio Bangladesh with effect from 1-7-78. In the meantime Mr. Habibullah Khan, a brother-in-law of respondent No. 3 took over charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. All on a sudden Shah Azharuddin Ahmed received an order dated 4-10-78 under section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 passed by Mr. M Yahia Khan, the then Director-General, Radio Bangladesh, compulsorily retiring him from service with effect from 5-10-78 without assigning any reason. Shah Azharuddin Ahmed alleged that Mr. Habibullah Khan, the Minister-in-Charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting himself asked the then Director General of Radio Bangladesh to pass the order of retirement of the petitioner. The Director General protested but under pressure from his Minister reluctantly passed the order of retirement. The respondent alleged that the impugned order was malafide as it was passed not in the public interest but only to satisfy the whims of the Minister and his brother-in-law, namely, the respondent No. 3.

5. The Writ petition was contested by the government by filing affidavit-in-opposition, wherein it was stated, inter alia, that the decision was taken to retire the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed under section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, (XII of 1974) with effect from 5-10-78 but he did not make over charge of office in violation of rules and by his action he created obstruction in the functioning of the Government and caused sufferings to the detriment of the public service. In the affidavit-in-opposition it was further stated that the Minister concerned did not pass any such order and the impugned order of retirement was passed by the Director General on examining the petitioner’s record as he completed 25 years of service.

6. The writ petition was heard by a Division Bench, which by the judgment dated 26-11-1980 declared the impugned order to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect. In the judgment the learned Judges made certain ad verse findings against Mr. Habibullah Khan, and arrived at the conclusion that the impugned order of retirement was passed by the Director General of Radio Bangladesh having been directed by the Secretary of .the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting in a malafide manner at the behest of Mr. Habibullah Khan, then in charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Government of Bangladesh. It was mentioned in the judgment that the said Mr. Habibullah Khan was being called upon separately to show cause why he shall not personally pay compensatory costs of the proceedings and compensations to the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed at an estimated amount of Tk. 10,000/-. A suo-motu rule was issued upon Mr. Habibullah Khan asking him to appear before the Court in his personal capacity through an authorized Advocate to show cause as to why he shall not pay an amount of Tk. 10,000/- in cash to Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, "the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978... as costs of the proceeding in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 and compensation for causing sufferings and harassment to the said Shah Azharuddin Ahmed.................."

7. On consideration of the affidavits filed by the parties the learned Judges accepted the case of respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed and found that he was illegally removed from service by invoking the provisions of Section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974, and this "was caused in an unmistakably malafide manner with a palpable bad faith" with the object "to impose exemplary punishment upon the petitioner." The impugned order of retirement dated October 4, 1978 was set aside and the Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Government of Bangladesh and the Director General of Radio Bangladesh were directed to reinstate the respondent in service forthwith with effect from the passing of the impugned order, with further direction that the period upon the date of his joining shall be deemed to be in actual service with all entitlements being admissible to him under the law.

8. The learned Attorney General appearing for the Government of Bangladesh in Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981 submitted that the government having been given the option under, section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 to retire government servants and such option having been exercised in the manner required by law the impugned order of retirement is valid and legal, but the learned Judges on a misconception of the law declared the order illegal and without any lawful authority. He also submitted that the order of retirement itself not having cast any stigma on the career of the respondent, nor having been said to have been passed by way of punishment, the High Court Division committed an error of law in going behind the order and setting aside the impugned order. He further submitted that the finding on the question of malafide which practically provided the basis of the judgment for declaring the impugned order of retirement illegal and without any lawful authority, does not get support from the facts as disclosed in the affidavits.

9. So far as the first contention of the learned Attorney General is concerned, there are sufficient materials to show that the order of retirement was made by way of giving punishment to the respondent and this has been practically admitted in the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the Government; and the learned Judges with refer-nee to the particular statement in the affidavit-in-opposition made the following observation:-

"In the present case in the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the Government Respondent No.1 subsequently on 6th November, 1980 it has been asserted at the bottom of paragraph 5 on page 3 that the provision of section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act No. XII of 1974 was applied in order to impose exemplary punishment upon the petitioner.

The learned Judges further observed that:-

"Since it has already been found hereinbefore that no one can he punished without being proceeded by a proceeding and without being followed by a finding on any specific allegation and that the provision for optional retirement under section 9(2) of the Act XII of 1974 is not a penal provision like the provision for compulsory retirement under clause (b) of sub-rule (3) of Rule 4 of the Government Servants Discipline and Appeal Rules of 1976."

10. In the course of argument the learned Attorney General finding it difficult to press his first point, namely the order of compulsory retirement was not by way of punishment, in view of the clear statement in the affidavit-in-opposition candidly submitted that he would rather press the second point, namely, the finding of malafide is without any basis. On perusal of the affidavits we find that the finding on the question of malafide is not based on materials. In a case where malafide is alleged against any person or authority, the person alleging facts constituting malafide is required to establish it. In the instant case apart from the possibility of Mr. Habibullah Khan in his capacity of Minister in-Charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting taking initiative in the matter of causing retirement of the respondent the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed could not bring any materials to substantiate that Mr. Habibullah Khan took initiative in the matter of taking disciplinary measures against the absentees with the mala fide object of giving exemplary punishment to respondent under the influence of his brother-in-law Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, former Director of News, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The learned Attorney General placed before us the papers from the relevant Government file to show that during the surprise visit of the Minister concerned to the Directorate of External Services, Radio Bangladesh, Dacca a number of-persons including respondent No. 3 were found absent and departmental action was taken against all of them and different punishments were given to them. So far as the case of respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed is concerned, as his record revealed that he was found absent by the Minister concerned, he was retired from service under section 9 (2) of Act XII of 1974 after thoroughly examining his case. According to the learned Attorney General there was no malafide in the matter and the action was taken in the normal course of administration by invoking the power of the government as provided under section 9 (2) of Act XII of 1974.

11. I have given anxious consideration to this aspect of the case and on consideration of the affidavits I am inclined to accept the contention of the learned Attorney General that the finding of malafide by learned Judges of the High Court Division cannot be said to be warranted by the materials on record, and as such the same cannot be sustained.

12. Now let me examine whether the impugned order of retirement is liable to be set aside in the absence of finding of malafide. The materials on record show that even without any finding of malafide the impugned order of retirement is still difficult to sustain. The affidavits reveal that respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed was given the exemplary punishment as he had been found absent by the Minister concerned when be paid a surprise visit to the office where the respondent was the Administrative Officer. On behalf of the government more than one affidavit were filed but not where there is any statement justifying the order of retirement other than on the ground that the respondent was found absent at the time when the Minister paid a surprise visit. The respondent categorically denied that he was absent when the Minister visited his office. He stated that as a matter of fact he “was very much in the office and was in the store room for his usual supervision work at the relevant time when the Hon'ble Minister visited the office." The respondent asserted that nobody informed him that he was marked absent and action was being taken against him. If he knew he could have explained that he was not absent from office but was at the relevant time engaged in the supervision in the store room. The learned Attorney General could not show from record that the retirement was not only for the respondent's absence on the solitary occasion and there were other considerations. It is also not the case of the Government that the respondent was absent for the whole day. According to their case the respondent turned up shortly thereafter. According to the Government the action was taken after due deliberation with a view to enforcing strict discipline in the office. Such justification for taking "exemplary punishment" only on finding the respondent absent for a short period, does not at all appeal to me. The action is undoubtedly arbitrary. Such arbitrary order depriving one of his service cannot be sustained. Section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 does not empower the government to pass such arbitrary order of retirement. There is nothing in the affidavits nor the learned Attorney General could submit that the service record of the respondent was not good. The respondent asserted that there was not a single instance of misconduct on his part prior to the passing of the impugned order of retirement. According to the respondent he was surprised when the order of retirement was given to him at the close of the office hours on 4.10.78 and it was-stated therein that order was to take effect from 5.10.78. He also stated that he was not asked to make over charge to anybody. It is not difficult to guess that placed in such a situation and the order was so sudden that the respondent naturally thought that the order might have been passed malafide at the instance of the Minister as he is a relation of Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, respondent No 3. Of course, it has been found above that this allegation could not be established. In the absence of any materials to justify such drastic action under section 9(2) of Act XII of 1947, the impugned order cannot be sustained.

13. It is true that the law empowers the government to retire a government servant if he has attained the age of 55 years or completed 25 year; of service without assigning any reason but in view of the protection in the Constitution, the authority concerned taking such action must satisfy the Court, when the order is challenged as arbitrary or malafide, that the order was passed in the public interest. In the absence of anything to justify the order of retirement, it is liable to be quashed. Therefore the appeal of the government challenging legality of the judgment and order of the High Court Division must fair.

14. Now let me take up Civil Appeals Nos. 67, 68 and 69 of 1981 filed by Mr. Habibullah Khan, which are directed against the adverse findings against Mr. Habibullah Khan, the suomotu rule and the order imposing compensatory cost against him. The judgment of the High Court Division shows that the learned Judges concluded their judgment with the following statement:

"Since it has been found that the impugned order was passed by the Director General of Radio Bangladesh having been directed by the Secretary of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting in a mala fide manner at the behest of Mr. Habibullah Khan, the then Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Government of Bangladesh on account of the petitioner's detection of administrative irregularities with regard to the use of transport and telephone by the then Director of News. Mr. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury being the brother of the wife of the aforesaid the then Minister-in-charge of the Information and Broadcasting, the said Mr. Habibullah Khan is being called upon separately to show cause why he shall not personally pay compensatory costs of the proceeding and compensation to the petitioner herein at an estimated amount of Taka ten thousand only."

15. After delivering judgment the learned Judges issued a suomotu rule calling upon the appellant Mr. Habibullah Khan to show cause in the following term:

"Let a suomotu rule issue calling upon Mr. Habibullah Khan, a member of the President's Council of Ministers, a former Minister in charge of the Ministry of information and Broadcasting and at present Minister in charge of the Ministry of Jute Affairs of the Government of Bangladesh, to appear before this Court in his private and personal capacity through an authorized Advocate to show cause why he shall not pay an amount of Tk. 10,000/- (ten thousand) in cash to Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, Administrative Officer in the External Services Directorate of Radio Bangladesh, Dacca being the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 in view of the finding of this Court that the said petitioner was made to retire under section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 by the Director General of Radio Bangladesh by its impugned order dated 4th October, 1978 upon a direction of the Secretary in the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting at the behest of Mr. Habibullah Khan, the then Minister in charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Government Of Bangladesh in a malafide manner on account of detection by said Shah Azharuddin Ahmed of certain administrative irregularities with regard to official transport and telephone by the then Director of News Mr. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, being the brother of the wife of the said Mr. Habibullah Khan, the then Minister in charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Government of Bangladesh as costs of the proceeding in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 and compensation for causing sufferings and harassment to the said Shah Azharuddin Ahmed or pass such other or further, order or orders as this Court may seem fit and proper.

This Rule is made returnable on 12th January, 1981 to come up on the top of the list.

This Rule shall be heard by this Bench since it arises out of, Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 being disposed of by this Bench on 26th November, 1980."

16. The appellant filed his affidavits showing cause in obedience to the Court's direction, explaining that he was not personally responsible for causing retirement of Shah Azharuddin Ahmed as alleged against him. He stated that in the course of his surprise visit to the Directorate of External Services, Radio Bangladesh, Dhaka, the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed along with several others were found absent from the office; and for the sake of improving discipline in the office, it was decided that some action should be taken against them. The Secretary and the Director General of Radio Bangladesh on examining the respective personal files of the delinquents decided as to what action should be taken against each of them. He pointed out that at the relevant time the said Anisuzzaman Chowdhury was no longer in the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting as he had been transferred to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs at the request of the said Ministry vide Ministry of Foreign Affairs Memo No. S.S.(1)-17/4/77 dated 8-8-78 for placing the services of Anisuzzaman Chowdhury at the disposal of the Foreign Ministry, and after his posting in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Anisuzzaman Chowdhury handed over charge of the, office of the Director of News of Radio Bangladesh on 31-8-78, and subsequently he was posted in the Embassy of Bangladesh in Islamabad, Pakistan.

17. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant Mr. Hgbibullah Khan in Civil Appeal Nos. 67, 68 and 69 of 1981 submitted with reference to the different findings in the judgment of the High Court Division that the appellant was found responsible for causing the order of retirement of the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed passed; and that the learned Judges after making several adverse findings against the appellant on the question of malafide alleged by the respondent, arrived at the conclusion that the impugned order was passed by the Director General, Radio Bangladesh having been directed by the Secretary of the relevant Ministry in a malafide manner at the behest of the appellant an account of detection of administrative irregularities of his brother-in-law Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, Director of News, by the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed; and that this adverse finding against the appellant was made although he was not made a party in the proceeding. The learned Counsel submitted that judgment was given against the appellant and pointing out from the concluding portion of the judgment that it was only a belated attempt to regularize the order awarding compensatory cost personally by issuing a suomotu rule against the appellant after disposal of the writ petition. According to the learned Counsel, separate proceeding was started only to decide whether the appellant should personally pay compensatory costs of the proceeding and compensation to the respondent at an estimated sum of Tk. 10,000/- already fixed in the judgment; and that the subsequent proceeding beginning from very issuance of the suomotu rule and its ultimate disposal is stained with judicial bias and it was also in violation of the principle of natural justice. The learned Counsel further submitted that the subsequent proceedings initiated with the suomotu rule in the instant case is bad "in law inasmuch as it lacked legal sanction.

18. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that subsequent proceedings started by the Court with the suomotu rule could not legalize the illegalities committed in passing the judgment on the question of malafide against the appellant; and that the findings must be quashed. The learned Counsel argued that in a proceeding arising from an application under Article 102 of the Constitution a person who has not been impleaded as a party to the proceedings cannot be proceeded against separately with the object of making him liable to pay costs of the proceedings in the writ petition and pay compensatory costs for causing sufferings and harassment to the person who initiated the writ proceedings. The learned Counsel raised a preliminary objection about the competency of the High Court Division to issue suomotu rule after disposal of the writ petition, only to determine the quantum of the appellant’s liability to pay personally the compensatory costs to respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed. Mr. Ahmed submitted that the Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 was disposed of on 26-11-80 and this news came out in different daily newspapers of the country, and subsequently the appellant was served with the suomotu rule. According to the learned Counsel the subsequent proceeding was nothing but an attempt to regularize the judgment dated 26-11-80 finding the appellant responsible for taking the action against the respondent retiring him from service and his liability to pay cost of the proceedings to this respondent. In this context the learned Counsel further submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court Division committed an error of law in awarding costs of the writ petition against the appellant on the assumption that it was a pending proceeding and all the reasons given in the judgment to justify the action impugned herein are not only untenable but also contrary to the record and actual facts, because the writ petition was finally disposed of on 26-11-80 awarding costs of Tk.10,000/- as compensatory costs against the appellant, who was not a party in that proceedings, but subsequently, as the judgment shows, a suomotu rule was issued treating it a pending matter, and if is alleged that the Rule was issued not in open court but in the chamber giving the date as 26-11-80. The judgment of the Court resulting from the suomotu rule was delivered on 13-4-81 it was made supplementary to the judgment dated 26-11-80. According to the learned Counsel this was just a device adopted by the Court in attempting to regularize the subsequent proceedings having no sanction of law.

19. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that the suomotu rule was issued by the Court only to determine why the appellant Mr. Habibullah Khan shall not pay an amount of Tk. 10,000/- in cash to Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, the petitioner in writ Petition No. 900 of 1978, his liability to pay compensatory cost had already been fixed in the judgment delivered on 26-11-80. The rule itself indicates that it was issued to make the appellant Mr. Habibullah Khan pay compensatory cost of Tk. 10,000/- to the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 90Q of 1978 in view of the findings of the Court in the judgment in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 which had already been delivered, wherein liability of the appellant Mr. Habibullah Khan for causing illegal retirement of respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed under, section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 was determined. The judgment contains a clear finding to the effect that the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed was retired from service by the Director General of Radio Bangladesh upon a direction from the Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting issued at the behest of Mr. Habibullah Khan in a malafide manner on account of the detection by said Shah Azharuddin Ahmed of certain administrative irregularities regarding use of official transport and telephone by the then Director of News Mr. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, a brother-in law of Mr. Habibullah Khan.

20. In the judgment dated 26-11-80 there are several findings imputing mala fide on the appellant, one of which is quoted here:

"In such circumstances when it has not been disputed that the Director of News Mr. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury is the brother of wife of Mr. Habibullah Khan, the then Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and when it is already on record to show that the proceeding against the petitioner was initiated at the behest of the then Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting Mr. Habibullah Khan, it is amply dear that the premature retirement of the petitioner invoking the optional provision of section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 was caused in an unmistakably malafide manner with a palpable bad faith."

<u>21. On perusal of the affidavits filed by the parties I find it difficult to arrive at the same finding. It is true that Mr. Habibullah Khan as the Minister-in charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Government of Bangladesh paid a surprise visit to the office of the Directorate of External Services Radio Bangladesh on 14-9-78 and he found some of the officers absent and the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed was also noted as an absentee. Proceeding was started against all the absentees and some disciplinary measure was taken. However, action was taken against Shah Azharuddin Ahmed also, but in his case the order was for his compulsory retirement. It is not the case of the respondent that he was singled out from the absentees for the purpose of punishing him. In the affidavit it has been explained that Shah Azharuddin Ahmed was retired from service on consideration of his age and length of service already put in. It has been already noted above that the active part alleged to have been played by the appellant has been categorically denied and the affidavits do not warrant such allegation. I have no doubt that the findings imputing malafide on the appellant are liable to be quashed, firstly, on the ground, that those were made in the absence of the person against whom malafide was alleged; and secondly, on the ground that the materials on record do not warrant such finding, in other words the allegation of malafide has not been established. If at the hearing of the writ petition the Court was of the opinion that the affidavits filed by the parties sufficiently showed that Mr. Habibullah Khan Was directly responsible for causing compulsory retirement of Shah Azharuddin Ahmed under the influence of his brother-in-law Mr. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, the Rules of the Court provide that in such a case the Court should adjourn the hearing of the writ petition and direct service of notice on such person. Rule 9 of Chapter A in Appendix IV to the Rules of the High Court of Judicature Vol. I provide that if at the hearing of the application the Court is of opinion that any person who ought to have been served with notice of the application has not been so served, the Court may order that notice may also be served on such person and adjourn the hearing upon such terms as the Court may consider proper. The learned Judges instead of following the Rule completed the bearing of the writ petition and delivered judgment. In view of the facts and circumstances the findings imputing malafide on the appellant cannot be sustained. Therefore, the objectionable findings set out above and the observations made in the judgment dated 26-11-80 are quashed.</u>

22. The rule issued unmistakably shows that subsequent proceedings was started not with a view to regularizing the findings made against the appellant but to make him pay costs of Tk. 10,000/- of the proceedings to the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978. The judgment delivered by the Court in the suomotu rule concluded as follows:

"In such circumstances it would appear that Shah Azharuddin Ahmed was duly compensated for his loss of service during the period in question and as such there is no occasion for any further order for awarding any compensation in that regard. In that view Mr. Habibullah Khan, a member of the President's Council of Ministers, a former Minister in charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting at the relevant time and at present Minister in charge of the Ministry of Jute Affairs of the Government of Bangladesh, is now therefore personally directed to pay only the costs of the proceedings taken in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 personally to Shah Azharuddin Ahmed. While awarding this costs the quantum thereof requires to be assessed properly before an appropriate authority of this court in presence of the concerned parties in accordance with the items enumerated in Rule 15 relating to writ petition as contained in Appendix IV(A.) of the High Court Rules. Since a writ petition before a High Court Division is an original proceeding under the Constitution it would be proper to apply the procedure relating to the taxing of costs in the original side of, the High Court Division. The Registrar of the Supreme Court being the Taxing Officer in the Original Side of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, is therefore. directed to assess the costs incurred by Shah Azharuddin Ahmed in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 in a proceeding upon an appropriate application by the said Shah Azharuddin Ahmed and tax the same against Mr. Habibullah Khan as aforesaid in accordance with Rule, 15 relating to writ petitions as contained in Appendix IV (A) of the High Court Rules and the relevant provisions relating to taxing of costs in the Rules of the Original Side of the High Court.

With the aforesaid observations and direction this rule is made absolute accordingly. This judgment in this rule being complementary to the judgment of this Bench made on,6th November, 1980 in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 is made supplementary thereto."

The course adopted by the learned Judges, according to the learned Counsel, is not supported by the rules of procedure. Since the appellant was not made a party in the writ petition on the basis of the adverse findings he could not be saddled with the costs of the proceedings. He submitted that the Bench after delivering judgment in the writ petition became functus officio in the matter and as such the question of payment of compensatory costs personally by the appellant could not be determined by initiating a separate proceeding by issuing a suomotu rule by the Court. He submitted that this course, that is, issuance of a suomotu rule for making the appellant personally pay costs of proceeding of the writ petition and compensation to the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed for causing sufferings and harassment to him, is not warranted by any rule or practice followed by the Court. From the judgment it does not appear that the learned Judges adequately dealt with this question although competency of the Court to issue suomotu rule was specifically raised in the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the appellant; and according to Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, it was also argued before the Court. From the judgment dated 13-4-81 it appears that the learned Judges were of the view that rule 15 by implication provides "a very wide authority to the Court to award costs against any party in any manner it considers fit and proper for the ends of justice in the circumstance of a particular case." The learned Judges however being conscious about their limitation answered the question stating that so far as the costs that may be awarded against any party is concerned, it is to be determined on consideration of the facts and circumstances of each case. It appears that the learned Judges were aware that Rules 14 and 15 are the only provisions relating to awarding or costs. They observed as follows:-

"The only limitations inevitably would be that no cost shall be awarded against any party finally if such party was not a party in the concerned writ petition unless such party is given a notice to show cause why such party shall not be saddled with costs and the reply thereto is heard and considered in due course."

23. The learned Judges further observed that "the writ petition was disposed of on the merit of the case but it remained partially pending with regard to awarding costs of the proceeding which, according to the learned Judges, would only be finally disposed of when this soumotu rule, is disposed of." In this context they referred to the concluding portion of the judgment dated 26.11.80 to show that the matter relating to awarding of costs in the said proceeding remained pending for which a separate suomotu rule was issued upon the appellant and such rule was in continuation of the proceeding taken in the writ petition. According to the learned Judges, the suomotu rule was limited only to the issue of awarding costs against a particular party. In conclusion the learned Judges observed as follows:-

"Thus the present suomotu rule being in continuation of Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 with regard to awarding of the costs against a particular party,may be considered as a pending proceeding under the aforesaid Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978."

In this connection the learned Judges referred to Rule 9 relating to writ petition as contained in Appendix IV (A) which read as under :-

"If at the hearing of the application, the court is of opinion that any person who ought to have been served with notice of application, has not been so served, the court may order that notice may also be served on such person, and adjourn the hearing upon such terms as the court may consider proper."

It appears that the learned Judges sought to derive authority from the above mentioned Rules, that is, rules 9, 14 and 15 to justify the issuance of the suomotu rule after disposal of the writ petition, The learned Judges without following rule 9 disposed of the writ petition by a lengthy judgment on 26.11.80 giving all the findings on the question of malafide, and, thereafter, according to the appellant, after a few days, suomotu rule was issued with the date as 26.11.80, that is, the date of the judgment in Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978.

<u>24. It has been already found on consideration of affidavits filed by the parties that the allegations of malafide made against the appellant are not well established and the Court's findings on these allegations cannot be sustained. The Court had already given its decision on the question of malafide alleged against the appellant, and the suomotu rule issued by the Court only provided the appellant with an opportunity to show cause why he should not pay compensatory cost of Tk. 10,000/- to the respondent, Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, because his liability to pay personally the cost to the respondent had already been determined. The judgment entered in the suomotu rule has been made supplementary to the judgment in the writ petition. I am constrained to say that the course adopted by the learned Judges was nothing but a belated attempt to regularize the irregular procedure followed in disposing of the writ petition.</u>

<u>25. Rule 15 of Chapter A in Appendix IV provides that where costs are awarded to a party, such costs, unless otherwise directed, shall include the court-fees paid on the petition and other documents, the costs of making of application, affidavit etc. the costs of service of notices, directions, orders, etc. as prescribed under rule 14 and the Advocate's fee. This rule provides no authority for the course followed by the learned Judges in awarding costs against the appellant by initiating suomotu a separate proceeding after disposal of the writ petition.</u>

26. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed rightly submitted that rule 9 clearly provides that if in the opinion of the Court the appellant ought to have been served with notice of the writ petition and since no notice was served upon him, only course open to the Court was to adjourn the hearing and issue direction for service of notice of the writ petition upon the appellant. There is no dispute that all the relevant findings as regards the allegations of direct involvement of the appellant in causing compulsory retirement of the respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, were made in the judgment delivered on 26.11.80. This is evident from the following observation:-

“It would be proper to observe that the Writ Petition No 900 of 1978 was disposed of so far it related to the adjudication about the legality of the impugned order and action of the Government in causing the retirement of Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, when it was found by the Court that such impugned order was passed at the behest of the then Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, a separate suomotu rule was issued by the Court upon such Minister calling upon him to show cause as to why he shall not pay personally costs and compensation to Shah Azharuddin Ahmed on account of such writ petition."

The observation shows that the learned Judges wanted to say that so far as disposal of the writ petition was concerned it was not disposed of on 26-11-80, but it was finally disposed of with the disposal of the suomotu rule, that is, on 13-4-81.

<u>27. I fail to appreciate the reasoning’s given by the learned Judges to support the initiation of a separate proceeding in the absence of any prayer from any quarter, and that too after making the rule in the writ petition absolute. Ongoing through the judgments dated 26-11-80 and 13-4-81 it becomes clear that the view taken by the learned Judges in the matter of issuance of suomotu rule after disposal of the writ petition is wrong and lacks sanction of any authority. It is true that the question of awarding costs was not finally decided by the Court in the judgment dated 26-11-80, which concluded with the statement that "Mr. Habibullah Khan is being called upon separately to show cause why he shall not personally pay compensatory costs of the proceeding and compensation to the petitioner herein at an estimated amount of Taka ten thousand only." The above statement clearly shows that the appellant's liability to pay costs had already been determined and only the quantum of the cost was to be determined, and this was done by issuing the suomotu rule. In an appropriate case the Court is competent to award costs against a stranger even in the absence of any prayer from the party, but that must be done according to the Rules of the Court. If the learned Judges after hearing the parties found themselves so much impelled by the sense of doing justice to the person who suffered on account of passing of the illegal order at the behest of the appellant, the proper course would have been to adjourn the hearing of the writ petition with direction to serve its copy upon the appellant who was considered responsible for the passing of the impugned order. The question for consideration is not whether-in a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution costs of the proceeding can be awarded against a stranger, but the question for consideration is whether liability to pay costs to the party in whose favour writ petition is decided, can by determined by starting a separate proceeding against a person not served with notice of the writ petition before its hearing concluded and judgment delivered. Another question has arisen on the facts of this case, that is, whether the liability to pay costs of the proceedings by a stranger could be determined by issuing a suomotu rule by the Court? There is sufficient force in the argument of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed that after delivering the judgment in the writ petition the Court became functus officio, and although the question of payment of costs by the appellant was kept open as the concluding portion of the judgment dated 26-11-80 shows, but this statement, in the absence of any legal sanction, would not justify issuance of the suomotu rule for determining the appellant's liability to pay compensatory costs to the respondent.</u>

<u>28. Authority for making a stranger liable to pay costs of the proceedings in writ petition cannot be found by construing Rule 15. As per Rule 14 costs is in the discretion of the Court, but it cannot be read to contain the authority to award costs against a stranger. In view of the specific rules in respect, of costs, that is, rules 14 and 15 the relevant sections 35 and 35A of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be referred to for providing the Court's power to award costs in writ petitions. Section 35A provides the power of the court to award compensatory costs. The powers as provided in sections 35 and 35A of the Code of Civil Procedure do not authorize normally awarding of costs against a person who is not a party to the suit, but in view of the language of section 35 it has been held in some cases that in exceptional cases the court may award costs, even against a stranger provided he is given an opportunity of being heard. Such bearing of course must be in the suit or proceeding itself and not after disposal of the suit or proceeding and then starting a separate proceeding for the purpose. The language of section 35 of the Code is wide enough to empower the court to award costs against a stranger, but it is subject to the conditions as indicated above. Sub-section (1) of section 35 reads as under:-</u>

<u>"35.-(1) Subject to such conditions and limitation as may be prescribed, and to the provisions of any law for the time being in force, the costs of and incident to all suits shall be in the discretion of the court and the court shall have full power to determine by whom or out of what property and to what extent such costs are to be paid, and to give all necessary directions for the purposes aforesaid. The fact that the Court has no jurisdiction to try the suit shall be no bar to the exercise of such powers."</u>

<u>29. The discretion as the above noted provision shows, is very wide, but in spite of that the provision cannot be construed to say that it empower the court to award costs against a stranger without giving him an opportunity of being heard.</u>

<u>30. It has been held that the adverse findings against the appellant in the judgment dated 26-11-80 cannot be sustained, because those were made in the absence of the appellant In the absence of those adverse findings there could not be any occasion, far less, raising the question of payment of compensatory costs to the respondent. Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent Shah Azharuddin Ahmed candidly submitted before us that his client was never keen to get costs of the proceedings from the Minister and so the question of his client claiming costs from the appellant did not arise. In this context the learned Advocate informed the court that his client Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, during pendency of the appeal, has gone on leave preparatory to retirement. In consideration of all these facts I am constrained to hold that the learned Judges of the High Court Division exceeded the judicial norms in their anxiety to do justice to the person aggrieved. They neither followed any practice or rule of the, Court in issuing a suomotu rule against the appellant nor they cared to follow the principles of natural justice while making the adverse findings against the appellant on the question of malafide alleged against him. The question of awarding costs is no doubt a matter of discretion of the Court, but such discretion must be exercised judiciously and in accordance with law or at least the practice followed by the Court. In that view of the matter the judgment dated 13-4-81 must be set aside.</u>

31. In Civil Appeal No. 88 of 1981 the appellant Anisuzzaman Chowdhury made a grievance against the findings and observations in the judgment dated 26-11-80 adversely affecting him when these are totally unwarranted by the materials on record. Anisuzzaman Chowdhury was a Director of News, Radio Bangladesh before he was deputed to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs with effect from 1-9-78 for training in anticipation of his posting in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and in due course he was posted in the Bangladesh Embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan. Mr. Habibullah Khan, the then Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting paid a surprise visit to the External Services and Transportation Services of the Radio Bangladesh on 14-9-78 at 8-30 A.M. and found some officers absent. Shah Azharuddin Ahmed was one of the absentees. Shah Azharuddin Ahmed alleged that at the behest of Mr. Habibullah Khan, a relation of the appellant, Director General of Radio Bangladesh by his order dated 4-10-78 caused compulsory retirement of Shah Azharuddin Ahmed with effect from 5-10-78. The fact that at the relevant time Anisuzzaman Chowdhury was no longer posted in the External Services of the Directorate of Radio, Bangladesh, and he had already joined in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, was not taken into consideration by the learned Judges while finding that Mr. Habibullah Khan must have acted with the ulterior object of punishing Shah Azharuddin Ahmed under the influence of his brother-in-law Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, because of the animus that grew between Shah Azharuddin Ahmed and Anisuzzaman Chowdhury as a result of the report of Shah Azharudnin Ahmed against Anisuzzaman Chowdhury pointing out some irregularities in the use of telephones, cars, etc. The other aspect which the learned Judges missed when making the findings and observations adverse against Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, is that the materials on record at the most showed that Mr. Habibullah Khan might have taken initiative in the matter of causing retirement of Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, but neither the materials on record nor the circumstances mentioned in the affidavits, lend support to the allegation that. Mr. Habibullah Khan took the initiative in the matter under the influence of Anisuzzaman Chowdhury. On careful consideration of the materials on record I am led to the conclusion that adverse findings and observations are more the product of speculation and conjecture than on consideration of facts. Mere suspicion that the personal interest of Anisuzzaman Chowdhury might have influenced Mr. Habibullah Khan to take initiative in the matter of causing retirement of Shah Azbaruddin Ahmed cannot justify the adverse findings. The very fact that Anisuzzaman Chowdhury was no longer in the Directorate of External Services of Radio Bangladesh and the report submitted by Mr. Kamaluddin Ahmed, Deputy Director General of News of Radio, Bangladesh was still pending enquiry by the Director General of Radio, Bangladesh is sufficient to take away the stings from the attack made against Anisuzzaman Chowdhury directly or indirectly.

32. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate on Record appearing for Anisuzzaman Chowdhury rightly pointed out from various affidavits that there was no direct allegation against Anisuzzaman Chowdhuy that he was in any way responsible for causing retirement of Shah Azharuddin Ahmed. According to him, the adverse findings are absolutely unwarranted in the face of the materials on record, and as such those cannot be sustained. On perusal of the record I find much substance in the contention of the learned Advocate and I find that the adverse findings made against Anisuzzaman Chowdhury cannot be sustained.

33. In the result Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981 is dismissed. Civil Appeal No. 67 of 1981 of Habibullah Khan allowed and the adverse findings made against him in the judgment dated 26-11-80 are quashed. Civil Appeal No. 88 of 1981 preferred by Anisuzzaman Chowdhury is allowed and the ad verse findings made against him in the judgment dated 26-11-80 are also quashed. Civil Appeal Nos. 68 and 69 of 1981 preferred by Habibullah Khan are allowed and the suo motu rule No. 4 of 1980 and the judgments dated 13-4-81 are set aside. I make no order as to costs in any of the appeals.

34. Badrul Haider Chowdhury J:-I have had the advantage of going through the judgment written by my learned brother Ruhul Islam J. in Civil Appeal Nos. 67 to 70 of 1981 and 88 of 1981 and also the dissenting judgment of my learned brother Shahabuddin Ahmed J. only in Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981 and I concur with the decision of Ruhul Islam J.

35. Shahabuddin Ahmed. J,- I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Ruhul Islam, J disposing of these five appeals. Except in the case of Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981. I agree with his views and concur with his conclusion that those four appeals, namely Civil appeals Nos. 67, 68, 69 and 88 should be allowed. But in respect of Civil Appeal No. 70 of 1981, I am of the opinion that this appeal also should be allowed, the impugned order of the High Court be set aside and the Writ Petition giving rise to it be dismissed. Reasons for this opinion are given below.

36. As has been stated in detail in the elaborate judgment of my learned brother the matter arises from Writ Petition No. 900 of 1978 filed by the respondent. Shah Azharuddin Ahmed challenging government's order retiring him from service on completion of his 25 years of service under section 9 (2) of Act XII of 1974 This section, as it now stand amended, empowers the government to retire a government servant at any time after he has completed 25 years of service 'in the public interest', 'without assigning any reason' on allowing him full pension and other service benefits, admissible under the "Rules. Respondent alleged that the order was malafide having been passed at the instance of the Minister whose brother-in-law, namely Anisuzzaman Chowdhury, another employee of the same Directorate, had some animus against him. The High Court Division accepted this allegation of 'malafide' to be wholly true, allowed the Writ Petition and declared the order of retirement invalid. Upon hearing the learned Attorney-General representing appellant No. 1, the Government of Bangladesh, and also Mr. Nurul Huq, learned Advocate-on Record for the respondent, I find that the allegation of malafide is not at all proved, and on this point I fully agree with my learned brother that 'the findings of malafide by the learned Judges of the High Court Division not being warranted by the materials on record cannot be sustained". If the allegation of malafide falls through, the impugned order of the High Court Division which was based upon a finding of malafide necessarily falls to the ground and consequently the order of retirement must stand.

<u>37. Mr. Nurul Huq contends that even if the High Court Division's order setting aside the government's order of retirement cannot be defended on the ground of malafide, it may be defended on the ground that it is 'arbitrary'. An arbitrary order means an order passed not in accordance with rules and procedures or according to established practices but is made whimsically without due consideration of material facts. On perusal of the order of retirement, Ext. 'D', it is found to be within the corners of law, namely, section 9 (2), An order when it is covered by the terms of a statutory instrument and passed by or under the authority of the government can in the absence of bad faith, be hardly assailed as 'arbitrary'. Secondly, every action of government must be regarded as having been taken bonafide until and unless the contrary is established. On this view I am supported by a decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Sai Mohammad Vs. West Pakistan, P.L.D.1958 S.C. 181. In the instant case the Minister paid a surprise visit to the External Services Section of the Directorate and found as many as eighteen (18) employees absent at 8.30 a.m., whereas the office work started at 7.30. a.m. The Minister noted down the names of all those absentees and directed that exemplary punishment should be awarded them. Respondent Azharuddin was one of those absentees. It appears from the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the Government in the Writ Petition that show-cause notices were served against all of them excepting Azharuddin and upon hearing their explanations some of them were given minor punishment by way of warning and others were let off. In the case of Azharuddin, the Minister directed that he should be retired according to law as he completed 25 years of service and was eligible for pension whereupon a file was started according to normal procedure and was disposed of in due course. The order of retirement was passed under the signature of the appropriate authority, namely, the Director General. It has been contended that though 18 employees were found absent only respondent Azharuddin was singled out for retirement. This argument is misconceived being based on ignorance of the broad fact that of these 18 employees only Azharuddin completed 25 years of service and came within the ambit of section 9(2). By unauthorized absence the respondent rendered himself liable for disciplinary action but to take or not to take disciplinary action under Rules against a government servant is a matter which lies absolutely within the discretion of the government. In the case of a government servant who has completed 25 years of service, 'the authorities may not take disciplinary measures but may retire him from service allowing him pensionary benefits if so considered necessary in the public interest. The authorities may even start proceedings against him on a given charge but thereafter may drop the proceedings and proceed under section 9(2) to retire him. In what case a proceeding should be drawn and in what case retirement should be resorted to, is a matter which lies within the absolute discretion of the authorities. The contention that, of the 18 persons only respondent was chosen for punishment is not at all tenable.</u>

<u>38. It has been next contended that the respondent has been punished under the colour of retirement and that this punishment having been awarded without any show-cause notice is violative of Article 135 of the Constitution. This contention is also totally misconceived, for retirement with full pensionary benefits after completion of 25 years of service is not a punishment nor does it contain any stigma and it is altogether different from 'dismissal', 'removal', or 'compulsory retirement' which are different kinds of punishment as specifically described in rule 3 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have observed that "the government admitted in their affidavit-in-opposition" that this retirement was ordered as an "exemplary punishment" as the Minister directed that the respondent should be given exemplary punishment for his unauthorized absence. This observation is also found to be based on misappreciation of the true import of the Minister's order on the spot that the absentees should be given exemplary punishment. When a higher officer makes a surprise visit to a section of his office and finds glaring irregularities or instances of breach of discipline he usually expresses his utter dissatisfaction in strong language threatening that drastic action would be taken against the persons at fault. Such statement should be understood as direction for initiating appropriate disciplinary measures according to law. Even if the respondent's retirement in this case has been referred to as an 'exemplary punishment' in the office file, still this action will not be a punishment. For retirement under section 9(2) which may be ordered "at any time" and "without showing any reason" is never a punishment. The impugned order Ext. 'D' shows that he has been retired under section 9 (2) of Act XII of 1974. The record shows that the case of retirement of respondent was initiated and dealt with in accordance with the normal procedure and the order was passed in accordance with law. How the question of the order being arbitrary can arise? The only ground to assail it was the ground of malafide in that the Minister allegedly acted at the instance of his brother-in-law, who was Director, News, when a dispute arose between the Director, News, and the respondent who was Administrative Officer in the same office about a year before the order of retirement. This matter has been set out in detail in the judgment of my learned brother Ruhul Islam, J, and as such it need not be repeated again. Suffice it to say that the respondent, an officer of the same Directorate, reported some irregularities committed by the Director in the use of office transport and residential telephone whereupon an enquiry was held and that because of this report this Director allegedly harboured a grudge which led to this retirement. But the record also shows that in spite of the enquiry the result of which has not yet been officially published, the Director was deputed to the Foreign Ministry which gave him a foreign assignment in higher rank and he was not in the Directorate of the respondent when the Minister paid a surprise visit to his office. Excepting the fact that the Director, Ashrafuddin was Minister's brother-in-law allegedly harbouring a grudge against the respondent about a year ago, there is nothing to prove that the Minister had acted malafide in the matter of respondent's retirement. As already observed, when any action of the government is found to have been taken in accordance with law and there was no malafide therein, it cannot be assailed as arbitrary. It is argued that the order was taken 'suddenly' without affording any opportunity to the respondent to submit explanation. When law does not require the government to give any notice or assign any reason for the retirement, government's action cannot be assailed as sudden, hasty or arbitrary. Such retirement being provided for by law, the respondent is supposed to know that as soon as he has completed 25 years of service, he is liable to be retired at any time without being shown any reason in the same way as he may himself opt for retirement under section 9, (1) at any time and without assigning any reason after completion of twenty five years of service. When the governments propose to take action under section 9(2) such action can be taken only" in the public interest."</u>

<u>39. It may be mentioned here that when the order of retirement in this case was made on October 4,1978, the provision as to "public interest" was not there in section 9(2) of the Act XII of 1974, In the case of Dr. Nurul Islam Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 33 D.L.R. 201 (A.D), this Court declared section 9(2) invalid being violative of Article 27 of the Constitution since in the absence of any guideline for selecting a government servant for the retirement this section was discriminatory. The President thereafter, on 24 July 1981, promulgated the Government Servants (Retirement) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1981, Ordinance VI of 1981, which amended section 9(2) of Act XII of, 1974 with retrospective effect from 1974. The amendment brought in the provision" if it considers necessary in the public interest so to do". The Ordinance further included a validation clause which validated all orders of retirement under section 9(2) made before the promulgation of the Ordinance. This clause provides, among other things, that notwithstanding anything to the contrary can tamed in any other law in force or in any judgment of a court "all orders of retirement made before the commencement of this Ordinance shall be deemed to be, and to have always been, made validly, lawfully and in the public interest". By virtue of this amendment of section 9(2) along with the validation clause, the order of the respondent's retirement is deemed to have been made in the public interest. Validity of this validation clause, namely, section 5 of the Ordinance was challenged by a Writ Petition which gave rise to Civil Appeals Nos. 73, 74 and 124 of 1981 of this Court, and by a judgment delivered on 10 March 1982 this Court upheld the validity of the Ordinance. This Court, however, observed that in spite of the validating law a person feeling aggrieved by retirement may contend that his retirement was not ordered in the public interest, in which case the government should place some materials before the court to show that the order of retirement was in fact made in the public interest. In the instant case the Government produced the relevant file showing certain facts on the basis of which the authorize formed the opinion that the respondent should be retired from service in the public interest. Now the question is who will decide as to what is "public interest". The answer is clearly that the Government is the better judge to decide whether a Government servant should be retired in public interest under section 9(2). There may be various reasons for which the Government may retire a government servant after he has completed the requisite period of service qualifying for pension; the government is in a better position to decide to whom to retire. It is not possible for a court to sit on judgment over government's action if from the facts disclosed it does not appear that government's action was malafide or colorable exercise of power. Subject to these limitations, the discretion of the government in such a matter is absolute. On a similar question coming up before the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Farzand Ali and others vs. West Pakistan, (1970) 22 DLR (SC) 208; 1970 P.L D. S.C. 98, Hamoodur Rahman C.J. in his well-reasoned judgment made the following observation:-</u>

<u>"It appear to me, therefore, that in the absence of any words in the statute limiting the discretion of the Government this must be so, for, it is difficult to lay down any yardstick by which "public interest" can be measured in this connection. There may well be circumstances apart from inefficiency or dishonesty which may be relevant for considering the suitability of an officer for being continued in public service. An over punctilious or over fastidious person may well in certain circumstances be just as unsuitable as a lax or careless officer having regard to the nature of his employment. But this is a matter which the employer alone can determine and therefore, it must of necessity be left to the subjective satisfaction of the employing  authorities."</u>

<u>40. It has been argued by Mr. Nurul Huq that the respondent was found absent only on one occasion and that the materials placed before the court by the government are not sufficient for considering the retirement of the respondent necessary in the public interest. This argument will be of no avail, for what materials are sufficient for retiring government servant are again for the government to decide. The law on the subject is that the government is not required to show any reason whatsoever for ordering retirement but government may form its opinion on consideration of over-all service performance of a government servant throughout his career. It may be true that the service record of the respondent does not contain any stigma but this can hardly be a defence against government's action in retiring him after 25 years of service. Government may think it expedient to infuse new blood into service by retiring persons whose record of performance is just average and not outstanding. The record of the respondent was called for and considered by the Minister before decision to retire him was taken. Be that as it may unless it is clearly established that retirement is malafide, insufficiency of its ground is not a matter for court's consideration and when law permits such retirement court's duty is only to see that the order of retirement is within the four corners of law, that the action has not been taken in bad faith and that it is not colourable exercise of powers. Satisfaction as to 'public interest’ in the case of retirement of a government servant after 25 years of service is subjective satisfaction of the government as distinguished from satisfaction of the government that a person should be held in preventive detention. A preventive detention can be questioned either by a petition under Article 102 of the Constitution or by any application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In a number of cases, particularly "Government of West Pakistan vs. Begum Agha Shorish Kashmiri" (1969) 21 DLR (SC) 1=P.L.D. 1969 (S.C) 14, the Pakistan Supreme Court held that satisfaction of the government that a person should be held in preventive detention is a satisfaction which should be tested objectively before the court on production of grounds for the detention. In the case of a preventive detention it is not only that the government is satisfied that the detention is necessary, but it is also for the Court to be satisfied that the detention is necessary in the public interest. Under both these laws, a duty has been cast upon the Court to examine the record of the case of a detenu in order to satisfy itself that the detenu is not held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner. No such duty however has been cast upon the Court under section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 or in any other law to examine the record of a person retired under section 9(2) to satisfy itself that the retirement was made in the public interest. The court may call for the record only to see that the government had some materials for deciding that retirement of a government servant was considered necessary in the public interest and that order of retirement was not made malafide. In this case, the order of retirement is found to be perfectly lawful. I would, therefore, allow the appeal, set aside the High Court Division's order and dismiss the Writ Petition without however, any order as to costs.</u>

ORDER OF THE COURT

By the majority judgment Civil Appeal No 70 of 1981 is dismissed. By unanimous judgment Civil Appeal No. 67 of 1981 of Habibullah Khan is allowed and the adverse findings made against him in judgment dated 26-11-80 are expunged; Civil Appeal No. 88 of 1981 of Anisuzzaman Chowdhury is allowed and the adverse findings made against him in the judgment dated 26-11-80 are also expunged; and Civil Appeal Nos. 68 and 69 of 1981 preferred by Habibullah Khan are allowed and the suo motu rule No. 4 of 1980 and the judgment dated 13-4-81 passed therein are quashed. We make no order as to costs in any of the appeals.

End.

Mr. Q. A. Hossain, AAG ----- For the Respondent Nos.1 and 2
