full_judgment:
AKM Sadeque, J.: By this Rule Nisi issued at the instance of the petitioner Aftabuddin Ahmed the Gazette notification No. See 140/65/8 EPS dated 7.1.66 and sec. III/IV-9/67/271 EPS dated 6.5.1967 and also the notice dated 10.3.81 issued to the petitioner for his summarily eviction from the properties described in the said notice Annexure G purporting to be in pursuance of the decision in an earlier Writ Petition No. 14 of 1974 Annexure E. by the Deputy Commissioner Sylhet (Respondent No. 2) have been impugned.

2. The following are averments in the writ petition necessary for disposal of the Rule.

3. The land of plot 6436 measuring .0956 acres recorded in khatian No. 3691 as cultivable vacant land within Sylhet Municipality. Kalighat, was acquired by purchase in 1949 (1356 BS) by one Duraram Upadhyaya, S/o. Late Thoparam Upadhyaya from the original owner Rakesh Chandra Kar and others. During the last Settlement Survey the said land was wrongly recorded in the names of the heirs of original owners and on a petition of objection by the said Duraram Upadhyaya, the CO (Rev) Sadar Sylhet by order dated 15.12.62 allowed the objection and directed correction of the record of rights in the names of the Duraram, as purchaser in possession without document. Thereafter in respect of the lands Duraram obtained a Registered kobala dated 25.4.63 executed and registered by Rakhal Kanti Kar and Jahar Kanti Kar, sons of late Rakesh Chandra Kar, This said Duraram Upadhyaya was in exclusive ownership and possession of the said plot of land for long over the period of limitation. Then he transferred the land to the petitioner for a consideration of Taka 3000.00 by a registered kabala dated 4.8.72. The kabala was executed and registered in pursuance of a Deed of Agreement for sale by Duraram earlier made on 5.1.68. Thereafter the petitioner mutated his name in the khatian vide order dated 19.8.72 passed by CO (Rev). Kotwali, Sylhet and he was continuing to be in possession thereof as exclusive owner of the land on payment of rents to the Government and Taxes to the Municipality. He also raised Bank Loan for his business by mortgaging the property within the knowledge of the Additional Deputy Commissioner Sylhet who was also the Chairman of the Loan Sanctioning Board.

4. It has further been averred that prior to the agreement of sale with Duraram, the petitioner and his brother Faizuddin Ahmed (added respondent No. 4) were jointly carrying on business as monthly tenants under Duraram on the land but subsequently Faizuddin severed his connections wish the said business and the petitioner by constructing a pucca building started carrying on business thereon as sole proprietor in the name and style of M/s. Karim Traders and M/s. Bengal Flour Mills The petitioner then applied for and got permission to convert his Flour Mill into a compact Flour Mill from the Government. Ministry of Food under Memo No 1327 dated 25.7.75 and then he installed the requisite machinery at huge cost and got recognition as an Industrial unit from the Director General. Department of Industries Government of Bangladesh vide Memo No. IP/PP/91 (I0831)/83/505 dated 8.3.84.

5. While in peaceful possession of the said land in plot No. 6434 bearing holding No. 91 B of Sylhet Municipality through his predecessor in interest Duraram Upadhyaya after acquiring ownership thereof by purchase by a registered instrument dated 4.8.72 the petitioner raised building and structures and installed machineries at huge cost thereon. The petitioner alleged that he came to know from the local Tahsilder that the said land was included within the list of Enemy Firm (Enemy Property) of M/s. Chandmal. Surujmal Bantia of Kalighat and on enquiry he got to know that in the Notification No. Sec.140/65/8 EPS-7th January1966 published in Dhaka Gazette dated 20th January, 1966, the Government of the then East Pakistan was pleased to direct that the following properties amongst others mentioned in the schedule below shall vest in the Assistant Custodian Enemy Property for Sylhet District. Item No. 16 of the said schedule reads as below:

"SCHEDULE"

(16) Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop of Messers Chandmall. Surujmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet,"

It further transpired that in the next year, by Notification No, Sec-III/lV-9/67/27I EPC dated 6th May, 1967, a Corrigendum was issued in respect of items 14, 15, 16 and 17 of the schedule of the aforesaid Notification dated 7.1.66 directing that "the following may be read in place of the existing ones" and in respect of the said item (16) it was to be read as follows:

"(16) Messers Chandmall, Surujmal Bantia including Duraram Upadhyaya, son of Lunaram Upadhyaya, Kalighat, Sylhet"

Thus the name of Duraram Upadhaya was tagged by this Corrigendum Notification with the shop Chandmall, Surujmal Bantia, appearing in the earlier Notification dated 7.1.66. It is alleged that Duraram was in no way connected with the shop of Messers. Chandmall, Surujmal Bantia which stands on Dag No. 6435 recorded as Gudamghar in Khatian No. 3431 measuring an area of .0800 acres while the aforesaid vacant land of Duraram was recorded in a separate Dag No. 6436 of a different Khatian No. 3691 measuring .0956 acres. This land of Duraram was vacant and not in any way connected or concerned with the Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop of Chandmall, Surujmal Bantia standing on Dag No. 6436 recorded as Gudamghar in Khatian No. 3431. There was no description of any property by Dag number, khatian or area in the said Notifications. The petitioner has alleged that what had vested cannot go beyond Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop standing on Dag No. 6435 and it never had attracted any vacant land, separately recorded in Dag No. 6436 which did never vest in the Government.

6. The petitioner's brother (added respondent No.4) turned inimical to the petitioner and he was trying to take lease of the property. So the petitioner had to file Title Suit No. 81 of 1972 in the Second Court as Subordinate Judge, Sylhet for declaration of Title and confirmation of possession with further declaration that it was not an enemy or abandoned property. He also prayed for temporary injunction restraining the Government and other defendants from disturbing his peaceful possession. The suit was, however, dismissed for default on 19.8.75 and the petitioner brought the Misc. Case No. 37 of 76 for its restoration. But this case also was dismissed on 30.10.78. The petitioner then applied to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms for release of the property from the list of vested properties and later he filed petition before the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade, Government of Bangladesh, who was pleased to stay all actions of proposed lease by the order dated 7.8.78. But the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet (respondent No. 2) took forcible possession of the petitioners' property on 15.11.78. Then the petitioner filed an application before the Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade but without any effect. Against this forcible possession of the property on 15.11.78 by the order of respondent No. 2 dated 14.11.78 the petitioner moved this court in writ petition No. 14 of 1979. Their Lordships Mr. Justice Chowdhury ATM Masud and Mr. Justice MH Rahman by judgment and order dated 18.7.80 were pleased to direct restoration of the properties to the petitioner, with an observation that, "this however will not stand in the way of the Respondents to take any legal action in the matter in accordance with law" In pursuance of this decision, the property was restored to the petitioner by an order of the ADC Sylhet under Memo No. SA/lI-I/ P-13/78/10628(4) dated 11.12.80. Thereafter, the petitioner was served with the impugned notice dated 3.10.81 by the Deputy Commissioner, Respondent No. 2 asking him to show cause within 7(seven) days of receipt of the notice as to why he will not be evicted being an unauthorised occupant in the said property on the ground that no right or title of the petitioner over the property was declared in the aforesaid Writ Petition No. 14 of 1979 (Annexure E).

7. The petitioner had shown cause by filing a petition of objection on 12.10.61 to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet. He pleaded that the disputed land in plot No. 6436 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality was a fallow land and not connected with or a part of "Tobacco Mollasses and Khamfia shop" of Messrs Chandmal, Surajmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet" with whom Duraram Upadhyaya had no connection or concern. The 'corrigendum' issued in Gazette Notification dated 6.5.67 did not vest the property of the petitioner in the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property for Sylhet and that the petitioner was in possession of the property on the basis of valid title by dint, amongst other things, of a registered kabala dated 4.8.72.

8. The respondent No. 2 rejecting the petition of objection passed the following order:

"Perused the records The earlier order stands in view of the fact that the Hon'ble High Court has not given any adjudication regarding right and title of the property. It is still considered to be a vested property and therefore please take action accordingly." The petitioner expressed his grievance that he was not granted certified copy of the aforesaid order passed by the respondent No. 2.

9. The petitioner has obtained this Rule mainly on the grounds that the impugned Gazette notifications do not attract the disputed properties which belonged to the petitioner and secondly that in the circumstances of the case, if the Government wanted to claim title in the property in question it could only do so by way of appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the petitioner's registered kabala and other deeds in view of decision of the Appellate Division, setting down principles governing cases of this nature.

10. This petitioner had sent a notice demanding justice to the respondents before obtaining this Rule.

11. The Rule was opposed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and also by the added respondent No. 4 who file affidavits in opposition. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and the added respondent No. 4 had controverted the material allegations. They, in substance, contended that the plot No. 6436 was not a cultivable land but a place of the shopping centre in the best commercial area within Sylhet Municipality. Rakesh Chandra Kar and others abandoned the land, left for India long before the final publication of the last Khatian Duraram Upadhyaya had no right, title or interest in the property. He got his name recorded in respect of the property through a got up objection case by practising fraud and influencing the settlement staff with a view to grabbing the property. Later on 25.4.63 he falsely created a kabala in his favour and recorded his name in the khatian. The kabala dated 4.8.72 by Duraram in favour of the petitioner was fraudulent and forged. The alleged agreement in pursuance of which the kabala was executed was also false. The order dated 19.8.72 relating to recording of the petitioner's name in the khatian was on the basis of his fraudulent agreement and sale deeds respectively dated 5.1.68 and 4.8.72, when Duraram was not residing in this country. He left for India during Indo-Pak war in 1965. Thus the petitioner had no right, title and interest in the property by virtue of his payment of Municipal or any other taxes, nor could he legally obtain any loan by mortgage of the land; nor did he ever file any application for loan to the officer concerned, i.e. the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue). It was further contended by the respondents that the land in question was Enemy Property. The petitioner had taken lease of the land in the name of his brother Faizuddin Ahmed but at the instigation of the petitioner, his brother instead of renewing the lease, filed Title Suit Nos. 334 of i967 and 163 of 1971 in the Courts of 2nd Sub-Judge and 1st Munsif respectively without any success, the petitioner claimed his own title in the land and filed Title Suit No. 81 of 1972 in the Court of 2nd Sub-Judge, Sylhet. His claim was false. So he allowed the suit to be dismissed. Then he filed Misc. Appeal No. 37 of 1975 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet for setting aside the order of dismissal and restoration of the case but that Misc. Appeal was also dismissed on contest. Then the petitioner got Title Suit No. 525 of 1976 of the Court of 2nd Sub-Judge by one Goura Chandra Das showing him as tenant under him. This suit was also dismissed. The respondents further contended that the petitioner had no title whatsoever in the land and the papers in support of the claim filed by the petitioner were fabricated. The respondents contended that the disputed property was declared as Enemy Property by Notification of January 7, 1966 as corrected by one dated 6.5.67. The plot Nos. 6436 and 6435 were contiguous plots and Messers Chandmahal Surjamal Bantia was a well-known business house that had several shops upon the same. When the owners of the said business house had left for India in September, 1965, the property came under the control and management of the authority concerned as vested property and it was taken lease of as such in the name of the petitioner's brother Faizuddin Ahmed (added respondent No. 4). It has been contended by the respondents that the petitioner was trespasser and he was asked to vacate the land. After he vacated the land possession was taken over by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. But in obedience to Writ Petition No. 14/79 the respondents restored possession to the petitioner and served him with a legal notice under section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966.

12. The added respondent No. 4 had supported the defence of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. He has stated that when he was in peaceful possession of the disputed land on the basis of lease, the petitioner got him arrested by lodging GR Case No. 1218 of 1978 and entered into the suit land forcibly. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 found the petitioner trespasser and took over possession from the petitioner. Then the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 14 of 1979 in which their Lordships observed:

"the respondents to take any legal action in the matter in accordance with law."

The respondents maintained that in the facts and circumstances of the case, this Rule should be discharged.

13. The main grounds urged by Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, are that the concerned Gazette Notifications do not attract the disputed properties and therefore, the disputed properties have never been treated as Enemy Property or vested properties. Again, when the petitioner has been in possession of the disputed property on the basis of title, the respondents are not entitled to evict the petitioner in pursuance of the impugned notice under section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order 1966 (Annexure G) without enforcing the claim of the respondents in a proper forum and the respondents cannot evict the petitioner summarily without having recourse to the civil Court for decision as to the title of the petitioner.

14. Annexure A to the petition is the Gazette Notification No. Sec-140/65/8 EPS dated January 7, 1966 and Annexure B is its Corrigendum Sec-III/IV-9/67/271 EPC dated 6th May, 1967. Gazette Notification No Sec-140/63/8 EPS 7th January, 1966 gives a schedule of properties which have been directed by the Government to be listed as Vested Properties of the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property Sylhet District, Serial No. 16 of the schedule to the notification is Tobacco, Molasses and khamfia shop of Messers Chandmal Surajmal Bantia Kalighat, Sylhet. The Corrigendum dated 6th May, 1967 says that the following may be read in place of the existing one. No. 16 "Messers Chandmal Surajmal Bantia including Dhura Ram Upadhyay, son of Lunaram Upadhyay, Kalighat, Sylhet", The stand of the respondents is that by means of this Corrigendum, the Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop of Messers Chandmal Surajmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet was also considered to be inclusive of the property of Dhura Ram. It was to be seen that neither in original notification nor in Corrigendum, the plot number or area of the property was given. Now the petitioner has appended Annexures C and D to the petition. Annexure C shows that the plot No. 6435 stood recorded in the name of Sushil Chandra Chowdhury and others and the property was described as 'Gudam Ghar' Annexure D, on the other hand, shows that Dag No. 6436 was vacant property of Sushil Chandra Chowdhury and others but possession was of Dhura Ram Upadhyay, son of Lunaram Upadhyaya, the vendor of the petitioner who was in possession of this plot No. 6436 with effect from 1356 BS and the petitioner Aftabuddin Ahmed had mutated his name in respect of this khatian by order dated 22.4.77. These two Annexures show that the plot Nos. 6435 and 6436 were two distinct lands both originally belonging to Shushil Chandra Chowdhury, The affidavit-in-opposition shows that these two plots are adjacent. Although these two plots are adjacent, they constitute two different khatians namely khatian No. 3431 and khatian No. 3691. The petitioner's case is that the Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop of Messrs Chandmal Surajmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet is situated upon dag No. 6435 and not upon dag No. 6436. Plot No. 6436 was originally the property of Sushil Chandra Chowdhury and from him Duraram Upadhayay purchased the land and he in his turn sold it to the petitioner Aftabuddin Ahmed in the year 1972. Now it is easy to see that the Gazette Notification Annexure A and its Corrigendum Annexure B are vague and they do not show whether the dag No. 6435 or 6436 or both of them were included in the Gazette Notification and in the Corrigendum. Therefore we find sound basis for the argument of the petitioner that his property was not as a matter of fact published in the Gazette as enemy property.

15. Secondly the petitioner has produced the certified copy of the kabala executed by Duraram Updhyaya on 4.8.72. The petitioner, as it appears from the Annexure L to the petitioner's affidavit- in-reply, had submitted certified copy of this document also before the respondent No. 2 in support of his objection filed on 3.10.81. It is at serial No. 8 of the Annexure. The petitioner has stated in his writ petition that he had submitted the original of this kabala to the Pubali Bank for obtaining loan for making construction upon the land of dag No. 6436. The petitioner has filed a certificate from the Ministry to the effect that the petitioner Mr. Aftabuddin Ahmed, Proprietor M/S Kalighat Flour Mills Kalighat, Sylhet has been enjoying a cash credit facility under BSCIC Loan from that Branch against which he offered certain documents of landed property. Serial No. I of these documents is Original Title deed comprising 9 decimal land under dag No. 6436, khatian No. 1809, JL No. 91 Mouza-Sylhet Municipality owned by Mr. Aftabuddin Ahmed, son of late Usman Ali of Kalighat, Sylhet, This serial No. 1 obviously refers to the original of the kabala furnished before this Court executed by Duraram Upadhyaya. The petitioner has also appended to this affidavit-in-reply Annexures I, J, and K which prima facie bear out that the petitioner had established Flour Mills upon the land in plot 6436.

16. The above documents and the averments supported by affidavit by the petitioner clearly show that the petitioner has a prima facie title. It appears that the petitioner was once dispossessed from the disputed land by the respondent No. 2 without any notice under section 4 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 and the petitioner had brought an application under Article 102 of the Constitution being Writ Petition No. 14 of 1979 before this court and their Lordships Mr. Justice Chowdhury ATM Masud and Mr. Justice MH Rahman found fault with the eviction, in that no notice was served upon the petitioner prior to the eviction. Their Lordships stated all the facts of the case but refrained from giving any decision as to the title of the petitioner or of the respondents. Their Lordships observed.

"He was adversely affected by that action but he was not given any prior notice to explain his position. In this view of the matter we hold that the impugned action was done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to restore possession of the properties to the petitioner. This, however, will not stand in the way of the respondents to take any legal action in the matter in accordance with law."

<u>17. Now it is this last sentence which was regarded by the respondents to authorise them to evict the petitioner only by complying with the requirement of section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966. The respondents have laboured under the impression that mere notice to the petitioner would be a sufficient step in law to evict the petitioner from the disputed premises. The learned Advocate for the petitioner, however, has argued depending upon the decisions reported in 22 DLR 48, 30 DLR (SC) 139, 32 DLR (AD) 29 and 32 DLR 252 (Division Bench) that in order to evict the petitioner mere notice will not do in the facts and circumstances of the present case. In accordance with Rule 5 (i)(b), only an unauthorised occupant of the enemy property is liable for eviction and before any action is taken towards that end, it must be established that he is an unauthorised occupant The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that the onus to prove that the occupant is in unauthorised occupation is upon the respondent Nos. I and 2. In support of his argument, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has cited decisions in the case of Shah Ghulam Nabi and others Vs. Vice-Chairman, East Pakistan Enemy Property Management Board Dhaka and others, reported in 22 DLR 48 and in the case of Benoy Bhusan Bardhan being dead his heirs Pronoy Bhusan Bardhan and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 139. In the decision in 30 DLR (SC) 139 the paragraph Nos. 37 and 38 are relevant, and these paragraphs had not been over-ruled by the decision in 40 DLR (SC) 22, although some other paragraphs have been over-ruled by the same judgment in the decision reported in 40 DLR (SC) 22 only paragraph 1-21 of the decision of 30 DLR (SC) 139 were over-ruled.</u>

18. In 30 DLR (SC) 139, amongst other things, in para 36, their Lordships observed:

"It has been consistently held, in our opinion rightly held in these cases, the vesting of property in the Custodian of Enemy Property did not transgress upon the title of the real owner and that nobody in possession of such property in exercise of a right, however imperfect or limited it may be, can be said to be in unlawful possession within the meaning of paragraph 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966," It was correctly observed by Chief Justice Siddiky (Abdul Hakim, J agreeing), who was incidentally a party to the judgment under appeal, on construing the provision of Rule 192 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, in the case of Ananda Mohan Kundu and others Vs. Province of East Pakistan 20 DLR 976, 980 "If after vesting of the enemy property in the Custodian, it is found on enquiry that a person who is holding some sort of document of title, though imperfect, from the real owner of the property who happended to be the enemy, then if the occupier is a citizen of Pakistan he cannot be Custed from the property because of mere vesting order of the Government. In paragraph 37, their Lordships observed:

………………………………………………..……………………………………………….

the illegality of the petitioner's possession being in dispute, the respondents could oust them only by obtaining an order of eviction in a properly constituted suit. Another proposition, which was laid down in the said case was that a citizen of a country could not be adjudged as enemy without definite evidence that the said citizen had been, as a matter of fact, residing in India.

<u>19. It appeared that for such view their Lordships had drawn reference to the decision in the case of Shah Ghulam Nabi and others Vs. Vice-Chairman, East Pakistan Enemy Property Management Board Dhaka and others reported in 22 DLR 48. It was held in this decision:</u>

<u>"Where circumstances of a case establish that a person in possession of a property treated as enemy property has set up and proved a prima facie title to the same, it amounts to this that the question that his possession of the property was illegal was in issue and therefore such possession cannot be treated illegal without a decision of this question in a properly constituted suit."</u>

<u>It was held in the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhury Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 32 DLR 252 by a Division Bench of this court that—</u>

<u>"A kabala executed and registered in Bangladesh in 1975 creates a presumption that the registration authority was satisfied that the executant was a valid citizen and national of Bangladesh since an Indian National as such could not transfer any property in Bangladesh by way of any registered deed".</u>

<u>The authority in the Government could not question and annul the validity of such title by an executive order. If the Government wanted to claim the title in such property it could only do so by way of an appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the registered kabala as such. Again in the case of Abul Khair Miah being dead his heirs Abul Kashem and others Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 29 DLR (AD) 29 their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed:</u>

<u>"The appellant on purchase of the property from his vendors is in possession of the property and it requires to be explained by the Enemy Property Authority, how the property could be treated as Enemy Property. It was for the Enemy Property Authority, to establish that the predecessor of the vendors of the appellant or they migrated to India earlier the Enemy Property law came into operation in 1965, so that the property left by them came within the mischief of enemy property law but the High Court Division has erroneously assumed as a fact which the Enemy Property Authority was to prove. The onus was thus misplaced on the appellant"</u>

<u>The aforesaid decisions lay down the principles that whenever an individual is in possession of a property on the basis of some sort of title deed either by way of purchase or unauthorised from the original owner said to be the enemy, the authority first of all has to establish that title in favour of the individual was invalid, void or fraudulent and this can be done at the instance of the authority by a properly constituted suit before the civil Court. In the instant case we find that the petitioner has furnished sufficient documents to establish this prima facie title and even if his title is invalid or bad in law it would be a matter to be decided by the civil Court.</u>

<u>It is for the authority to go to the civil Court and to get decision as to title and find whether they are allowed to evict the petitioner by means of notice under section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966.</u>

20. A question arose whether the dismissal for default of Title Suit No. 31 of 1972 would be a bar to the present writ application. We have given our consideration to the aspect of the case as well. The suit appears to have been dismissed for default under Order 9 rule 9. The petitioner filed an application for setting aside the dismissal order and to restore it to its original file and number in accordance with Order 9 rule 9 CPC. The Misc. Case was also dismissed on contest. Order 9 rule 9 precludes the plaintiff from bringing a fresh suit. But if a suit is dismissed for default in presence of defendant or defendants, the only remedy is under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure Order 9 rule 9, therefore, does not preclude the writ application before this court.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. We declare that the Notification No. 140/65/8 EPS 7th January, 1966 (Annexure A) and No. Sect III/lV-9/67/271 EPC dated 6th May, 1967 (Annexure B) in so far as they concern the disputed property of the petitioner are void and of no legal effect and further declare that the impugned notice Annexure G is also without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

End.

Abdul Quayum with Abdul Malek Munshi and Abdul Karim, Advocates ------- For the Opposite Party Nos. 1-3.

full_judgment:
In this Rule under section 25 of the Small Causes Court Act I am invited to examine the legality of the Judgment and decree dated 27.12.87 passed by the learned Assistant Judge and Small Cause Court Judge in Small Causes Court Suit No. 6 of 1984.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted the suit against the opposite parties as defendants for ejectment, realisation of arrear rent and for compensation in the said Court of the learned Small Cause Court Judge stating, inter alia, that the defendants were monthly tenants in the suit premises under the Sonaullah Waqf Estate of which the plaintiff is the Mutwalli at a monthly rent Tk. 125/- which was subsequently enhanced to Tk. 150/- per month since 1st of Baisakh,1390 B.S. The rent was payable according to Bengali month within the expiry of the month for which it was due as per an oral agreement. The defendants did not pay rent regularly. They paid rent for 2/3 months at a time in spite of demand by the landlord. The rent since Baisakh, 1391 B.S. was in arrear. The defendants were habitual defaulters. The plaintiff terminated the tenancy on the expiry of the last day of Sravan, 1391 B.S. by issuing notices on the defendants under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 15th Ashar, 1391 B.S. The defendants received the notices and replied through their Advocate Mr. M.A. Karim on 7.7.84 stating that the contents of the notices were not true. The defendants are trespassers since 1st of Bhadra, 1391 B.S. and for their illegal Occupation of the suit premises since then the plaintiff was entitled to get compensation from them at a rate of Tk. 20/- per day. The plaintiff claims arrear rent from Baisakh to Sravan, 1391 B.S. and also compensation and prayed for khas possession after evicting the defendants from the suit premises.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. They also filed two additional written statements. Their case, inter alia, is that there was oral agreement with the former. Mutwalli Mvi. Rahmatullah to pay the annual rent by instalment and there was no agreement with him for payment of rent within the month for which the rent was due. The defendants offered rent to the plaintiff for the month of Baisakh to Ashar, 1391 B.S. But he refused to accept the same. The defendants thereupon sent the rent for the aforesaid months to the plaintiff on 7.7.84 through rent money order which was refused on 10.7.84 and the defendants received back the same on 14.7.84 and the defendants have been depositing the rent since then in the House Rent Control Case No. 38 of 1984 and as such they are not defaulters. The defendants further case is that they paid rent to the Government and taxes to the Pourashava for the suit premises amounting to more than Tk.500/-. The plaintiff demanded illegal money for the premises from the defendants which they did not agree and for that the plaintiff filed the suit for same illegal gains and to earn a handsome amount by letting out the premises to 3rd party.

4. By the impugned judgment and decree the learned Small Cause Court Judge dismissed the suit on the findings that the four rent receipts Exts. Ka-Ka(3) and the six counter foils of rent receipts up to 30th Aswin, 1387 Exts 1-1(e) B.S. show that the plaintiff accepted the rent from the defendants in lump for few month at a time, that the plaintiff failed to prove that there was written agreement for payment of rent due for a month within the expiry of the months for which it was due and that it appeared from the rent receipts produced in Court that there was an oral agreement between the former Mutwalli and the defendants for payment of rent in yearly instalment and in such circumstances when the defendants paid rent in yearly instalment they could not be called defaulters.

5. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Small Cause Court Judge the plaintiff has obtained the present Rule in this Court.

6. Mr. Subodh Ranjan Dutta, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has submitted that in the absence of any written contract between the plaintiff-landlord and the tenant-defendants the rent was payable within the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent was payable under the provision of section 18(5) of the Premise Rent Control Ordinance, 1986 and as such the learned Small Cause Court Judge committed an error of law in holding that the rent was payable in yearly instalment.

7. Mr. Dutta has further submitted that the acceptance of rent by the plaintiff by instalment or in a lump will not disentitle the plaintiff to get a decree for ejectment if the defendants are found to be defaulters.

8. He has next submitted that when the relationship of the landlord and the tenant is established and the landlord makes an allegation of default the onus will be on the tenant and as such the defendants have to prove that they are entitled to protection under section 18(5) of the Ordinance. In support of his submissions he has relied upon the cases of M/s. A. Hague and Co. & another Vs. Alhaj Zakir Hossain, 40 DLR (AD) 109 and M/s. Binning & Co. (Bangladesh) Ltd. Vs. M/s. Nasirabad Properties Ltd. 4 DLR (AD) 89.

9. The last submission of Mr. Dutta is that the learned Small Cause Court Judge failed to consider that the transmission cost was not deposited along with the monthly rent in House Rent Control Case No. 38 of 1984 and the deposit having not been made as per provisions of section 19(1) (b) read with section 18(5) of the Ordinance the said deposit would not be considered as valid deposit. In support of his submission be has relied upon the case of Mir M.A. Razzaque and others Vs. Md. Abdul Hai Patwari 5 B.L.D (AD) 97.

10. In reply to the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, has submitted by making reference to the case of Md. Golam Hossain Vs. Mst. Asia Khaiun Chowdhury, 40 DLR (AD) 1 that in view of the pleadings and evidence on record the present case is an example of waiver and acquiescence and as such although the defendants made payment of rent in a lump in yearly instalment they cannot he called defaulters and in this connection Mr. Quayum has pointed out that in paragraph 2 of the plaint the plaintiff stated that whenever the plaintiff demanded rent from the defendants they deferred payment on various pretexts and ultimately they would pay rent for 2/3 months at a time and the plaintiff would accept the rent out of kindness, that the defendants pleaded waiver and ac-quiescence in paragraph 6 of the written statement, that the petitioner as P.W. 1 stated that the defendants entered the suit premises in 1380 B.S. on same terms with the former Mutwalli Rahmatullah and accordingly the former Mutwalli used to receive rent in lump by instalment and the plaintiff signed the rent receipt Ext. A series dated 1.7.87 B.S. for the months from Chaitra to Aswin, 1387 B.S.

11. In reply Mr. Dutta has submitted that the statement in the plaint that the defendants would not pay rent in spite of demand and that they paid rent for 2/3 months at a time and the plaintiff accepted the same out of kindness does not amount to waiver as contended on behalf of the defendants. He has referred to the statement of D.W.1 (defendant No. 3) to the effect that when the present Mutwalli was appointed the defendants had an understanding with him with regard to the mode of payment of rent.

12. Mr. Quayum has further submitted that the payment of municipal taxes by the defendants in addition to their payment of rent shows that they were not defaulters.

To this Mr. Dutta has submitted that payment of municipal taxes in excess of payment of rent does not and cannot show that the defendants are not defaulters.

13. Mr. Quayum has next submitted that the plaintiff sought to evict the defendants only for getting salami from new tenants which is not allowed under section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1986. In elaboration of his submission he has pointed out the statement of plaintiff P.W. 1 to the affect that there is provision for letting out the premises on receipt of salami and that the salami of the suit premises would be Tk. 20,000/-, 25,000/-.

14. In reply Mr. Dutta has submitted that the plaintiff as P.W. 1 denied the suggestion that in order to get salami money he brought the suit for eviction and that the defendant No.1 admitted in his cross-examination that the plaintiff is a well-to-do man and as such he does not hanker for salami money.

<u>15. In 40 DLR (AD) 109 the Appellate Division has held:—</u>

<u>"From the evidence it appears that the defendant-appellants have on various occasions paid rents for several months at a time. There is no controversy regarding such lump sum payments of rent. What is, however, important to notice about such payments is that while granting receipts for them the plaintiff respondent took care in giving such receipts month wise. A question is do the facts constitute an evidence of a contract between the parties waiving the right to receive rent within the 15th day following that month for which rent has become due. Secondly even if it does whether sub-section (5) of section 18 of the Ordinance contemplates this kind of contract or an oral agreement. On referring to the precise provisions of this sub-section it is seen that the expression used therein are within the time fixed in the contract or by the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable." The portion under-lined by me refer to the existence of the contract between the landlord and the tenant. From the use of the preposition "in" before the expressions "the contract", the intention of the legislature seems to be clear. There might have been some scope for controversy if the preposition 'by' was used instead of the preposition 'in'. As it is, the contract referred to here in this sub-section means a written contract, and not an oral contract. The Ordinance lays down the deadline for rents to be paid by a tenant, that is, by the 15th day of the month next following that for a which the rent is payable'. If this time limit has to be varied by a landlord and his tenant, it obviously implies something in writing, which is not the case here. Moreover, defendant-appellants tried to establish the so-called con-tract by referring to the practice of the parties of payment of rent in lump sum amount and the acceptance of the same by the landlord at a time. It has been pointed out by the respondent's Counsel that though there has been lump sum payments and receipts, the plaintiff-respondent never accepted such lump sum amounts by granting one receipt. Receipts issued by the Plaintiff-respondent show that they were issued month-wise, that is, one receipt for one month and the date of granting receipt was put within the month before the 15th day of the following month. The learned counsel further submitted that the regular payment of lump sum rents for several months at a time and the receipts thereof granted in the aforesaid manner did not create any express or implied contract varying the deadline of payment of rents by a monthly tenant as provided in the Ordinance, nor did such conduct constitute a waiver of the respondent landlord's right to receive rents by the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable. In the absence of any contract and also on the failure of the defendant-appellants to prove the extistence of an oral contract between the parties to the effect that the respondent would collect rents for several months at a time according to his convenience the defendant-appellant must be held to be defaulters within the meaning of the terms used in sub-section(5) of section 18 of the Ordinance."</u>

16. In 40 DLR (AD) 89 the Appellate Division by a majority decision has held:

"under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance a tenant is under an obligation to pay rent within certain period after the same has become due. Section 18 provides that in the absence of any contract to the contrary between the landlord and tenant to pay the monthly rent within a certain date it must be paid within the 15th day of the next month. These statutory restrictions relating to payment of monthly rent within certain date, if disregarded by the tenant, disentitles him to the protection against eviction for default in payment of rent. By judicial interpretation of these provisions which impose such restrictions the only exception which, if established, can take the tenant out of the mischief of those restrictions, is waiver, that is, if the tenant succeeds in showing that though he defaulted in paying rent within the due date or dates, the landlord accepted the rent without any objection or protest. Mere acceptance of rent is not sufficient to constitute waiver. Whether there has been any waiver by the landlord must be gathered from the facts of the case. Vide Ramzan Ali Mistry Vs. Hedayetullah (1979) 31 DLR (AD) 183:

"There may be a case of waiver or acceptance or such supervening facts and circumstances as to make the compliance with the enactment beyond the control of the tenant. However, it will depend on the facts of a particular case to see whether there has been default in the payment of rent in terms of the statute but once the fact is established in terms of the Ordinance, legal consequence following therefrom cannot be averted.

Evidence, as already observed, must be given to establish the plea of waiver. Quite necessarily the tenant is required to take the plea of waiver at the earlier opportunity, that is, in his pleading and at the trial where it should be raised as an issue.

17. In 40 DLR (AD) 89 the Appellate Division has further held:-

"Once a default occurs subsequent acceptance of the rent in lump by the landlord, docs not, in the absence of any positive proof of his intention to waive such default, amount to waiver so as to entitle him to the protection against the consequence of default, that is, eviction."

18. In the case reported in 40 DL.R(AD) 1 the Appellate Division has held:-

Thus even on the ratio of the case of M.A. Haque (40 DLR (AD) 109) and the majority view of Binning & Co. Ltd. (40 DLR AD 89) there is no escape from arriving at a conclusion that the defendant had made out a case of waiver and acquiescence in the facts and circumstance of the case at the earliest opportunity. Evidence that has been led shows that this was the arrangement between the landlord and the tenant that the Karmachari would come and collect the rent. This practice continued for 16 years. In the meantime the original lessor died and his son for some time managed the property and ultimately it devolved upon the plaintiff. It is the plaintiffs son who is now looking after the property. The trial Court noticed that the management of the property had been well established by the rent receipts Exts A(1) to A(61) which were issued in lump and it was not granted in month wise receipt as was the case in the earlier decision e.g. M/s. M.A. Hoque.

19. It has been further held in this case:

"Then the oral evidence was considered and the trial court found that P.W. 1 himself admit ted that they had no grievance as to the mode of payment till 1976. The consistent view of this Court is that the waiver is a question of fact and is to be taken at earliest opportunity and must be established on evidence. The present case is an example of waiver and acquiescence."

<u>20. In the instant case the plea of waiver was not raised or agitated at the trial and no such issue was framed there. In the Appellate Division Case in a 40 DLR (AD) 89 it has been held that the tenant is required to take the plea of waiver in the pleading and at the trial where it should be raised as an issue. In the plaint the plaintiff asserted that whenever he demanded rent from the defendants they deferred payment of rent on various pretexts and ultimately they would pay rent for 2/3 months at a time and the plaintiff would receive the rent out of kindness.</u>

21. The statement of P.W. 1 when considered with the statement of D.W. 1 in the cross-examination referred to above docs not show that the same in any way amounts to waiver or acquiescence. Therefore the case in 40 DLR (AD) 1 does not help the defendants as the instant case is not an example of waiver and acquiescence.

<u>22. In the instant case apparently the facts are different from those of the case in 40 DLR (AD) 1 inasmuch as in the said case that evidence showed that there was an arrangement between the landlord and tenant that the Karmachari would come and collect the rent and this practice continued for 16 years and that it was noticed by the trial court that the management of the property had been established by rent receipts Ext. A(1)-A(61) which were issued in lump and not granted month-wise. But in the instant case there was no arrangement between the plaintiff and the defendants for collection of rents by Karmacharies in lump for few months and no such practice continued for a long time. Again, there is no admission by the plaintiff in the instant case that he had no grievance as to mode of payment of rent in lump and the instant case is not a case of waiver and acquiescence. In these circumstances, the case in 40 DLR (AD) 1 has no application in the instant case.</u>

23. As already noted it has been held in 40 DLR ( AD) 109 that in the absence of any contract if the rent is not paid within 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable as per section 18(5) of the Ordinance the tenant will become a defaulter. It has been further held in the said case that the word 'contract' means written contract. In the instant case there is no written contract between the landlord and the tenants and as such the tenant defendents are liable to pay the rent by the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable.

24. In 40 DLR (AD) 89 the Appellate Division has held that the payment of rent in lump does not save a tenant from making him defaulter and once a default occurs subsequent acceptance of rent in lump by the landlord can not protect the tenant from being a defaulter in the absence of any positive proof of his intention to waive such default and as already noticed there is no positive proof of the intention of the plaintiff to waive the default in the instant case.

25. The payment of municipal taxes by the defendants in excess of payment of rent, I think, can not save the defendants from being defaulter if they are otherwise found to be defaulters.

26. The statement of the plaintiff as P.W. 1 as referred to above docs not show that he sought to evict the defendants only for getting salami from the new tenants but the plaintiff sought to evict the defend ants because they did not pay rents regularly. That being so section 10 of the Ordinance is not attracted.

27. The information slip Annexure A showing that the transmission cost was not deposited in the Rent Control Case, I think, can not be looked into at this stage because it not being a public document the matter should have been raised before the trial Court and considered there on evidence and for that the case in BLD (AD) 94 need not be considered.

28. In the above circumstances, it is found in the light of decisions in 40 DLR (AD) 109 and 89 that the defendants are defaulters and the learned Small Cause Court Judge is not correct in holding the view that the defendants are not so merely because of the fact that the plaintiff accepted payments of rent from them in lump for few months by instalment. The judgment and decree of the learned Small Cause Court Judge are therefore liable to be interfered with.

29. In the result, the rule is made absolute.

The judgment and decree passed by the learned Small Cause Court Judge are set aside and the suit is decreed.

End.

caseno: Appeal From Original Order No. 109 and 110 1984.with Civil Rule No. 298 (FM) of 1984. and Civil Rule No. 297 (FM) of 1984
lawyer:
Md. Khondker, M. GholamRabbani with A.I. Mohammad Ali, Advocates. ------- For the Appellants. 
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocates. ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Sagir Ahmed and ors ------ Appellant 
vs.
Dclwar Hossain and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Choudhury, J: - These two appeals were heard together and are disposed of by this one judgment. 

2. Facts are that the appellant-petitioners No. 1 and 2 filed two Miscellaneous Cases under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the property described in the schedules. Opposite party Nos. 1 to 8 namely, Delwar Hossain and others are the purchasers. Opposite party No.9 is the seller and Opposite party Nos. 10-21 are the other co-sharers of the holding. The case of the petitioner pre-emptors, who are father, son and daughter, is that the properties mentioned in C.S. Khatian No. 12223 appertaining to Mouza Sahar Dhaka originally belonged to one Parbati Charan Datta Kabiraj in raiyatijote right. He died leaving one widow Khiroda Sundari and 4 sons, Profullah Chandra Datta Kabiraj, Pizus Kiran Datta Kabiraj, Pran Goura Datta Kabiraj and Khitish Chandra Datta Kabiraj. Khiroda Sundari died leaving those 4 sons where after Khitish Chandra Datta Kabiraj transferred his entire interest in the suit property to his other three brothers. The three other brothers there sifter transferred their entire interest in the said to one Moulvi Yahayia Bawani who again transferred the same to opposite party Nos. 9.10 and 11 and Mujibur Rahman who are 4 brothers by executing a registered sale deed dated 6.1.1959 and delivered possession. The 4 brothers having gone into possession continued to possess the entire property so purchased from Bawani and during the S.A. and R.S. operation the name of the four brothers have been correctly recorded in Khatian No. 895 and 1708 respectively and the brothers, though separated the property amicably amongst them for convenience, continue to remain in ejmali in payment of rent as the tenancy remained one. When that was the position one of the brother namely, Habibur Rahmar., opposite party No. 10 transferred part of his share in the land of the holding together with the structures standing thereon to appellant-petitioner No. 1 namely, Sagir Ahmed by two registered sale deeds dated 22.3.1982 and 23.3.1982 and also transferred in favour of petitioner No.2 Reaz Ahmed minor son of petitioner No. 1 some other portion of the holding by two registered sale deeds dated 19.3.1982 and 20.3.1982 and delivered possession of the same to the appellants-petitioners. The petitioners' case is that they thus remained co-sharers in the case holding with other co-sharers namely, Habibur Rahman Matiur Rahman and Mozaffar Rahman. It was their further case that opposite party No. 22 wife of Sagir also purchased the remaining share of Habibur Rahman by separate sale deed and got delivery of possession of the purchased land. When that was the case Matiur Rahman one of the other brothers Opposite party No. 9 of the Misc. Case No. 327 of 1983 transferred his entire interest in the holding to opposite party Nos. 1-8 by registered sale deed dated 26.3.1982 for a consideration of Tk. 6,00,000/-. In the same way Mozaffar Rahman, the other brother transferred his entire interest in the holding to opposite party Nos. 1-6 by a registered sale deed dated 31.3.1982 for a consideration of Tk. 6,00,000/-. It is the appellants-petitioners' case that the two brothers transferred their respective properties without giving any notice to the petitioners though the petitioners are co-sharers in 'the case holding. The petitioners came to know of it long afterwards and after depositing the consideration money along with the statutory compensation then prayed for pre-emption. 

3. The cases were contested by opposite party Nos. 1-8 by filing two similar written objection in both the cases denying the material allegations made therein contending that the petitioners are not co-sharers in the lands sought to be pre-empted. It is the case of the opposite party Nos. 1-8 that the four brothers namely, Matiur Rahman, Majibur Rahman, Habibur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman became owners of holding No. 221 and 221/1 now holding Nos. 56 and 57 at Mitford Road, Dhaka by purchase. After the said purchased, one of the brothers, who had other ejmali properties also in the District Bogra along with the brothers filed a suit being Title Suit No.161 of 1981 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bogra for partition of their ejmali property including the case holding. The said suit was decreed on com- promise on 1.12.1981 in terms of the solenama in the preliminary. form: As per direction of the said decree, the case holding was partitioned as per map and four separate blocks were created in blue print in pursuance of which Majibur Rahman obtained Block No. 1, Habibur Rahman obtained block No. 2, Matiur Rahman obtained Block No. 3 and Muzaffar Rahman obtained block No.4 and by that they accepted the partition map between the parties and the parties went into possession of the respective saham each having a compact plot of land and building separately. Thereafter the partition map was readjusted for convenience of possession and blocks Nos. 1-4 were readjusted, according to which Matiur Rahman got 'C' block, Muzaffar Rahman got 'D' block. When that was the position, opposite party Nos. 1-8 purchased block Nos. 'C' and 'D' from Matiur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman and possession of those blocks were delivered to opposite party Nos. 1 and 8 by their vendors by raising pucca boundary wall in between the land. Thereafter Md. Habibur Rahman, vendor of the appellant-petitioners ceased to become co-sharers of Matiur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman, vendors of the opposite party Nos. 1 to 8. It is the further case that the petitioners-appellants also separated their jama and paid rent separately by opening a khatian as also the opposite parties and that the opposite party Nos. 1-8 are owners of separate land and holding having no jointers .of the tenancy and as such they being not co-sharers, they are not entitled to pre-empt. In the court below the parties fought out the suit on specific issues. After a consideration of the pleadings of the parties the evidence on record the court below came to a finding that as the property had been partitioned among the brothers, each brothers having a separate possession and the appellant-petitioner Sagir Ahmed after purchase having separated his jama paying rent separately creating two separate tenancy, the petitioners-appellants arc no longer co-tenant in the case holding and in that view of the matter the court held that the petitioners are not entitled to pre-empt the case land and in holding so the court has referred to the principle enunciated in 35 DLR (AD) page 230. As against that the appellants-petitioners have preferred these appeals which are heard together and disposed of by this one judgment. 

4. Mr. M.H. Khondker along with Mr. M. Gholam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appeared for the appellants in this case when Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan along with Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed appeared for the Respondents in both the appeals. 

5. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, the learned Advocate who argued the case at length for the appellant having taken us through the judgment and the various exhibits, has submitted that the court below erred if law in not holding that what the four brothers has was an amicable partition for convenience and not a partition by metes and bounds when in fact there was no final decree in that partition suit, for the partition to take any legal effect. He has further submit- ted that the court below erred in not holding that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 161 of 1982 being not a final decree and not admissible in evidence for want of stamp papers, the decree proved nothing and hence the finding of fact arrived at on a consideration of the inadmissible evidence, can not be sustained in law. It is his further case that the appellant-petitioner remained co-sharers in the tenancy and unless the tenancy is separated the co-tenant would be a co-sharer and the decision referred to in 32 DLR (AD) has no application in the fact and circumstances of the instant case. Mr. Gholam Rabbani the learned Advocate having referred to certain exhibits on record and to the deposition of Sagir before the court below, submitted that there are assertion made by the appellant that he had not supplied the names of the other co-sharers in his petition for separation of jama and no notice were in fact served upon the co-sharer and this having been corroborated by the testimony on record the court ought to have held that the separation of jama or tenancy behind the back of other co-sharers had no basis in the eye of law and, therefore, they remained co-sharers in tenancy inspite of the separation of the jama which was illegal. In support of this contention he has referred to the decision reported in 33 DLR(AD) page 323 and 12 DLR (Dhaka) at page 785 and 17 DLR (Dhaka) page 77. 

6. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate, arguing the case for the opposite parties has submitted that the decree passed in the title suit for partition was in fact a final decree with a direction to separate the specific possession as already effected by the parties on compromise as evidenced by Exhibit- H dated 30.11.80 on which the decree was passed on 1.12.81 and the parties having acted on it and having partitioned the properties on the basis of the said mutual partition it cannot be said that there was no partition in law. He further stated that there is evidence on record that the brothers were possessing the property separately and distinctly and that Sagir Ahmed, the appellant No.1 being in possession of the distinct portion of the holding under his vendor and paying rent only to that brother as his landlord should not be allowed to say that his vendor and landlord was a co-sharer with others. It is the further contention of the learned Advocate that Sagir himself separated his tenancy and against that separation of jam a no appeal was preferred and the tenant having paid in a separate jama his specific amount of the rent, the said matter cannot be agitated now before this court on appeal.In support of this contention he has referred to certain decision to which we shall advert at the relevant portion of the judgment. Mr. Habibul Islam lastly submits that the principle enunciated by the Appellate Division in S.M. Basiruddin case reported in XXXV DLR (AD) at page 230 is the law in this field and it is that in case of non-Agricultural tenancy it is the factum of separate possession of the co-owners of the holding which is relevant and not the tenancy and that inspite of one tenancy, the possessors having possessed separately it cannot be said that one is a co-sharer to the other. 

7. In the instant case when one looks at the petition for pre-emption one would find that the averment made initially before the court, asking for pre-emption was that the four brothers were in separate possession for their convenience but there was no separation of the tenancy but there is no averment to the effect that there was no final partition decree and no Partition according to law and hence the court at the first instance had to frame issues relevant to the averment made in the petition and it was to the effect whether the petitioners are co-sharers of the case land and whether the tenancy had been separated. The parties in fact fought out the suit on this two specific issues and that being the position we would limit ourselves within these two issues to find out whether the court below had committed any error of law in arriving at a finding of fact regarding those two issues. 

8. On a reference to the impugned judgment it is seen that the courts below had examined carefully the various sets of documents executed by the broth in favour of the strangers namely the present appellants Nos. 1 and 2 and also the documents of opposite party No. 1-8 and from the evidence on record the court found that the holding was physically partitioned among the four brothers and exhibit 8, the amicable partition map dated 30-11-80 was prepared to that effect and signed by the brothers and the said partition map was confirmed in the Partition Suit No. 161 of 1981 filed by one of the brother for partition of their other properties at Bogra including the instant property at Dhaka. The court had also examined the documents, Exhibit 3 series, and found that the petitioners had purchased block No. B which is well demarcated. In Exhibit 3 the boundary of the appellants-petitioners Kabala land had been stated to be bounded on the north by Vendors land, on the south by Haji Muzaffar Rahman Bhandari land and on the East-Azizullah Road and on the west by the land of the heirs of late Majibur Rahman Bhandari. The court after examining Exhibit 3 series found that on the south of appellant petitioner's purchased land is the land of Muzaffar Rahman, Vendor of opposite party Nos. 1-8 and to the west is the land of the heirs of Muzaffar Rahman and on that the court found that if the land had not been separated amongst the brothers, the vendor of the petitioner would not have mentioned in the sale deed that on the south is the land of Haji Muzaffar Rahman and to the west is the land of the heirs of Mujibur Rahman. The court found from the recitals of the deeds that there was a partition effected by metes and bounds amongst the co- sharers in terms of the compromise decree. The court also found from Exhibit K, K(i), L and L(L), the documents in favour of opposite party Nos. 1-8 that those documents also specifically sold block Nos. 'C' and 'D' by two other brother namely, Matiur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman specifically mentioning that those are their separate blocks. From the said documents the court below found that in fact separate land and building having no connection with block Nos. A and B had been sold by two brothers namely, Matiur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman and that those documents also supports the re-adjusted blocks. It appears that in coming to that finding of fact the court below had examined those documents carefully. We have also re-examined those and find from the recitals appearing in the sale documents in favour of the appellants-petitioners Sagir and other that on the east and on the west the lands of other brothers have been specifically mentioned and that in fact separate blocks have been sold with specific boundary. From a reading of the documents in favour of opposite party Nos. 1-8 we also find that clear recitals have been made therein to the effect that the blocks of lands sold were acquired by the brothers by mutual partition and hence it is seen that the finding of fact arrived at by the court below as to the factum of partition of the land amongst the brother as evidenced by the compromise decree, appears to have been arrived at with cogent reasons and on evidence on record with which we find no illegality to interfere in this appeal. 

9. It has been argued by the appellants that there was no separation of the tenancy and in case of both a Non-Agricultural Tenant and a tenant under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is the co-tenancy of the holding which would determine the status of a tenant as a co-sharer and not possession by amicable partition. In support of that he has referred to certain decisions. 

10. This brings us to the case of S.M. Basiruddin Vs. Zahurul Islam Choudhury and another reported in 35 D.L.R. (AD) page 230. In that case the court had to consider whether the expression such as "non-agricultural land" appearing in the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act and the expression "holding" appearing in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are synonymous, carrying the same meaning for the application of the principle which is applicable to agricultural land that partition alone would not extinguish co-tenancy and the right of pre-emption. It was held by the Appellate Division in that case under report that those two expressions are not synonymous but arc distinct expressions which were used consciously by the legislature. Their Lord-ships of the Appellate Division, having reiterated the principle of law that the right of preemption is not extinguished by mere partition but by a partition of the tenancy itself, had held that the legislature in the case of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, maintained a distinction between the expression "Non-Agricultural land" and "holding" with a purpose which may be to limit the number of applicants for pre-emption of non-agricultural land by making it available only to the co-sharer in the land and not to the co-sharer in the tenancy. It was held, at para 34, thus:- 

"In my opinion the respondent not being co-sharer in the case land transferred though they may be co-sharer in the tenancy, the right of pre-emption did not accrue in their favour" and after finding so it was held that the application for pre-emption must fail. 

11. The court of first instance however on evidence on record found that there was in fact a separation of tenancy when it was the case of the petitioner that no notice of that proceeding were served upon others. Against that it was argued that the matter having not been taken on appeal before the appropriate authority, the said matter can not be agitated here in appeal before this court. The learned advocate has referred to a decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 in support. There is substance in this contention and it need be considered in the affirmative but here we do not have to consider that as we find that the principle enunciated by the Appellate Division in Basiruddin's case reported in 35 DLR(AD) would be relevant in the instant case and that being so the question of joint tenancy-would be irrelevant. 

12. That being the legal position we do not find any illegality committed by the court of first in- stance on this ground as to co-sharer. 

13. Mr. Gholam Rabbani the learned Advocate lastly submits that the court of first instance erred in law in taking into evidence certain documents which on the face of it is inadmissible, namely, the decree passed in the partition suit and the said decree being preliminary in nature and not final the partition had not reached its finality and the final partition decree having not been drawn up on Stamp papers as required under the law, it ought not to have been taken into evidence by the court. There lies the error affecting the merits of the case. 

14. This objection was not taken initially at the time when the court framed the issues or initially when that document or the decree was exhibited in court. A point of law can be agitated even at the appellate stage but not if that point of law calls for de- termination of certain points of fact initially. It appears that objection is now taken on the ground that as the decree was not drawn up in stamp papers it is barred from being admitted to prove any thing. It appears that when that document was admitted no objection was taken as to stamp paper and on the basis of that documents the parties were asked to depose and they in fact deposed on that point. When that is the position we hold that the legality of the admissibility of that document can not be agitated at this stage on appeal as section 36 of the Stamp Act would be a bar. 

15. Section 36 of the Stamp Act provides:- 

"When an instrument has been admitted in evidence, such admission shall not except as provided in section 61, be called in question at any stage of the same suit or proceeding on the ground that the instrument has not been duly stamped." 

16. A similar matter came for decision in the case of Javer Chand Vs. Pakhraj Surana reported in A.I.R. 1961(SC) at page 165. Sinha C.J. in delivering the judgment, at the relevant portion, held, thus:- 

"Where a question as to the admissibility of a document is raised on the ground that it has not been stamped or has not been properly stamped, the party challenging the admissibility of the documents has to be alert to see that document is not admitted in evidence by the court. The court has to judicially determine the matter as soon as the document is tendered in evidence and before it is marked as an exhibit in the case. Once a document has been marked as an exhibit in the case and has been used by the parties in examination and cross-examination of their witnesses; Section 36 comes into operation. Once a document has been admitted in evidence, as aforesaid it is not open either to the Trial Court itself or to a Court of Appeal or Revision to go behind that order. " 

17. We are in respectfully agreement with that. We thus find no substance in the contention that this appeal must be allowed as the decree was exhibited illegally having not been admissible in evidence. 

18. Further, we find that this decree in the partition suit was obtained on the basis of a solenama and the solenama was made part of the decree. The said solenama speaks of a mutual partition amongst the brothers of the property in question by means of a partition map exhibit-H of the year 1980. This partition map has been confirmed by the court by decreeing the suit on compromise making the solenama a part of the decree. It therefore can be said that the decree itself partitioned the property or that there was no final partition decree on compromise. 

19. In the case of Raghubir SahuVs. Ajodhya Sahu & ors. reported in A.I.R. 1945 (Patna) at page 482 it was held thus :- 

"When in a partition suit the properties allotted to the share of each party are clearly specified and schedules of properties allotted to each are appended to the compromise petition, no further enquiry is at all necessary. In such circumstances the compromise decree does not merely declare the rights of the several parties interested in the properties but also allots the properties according to the respective shares of each party. Therefore, it is not a preliminary decree but it is the final decree in the suit. The only thing that remains to be done is to engross it on a stamp paper under Art. 45, Stamp Act There is no time limit prescribed by the statute for the engrossment of a partition decree on stamp of requisite value. Therefore, mere delay in engrossment of the decree on stamped paper of the requisite value will not in any way affect the interests of the parties in respect of the properties though changes may have taken place in regard to the properties since the decree has been made." 

20. We are in respectful agreement with the above observation which are in complete accord with the view we have taken herein before to the effect that the compromise decree affirms what had already been done by the parties and the parties having acted as directed by the court by going into specific possession of respective portion the partition decree though in preliminary form is final. No other points urged and all having been found in the negative we find no substance in these appeals which are thus dismissed without any order as to costs. 

21. The injunction orders passed by this court in Civil Revision No. 298(FM)/84 and No. 297 (FM)/84 are hereby vacated and the Rules are disposed of accordingly. 

Send down the records. 

End.

lawyer:
M. Latifur Rahman—For the Appellant
A.K. Badrul Huq for Syed Mokaddas Ali—For the Respondents
parties:
Ananda Charan Halder-----Appellant
Vs.
Shubhadra Bachar & ors ------Respondent
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 4th December, 1962 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Khulna  in Title Appeal 208/1961 reversing the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif in Title Suit No. 526 of 1959 on 7.8.59. The appeal arises out of the suit for declaration of title over the suit land and for recovery of khas possession.

2. Plaintiff's case in short, is that the suit land comprising an area of 3.14 acres of land belonged to plaintiff's brother Jadab who died 20 years ago leaving behind his widow Jatri, an unmarried daughter Shubhadra was inherited by his Widow Jatri for lifetime and this land  were managed by the plaintiff on behalf of the Jatri who gave the usufructs thereof to her who died in 1360 B.S. the plaintiff inherited the said land as reversionary Subhadra, the daughter of Jatri in. the meantime was married. But she was also sonless Subhadra obtained a patta with respect to the suit land from her mother. The patta is a collusive document and without consideration and there was no legal necessity for Jatri to transfer the same to Shubhadra. As the same patta has clouded the title of the Plaintiff, the plaintiff has been compelled to file this suit. Defendant contested the Suit by filing a written statement. The defdt's ease is that the patta was executed by Jatri in favour of Subhadra for legal . necessity and for a consideration of Tk. 900/- and the defdt is in possession of the suit land from the date of execution of the patta as such the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree. The learned, Munsif decreed the suit.

Being aggrieved the plaintiff filed an appeal. The appeal was allowed and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif was set aside.

Being dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Appellate Court the plaintiff has filed the 2nd appeal.

3.  Mr. Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate has appeared on behalf of the appellant. He submits that the lower appellate court erred in law in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial court without reversing his finding and referring to the material on which the trial court based his finding. He further submits that the learned appellate court erred in law in holding that the transfer in question by Jatri in favour of Subhadra was for legal necessity. According to him this transfer was not genuine and no consideration was passed and the defdt could not prove that the said transfer was for legal necessity. He further contested that in the absence of any proof that the transfer was for the purpose of legal necessity the said transfer cannot he treated as valid transfer by a widow because of the fact she had only life interest in the suit property. In support of his contention Mr. Latifur Rahman has relied on a case reported in 29 DLR pages 6 and 239 as well as a case reported. in 21 DLR page 673.

4. Mr. A. K Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate has appeared on behalf of the respondents. He submits that the rower appellate court was perfectly justified in holding that the transfer in question was  for the purpose of legal necessity lie further submits that in coming to his decision he has referred to the evidence on record and reversed the finding of the learned Munsif referring to the material on which he relied. According to this finding of fact Should not be interfered in support of his contention he has relied on several decisions namely, 17 DLR page 729, 28 DLR page 421, 29 DLR (SC) 268 and 34 DLR page 290.

<u>5. Plaintiff's case is that the suit property originally belonged to Dharma Halder who died leaving 4 sons. Nibaran, Jadab, Baroda and the plaintiff Ananda Jadab died leaving his widow Jatri. After the death of Jadab his widow Jatri inherited his share of interest and used to possess the same. She had a daughter namely Shubhadra who had no son it is the case of the defdt. that Shubbadra's husband sold his property and thereafter purchased the share of Jadab inherited by his widow Jatri for a consideration of Tk. 900. Since then he is in possession Ananda, one of the brothers of Jadab claims the property left by Jadab as a reversioner as Jadab had no son. Defdt's case is that she had purchased the suit land from Jatri, her mother who sold the same of legal necessity. Now the whole question is whether the said sale was for legal necessity or not. In this connection reference may be made to the case reported in 29 DLR page 6 in the case of Mohendra Kumar. Roy and others vs. Akbar Mona and others. It as held:-</u>

<u>"Recital in the document in such a case as to the existence of necessity would be clear evidence of the legal necessity of the alienation, if circumstances are such as to justify a reasonable belief in the mind of the court."</u>

<u>From the above quotation it appears to ascertain whether there was a legal necessity or not recital in the document concerned can be looked into. In the present case document in question has been marked as Ext. A from the recital of his document, it appears that Jatri sold the land to Shubhadra for the purpose of payment of loan and for the purpose of Sharadha of her husband after going to Gaiya and for the purpose of her maintenance. From the recital it appears that the land in question was told for the above noted purposes which can be termed as for the purpose of legal necessity. In this connection reference may be made to a case reported in AIR 1960. Mysore page 260, It was held in that case:—</u>

<u>"Ramappa Gudadapa vs. Chandanagouda Neelangouda. The question of legal necessity is one of fact and the High Court will not interfere with the findings in Second Appeal."</u>

<u>In the present case it appears that the learned lower appellate court on consideration of material on record categorically found that the transfer in question was for legal necessity which finding being a finding of fact and based on evidence on record I think cannot be disturbed in second appeal. In this connection it, may be mentioned that the defdt. adduced evidence in support of her purchase and also to show that the sale in question was for legal necessity which were accepted by the lower appellate court. This finding being based on evidence on record I think cannot be disturbed in 2nd Appeal.</u>

<u>6. Mr. Latifur Rahman next submits that finding of the lower appellate court being based on no evidence and mere surmises and conjecture can be interfered by this court. In support of his contention he has relied on a decision reported in 29 DLR page 239 wherein it was held:—</u>

<u>"A finding of fact not based on evidence but on mere surmises and conjectures is open to interference in second appeal undo section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure."</u>

<u>From the above quotation it appears that the finding of fact arrived at by the final court of fact i.e. the lower appellate court can be interfered with if that finding is based on surmises and conjectures.
