But in the present case I find that the finding of the lower appellate court as to the legal necessity was based an evidence on record and not barely on mere surmises and conjectures. As such I think this cannot be interfered in Second appeal.</u>

<u>7. Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate has referred to several decisions in support of his contention that this Court Should not interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the final court of fact i.e. lower appellate court. In this connection reference may be made to the case reported hi 28 DLR page 421 wherein it was held:</u>

<u>"However gross may be the error on findings of fact the High Court cannot interfere under section 100".</u>

<u>In this connection reference may be made to the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) page 268 in the case of Fakhruddin Mia and another vs Mohammad Khodabaksh Shaikh wherein it was held:</u>

<u>"The finding of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate court is binding on the High Court, both as a second appellate Court and a revisional court, except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances".</u>

8. These are all settled by the decision of this Court as well as by other courts of this subcontinent that the finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court which is a final court of fact cannot be interfered by the High Court in its jurisdiction under sections 100 and 115 of the C.P.C. i.e. in exercising the power in appeal as well as revision. In the present case the fact arrived at by the lower appellate court as to legal necessity in respect of the transfer in question being based on evidence on material on record I think cannot be disturbed in 2nd Appeal.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed, however, without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Asrarul Hossain; Sr. Advocate; (Md. Azim, Advocate with him) instructed by Syed Sakhawat Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant. 
Rokanuddin Mahmood, Advocate instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on- Record ----- For the Respondent No.1.
parties:
General Manager, Jamuna Oil Company Ltd. ----- Appellant
Vs.
Golap Rahman & another ----- Respondents
case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated July 18, 1980 passed by the High Court Division in Writ petition No. 672 of 1978)
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, J:- This appeal arises out of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 672 of 1978 on July 118, 1980.

2. The petitioner which is a company incorporated under the Companies Act challenged the legality of the order of the Labor Court, Chittagong directing it to give termination benefits to respondent No. 1 under section 19(1) of the Employment of Labor (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. Respondent No. 1 who was at first appointed a Driver of an Oil Tanker belonging to the petitioner company was subsequently upgraded as Chief Driver of the taker and since then he had been enjoying the pay scale, facilities and privileges of a member of the Management staff in Group III. According to Marine Rules the, service of respondent No. 1 who attained 57 years of age was terminated. He was given one month's salary in lieu of notice and other benefits to which he was entitled Respondent No. 1 filed an application under section 25(1)(b) of the Standing Orders Act before the Labor Court Chittagong on 13.10.77. He prayed for setting aside the order of termination of service dated 17.8.77 and also for reinstatement with back wages. After hearing the parties the Labor Court held respondent No. 1 to be a worker and directed the petitioner company to give him termination benefits under section 19(1) of the Standing Orders Act. Being dissatisfied with the judgment of the Labor Court the appellant company moved the High Court Division by filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. In agreeing with the decision of the Labor Court the learned Judges of the High Court Division held that respondent No. 1 was a worker as he did not exercise any managerial or supervisory function. They also held that commission to consult a member did not vitiate the decision of the Labor Court. The petitioner company moved this Court and obtained leave to consider three points, namely:-

"1. The respondent is not covered by the definition of worker under the Employment of Labor (Standing Orders) Act 1965 as a Tanker is not an Industrial Establishment under the said Act;

2. Non-consultation of a member had vitiated proceeding;

3. Ext. A(1) of the evidence has excluded the respondent from the category of workers."

3. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, Counsel for the appellant company, made strenuous efforts to show that the views taken by the Labor Court and the High Court Division on the status of respondent No 1, namely, whether he is a worker or a member of the management staff of the petitioner company, were wrong, According to him respondent No. 1 ceased to be a worker when he was promoted as the Chief Driver of the oil tanker. His promotion put him in the category of administrative or managerial staff, and it will be seen that after his promotion he had enjoyed salary and other fringe benefits of the management staff. He was debarred from claiming that he was still a worker. The learned Counsel referred to Ext. A, dated 11th June, 1973 which is a letter of the petitioner company informing respondent No. 1 that he was being promoted to the management staff. It is as follows:-

"I am pleased to advise you that with effect from Its January, 1973 you will be treated as a Management Staff in Croup-Ill and that as from that date (i.e. 1.1.73) your revised salary will be as under, subject to Government restrictions thereon:

Basic…………………….Tk. 685/-

D.A, (@ 40 %) …………Tk. 274/-

Total …...................……Tk. 959/-

2. With effect from 1.1.1973 you will be entitled to House Rent Allowance as applicable to other Management Staff in Group-III.

3. I am confident that you will keep up the standard of good work already attained by you and will also maintain the spirit and zeal that you have shown so far.

4. I take this opportunity to stress that your salary and terms of service are a matter between you and the Company only and as such the same should be treated by you as strictly private and confidential."

4. It is true that this letter refers to the inclusion of the respondent No. 1 in Group III of Management staff with effect from January 1, 1973. Under this letter his salary is revised and he became entitled to house rent allowance payable to other Management staff in Group- III.

5. The learned Counsel therefore, asserted that the managerial capacity of the respondent disentitles him to be treated as a worker. His application under section 25 (1) (b) of the Act is not, therefore, maintainable.

6. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmood, Counsel for respondent No. 1, referred to Ext. A( 1) dated 1.3.73 to show that he did not enjoy all the facilities of Group III Management staff. The relevant portion from this exhibit is quoted below:-

"It is agreed that the crews of QUAMI one excepting Masters and Chief Driver shall be treated as regular employees of the company and shall get benefits of the agreement applicable to shore employees.

As regards Masters and Chief Driver, it is agreed that they will, be treated as management staff ant the existing facilities of management staff in Group- III shall be applicable to them. This will be effective from 1.1.1973.

Note: The following facilities of Group-HI management staff shall not be applicable to Qaumi One Master and Chief Driver:-

(ii) Halting Allowance and

(iii) Any other allowance that may not be applicable to them."

<u>7. It is seen that though the existing facilities of management staff in Group-VI have been made applicable to respondent No. 1 who is the Chief Driver of the oil tanker, the note shows that he will/not enjoy certain facilities of Group-Ill management staff. It will not be, therefore, wrong to suppose that some discrimination existed between the respondent No. 1 and employees in Group-III management staff. Such discrimination obviously negatives the contention that respondent No.1 is not a worker.</u>

8. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, Counsel for the appellant contended that the decision of the Labor Court was without jurisdiction as the Chairman of the Court consulted only one member. According to the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 35 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance a Labor Court is to consist of 2 members to advise the Chairman one of the members to represent the employers and the other to represent the workman. In the present case the Labor Court consisted of the Chairman and two other members. The judgment of the Labor Court shows that only one member who attended the sitting of court was consulted but the Chairman of the Labor Court being unable to agree with him pronounced the judgment as it is.

9. In this connection the learned Counsel for the appellant drew our attention to the relevant provisions of law in two enactments. First, he referred to sub-section (6) of Section 9 of the East Pakistan Labor Disputes Act, 1965 which is as follows:

"If a member is absent from any sitting of the Court or is otherwise incapable to sit as a member or has ceased to be a member of a panel, the Court not withstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, may function in the absence of such member and no act, proceeding, decision or award of a Court shall be invalid merely by reason of absence of any such member from any sitting of a Court and no Court shall call in question any such fact proceeding, decision or award."

Reference was also made to the provisions of sub-section (7) of section 35 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 which provide as follows:-

"If any member of the Labor Court is absent from or is otherwise unable to attend any sitting of the Court the proceeding of the court may continue and the decision or award may be given in the absence of such member; and no act proceeding decision of the Court shall be invalid or called in question merely on the ground of such absence."

10. Mr. Hossain referred to three cases, namely, the case of National Bank of Pakistan vs. Md. Golam Mostafa, (1975) 27 DLR 158, the case of Aminul Islam vs. James Finlay, (1974) 26 DLR (SC) 33 and the case of Project in Charge, Paruma Ltd. Vs Mr. Aminur Rahman Khan, (1979) 31 DLR 124.

11. In the second case, while considering the provisions of sub-section 6 of section 9 of the East Pakistan Labor Disputes Act, 1965, which provide for the functioning of the Court in the absence of a member, it was observed that there was no question of obtaining the advice of a member where he is incapable to sit as a member or ceases to be a member of the panel, as under both the circumstances the said member ceases to be a member of the Court. It was further observed that since the legislature authorised the Labor Court to function in the absence of such member, this clearly indicates that the advice is not intended to be mandatory but directory. It was held that if the award was made without any advice from either member it will not be vitiated. 10 answering the question whether the advice of the members of the Court is mandatory, Ahsanuddin, J. who delivered the judgment, said

"Needless to say that difficulties are sometimes felt to determine whether a certain provision of statute is directory or mandatory. When the legislature itself expresses its opinion as to the consequence of non-compliance with a certain direction, no difficulty arises but in a case where the legislature does not indicate its mind as to the consequence of violation of such direction, the Court is to consider whether the direction is merely directory or mandatory and this is to be determined on the construction of the provision in question and the importance attached to the direction therein."

It was further observed:

"It can hardly be disputed that if the advice is said to be mandatory it shall be mandatory with respect to advice of both the members of the Court and no exception can be made with respect to any of them. It will however become impossible to fulfill the requirement of law as regards and vice when a member ceases to be a member of the panel or when he becomes incapable to sit as a member. If the legislature intended the advice of the members to be mandatory, it must have made necessary provisions to meet such eventualities either by reconstitution of the Court or by substitution of a member from the penal in the place of the one becoming incapable to sit as a member or ceasing to be a member of the panel. Instead, the legislature has authorised the Court to function in the absence of such member. No advice can be sought or obtained from the said erstwhile member. This situation does not indicate that the advice is intended to be mandatory,

12. The provisions of sub-sec. (7) of section 35 of toe Industrial Relations Ordinance-which are similar to the provisions of section 9(6) of Labor Disputes Act, 1965 were considered in the first case mentioned above. There it was observed that the total absence of a member would render the decision of the Labor Court void as the section did not contemplate the total absence of member. For, such absence would reduce the Labor Court to a one member tribunal.

K. Hossain, J. as he then was, observed as follows:

"The expression requiring interpretation is any sitting. According to the learned Advocate for the bank any sitting may mean one sitting or more than one sitting. "but it cannot mean all the sittings, According to Mr. Huq any sitting means each sitting taken singly on each occasion and must be taken in that isolated sense, even though it may turn out that the absence was from all the sittings. The submission of Mr. Huq is no doubt ingenious, but it does not stand the scrutiny of either the logic or the section. Logically, it is fallacy to say it is one and not one at the same time Nothing can be more fallacious than to take each sitting in the proceeding in isolation and to ignore the aggregate. If we look to the tender of the enactment specially sub-section (2) of section 35, it is manifest that law makers contemplated the tender of advice obligatory. True, advice is not binding on the Chairman, but the tender of the advice has not been dispensed with There is no language to that effect. To construe otherwise will make the effect of sub-section (2) illusory. Such an interpretation making a provision illusory is against all principles of Interpretation of Statutes.

In our opinion, therefore, 'any sitting' means one or more than one sitting, but it does not mean all the sittings, or in other words a total absence. Had that been the purpose of the law makers, they would have employed some other language, and there is nothing in the language of the section to convey a case of total absence.

To hold otherwise would be to reduce the Labor Court to a one member instead of two members Tribunal."

13. These two cases were referred to in the last mentioned case where it was held that if the proceeding of a Labor. Court started with the required number of members the subsequent absence of any member, or his ceasing to be a member or his incapacity to sit as a member of the court need not be considered as a bar to the functioning of the Court. Shahabuddin J, as he was then observed:

"Sub-Section (7) of section 35 appears to be an enabling provision, i. e. that is to say, if a member of the Labor Court is absent from any sittings the proceeding "may continue" in his absence. The words "the proceeding may continue" in this sub-section show that the proceeding has already started with the required number of members. If thereafter there is any casual absence of any member or if he ceases to be a member or is incapable of sitting in the Court further, the proceeding need not be stopped but it may be carried to its conclusion. We, therefore, are of the opinion that sub-section (7) provides for continuation of a proceeding in absence of a member if the proceeding already started with the Chairman and both the members, and that thy total absence of a member means in effect that, the Court has not been duly constituted."

<u>14. Question is whether the provisions of sub-section (7) of section 35 are mandatory, or merely directory. From the provisions of this section it would appear that if after the constitution of the Court, a member is absent from any sitting of the Court such absence will not invalidate the decision of the Court. Expression "any" which qualifies the word "sitting" means one or all the sittings of the Court. If therefore a member is absent from the sitting of the Court or fails to attend any sitting of the Court after his, inclusion in the panel of the Court, there is no obligation upon the Chairman to obtain his advice. To try to obtain advice from a member who has been partially or wholly absent from the sittings of the Court will itself be meaningless.</u>

<u>This however, does not lead to the conclusion that a Labor Court may proceed to function without any member being present at all, On the other hand, even if a member is absent or ceases to be a member or incapable of sitting as a member, it has been empowered to continue to function. As no obligation has been imposed upon a member to attend the sitting of the Court, no consequence follows his failure to attend the sitting of the Court. What appears to be incumbent is that a two-member panel was to be created to assist the Court. What has not been provided in the section itself cannot be provided by the Court by stretching the language of the section beyond its normal meaning. Accordingly, the proceeding before the Labor Court cannot be declared to have, been illegal.</u>

<u>15. To me it appears that the intention of the legislature as appears from the language employed in sub-section (7) of section 35 of the Ordinance shows that the Court itself either cannot compel the attendance of such member or extract his advice.</u>

For the reasons stated above, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 6025 of 1991 (Dhaka) and Civil Revision No. 256 of 1986 (Jessore)
lawyer: Md. Abdur Rahim, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners.
parties:
Abul Hossain Molla and another ----- Petitioner
Vs. 
Khoteza Nessa Bibi and others ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
In this Rule plaintiff-respondent-opposite parties were directed to show cause as to why the Judgment and Decree passed by the learned District Judge, Magura-Narail, (at Magura) in Title Appeal No. 45 of 1985 affirming the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif at Sreepur Upazila in Title Suit No. 113 of 1984 decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted on 20.3.84 the Title Suit No. 113 of 1984 in the Court of the learned Munsif, Sreepur, praying for declaration that the registered deed of Heba dated 16.1.71 executed by one Hazi Abdur Rahman in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, namely the resent petitioners, is bogus, tainted with fraud, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiffs. It is stated that Hazi Abdur Rahman was the owner of the suit land and after his death the present plaintiffs became the owners of the suit land by inheritance. Hazi Abdur Rahman was issueless. He died leaving behind his wife plaintiff No. 1 and heirs namely, plaintiff Nos. 2-3 who took care of him but the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 fraudulently got the Heba deed executed and registered by Hazi Abdur Rahman on 16.1.71 through fraudulent means. Since the deed of gift was fraudulent and collusive plaintiff prayed for declaration for cancellation of the aforesaid Heba deed.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2, the present petitioners, contested the suit by filing written statement contending that the plaintiffs never took care of Hazi Abdur Rahman. The story made in the plaint is absolutely false and fabricated. Abdur Rahman at the age of 80 years was killed by some unknown persons. Hazi Abdur Rahman had no issue, His wife took defendant No. 1 as adopted son. The fathers of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 died in their boyhood and deceased Hazi Abdur Rahman loved them. He spent money for their education and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 also took care of him. The plaintiffs did never take any care of the deceased Hazi Abdur Rahman though they were near relations of deceased Hazi Abdur Rahman. It is their case that out of love and affection and without any influence from any quarter Hazi Abdur Rahman voluntarily executed and registered the impugned deed of gift and as such the suit was not maintainable. Both the parties adduced evidence both oral and documentary. After hearing the parties and perusing the materials on record the learned Munsif by his judgment dated 31.3.85 decreed the suit declaring the deed of gift dated 16.1.71 bogus, tainted with fraud, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiffs. Against the aforesaid Judgment and decree the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 preferred appeal being Title Appeal No. 43 of 1985 and the learned District Judge, after hearing the parties and perusing the materials on record by his Judgment dt. 15.7.86, dismissed the appeal affirming the Judgment and decree of the trial Court. The present petitioners defendant Nos. 1 and 2 being aggrieved by the aforesaid Judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court preferred this revisional application and obtained the-present Rule.

4. In this case it appears that both the parties are near relations of late Hazi Abdur Rahman and the plaintiff claimed that the deed of gift in question is a fraudulent one and they by inheritance are the owners and possessors of the suit land. The moot question comes up in this case as to whether the deed of gift is genuine or not.

5. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that plaint itself in the present case is not maintainable in view of provision of Order 6 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, He submits that in a cause in which anybody pleads any misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, wilful default, or undue influence he must specifically spell out the same in the plaint itself, He submits that in this plaint the pleadings as regards fraud have not been specifically spelt out in it, only an assertion has been made that through fraudulent means the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 got the deed of gift executed and registered by Hazi Abdur Rahman. I have gone through the plaint. It appears that allegation of fraud has been made no doubt but as to how and by what means fraud was committed or practised has not been clearly described in the plaint. DW 1 is the son of the cousin and DW 2 is sister's son of late Hazi Abdur Rahman. It is the defendant's case that since Hazi Abdur Rahman was childless they used to look after Hazi Abdur Rahman and out of love and affection late Hazi Abdur Rahman executed the deed of gift on 16.1.71 in their favour. In this connection Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim has referred to the Judgment of both the courts below and has tried to argue that the courts below did not spell out in their Judgment as to how and by what means fraud was committed and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 got the deed of gift registered from Hazi Abdur Rahman. In a case like this the plaintiffs are required to prove their own case on the basis of the evidence, both oral and documentary, In this conrection Mr. Rahim has referred to the case of Ananta Kumar Bepari Vs. Jamini Mohan Das and others reported in 4 DLR 487 wherein it is held by their Lordships that party pleading fraud must prove it specifically and general allegation of fraud cannot be entertained. Similar view was taken in the case of Mr. Ghaus Bakhsh Bizenjo, Chief Election Commissioner of Pakistan & others, 22 DLR (WP) 178. So, in the plaint as well as in the deposition of PW 1 general allegation of fraud is made but there is no specific description as to how, when and by what means fraud was committed and as such fraud could not be proved by material evidence on record by the plaintiff.

6. Mr. Rahim further submits that onus of proving fraud is heavily upon him who alleges fraud. In this connection he has referred to the case Subitri Bari Vs. Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and ADC (Revenue) Patuakhali & others 39 DLR 172. Now let me consider the evidence on record, both documentary and oral to see as to whether the plaintiffs have discharged their onus to prove fraud. In this connection it may be noted that this deed of gift was registered on 16.1.71 and plaintiffs claiming themselves as heirs of late Hazi Abdur Rahman had filed the suit on 20.3.84 that is, after about 13 years.

7. The general allegation of fraud is made in the plaint and the general allegation is also made by PW 1 in his deposition. The plaintiffs examined Imanuddin MondaI as PW 2. He stated that he heard that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 got a deed of Gift. In cross examination this PW 2 stated that about 10 years back he heard about this deed of gift. He further stated that late Hazi Abdur Rahman had given some land to his wife through a deed of gift. His wife is plaintiff No. 1. She is not coming to depose before the Court. This witness further stated that by that deed of gift plaintiff No. 1, the wife of late Hazi Abdur Rahman, got the homestead. Part of the suit land was possessed by the defendant No. 1. I have gone through the deposition of PW 3 Siddique Miah. He stated that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 had dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land. He stated that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have been possessing the suit land. Now excepting the general allegation of fraud as made in the plaint as well as in the deposition of PW 1, who is the most vitally interested witness in this case, I find no other evidence to show that fraud has been proved by the plaintiffs. PWs 2 and 3 did not say a single word as regards commission of fraud by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in respect of getting the impugned deed of gift. So I find that plaintiffs totally failed to discharge their onus that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 got the suit land by way of the deed of gift through fraud.

8. Now let me consider the Judgments of the two courts below. I have carefully gone through the Judgment of the trial Court which has given reasonings in details but, unfortunately, it appears that the trial Court had found some defects and discrepancies of the evidence of DWs here and there. Solely replying upon some defects in the oral deposition of the DWs it decreed the suit. As I have stated above that since fraud has been alleged and since plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of the deed of gift being void, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs, they are required to prove fraud but thereby failed. The trial Court found all faults in the oral depositions of the DWs. He has not considered and discussed anything about the oral evidence of the PWs. It is now established principle that on the weakness of the defendants, the plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree in a suit like this rather plaintiffs are required to prove their own case in order to get a decree. The judgment of the trial Court shows that only on the alleged defects of the depositions of the DWs it came to a conclusion that the deed of gift was bogus, fraudulent and illegal. He did not even care to go through the depositions of the PWs 2 and 3 which admitted possession of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 of the suit land. Further PW 2 admitted that he heard about this deed of gift about 10 years back, it means that in the year 1975 he heard it. So the Judgment of the trial Court solely relying upon some defects and discrepancies of oral evidence of DWs cannot be sustained in law.

9. Now let me see the Judgment of the lower Appellate Court. In fact it is a Judgment of one and half pages; He did not discuss any evidence whatsoever, either the deposition of DWs. He simply accepted the conclusion of the trial Court that the deed of gift was collusive and fraudulent He stated that PWs. proved the contention of the plaintiffs and corroborated each other. This finding is absolutely wrong and contrary to the evidence. PWs 2 and 3 did not in any way corroborate with the evidence of PW1 Even lower Appellate Court has not discussed anything not even a sentence about the deposition of the PWs. He further found that conduct of the defendants was not fair as the defendant did not produce the original document for fear of detection of fraud. The defendants filed the certified copy of the impugned deed of gift with an explanation as to how original was missing. Merely because the defendants failed to produce the original registered deed of gift, a registered deed of gift cannot be called a fraudulent one without considering and discussing other material evidence on record.

10. Mr. Rahim submits that the Judgment of the Appellate Court below is not a proper Judgment of reversal and also not proper Judgment of the Appellate Court itself. The Lower Appellate Court has neither discussed the evidence of the PWs nor the DWs. In a short-cut manner he just approved the Judgment and decree of the trial Court, I have found above that the Judgment of the lower Appellate Court cannot be sustained in law as it discharged its onus only by writing a few sentences. This deed of gift was registered on 16.1.71 and the suit was filed on 20.3.82. PW 2 said that about 10 years back that is in 1975 he came to know about this deed of gift. PWs 2 and 3 also stated that they found the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 possessing part of the suit land. On this point Mr. Rahim submits that the present suit is absolutely barred by limitation. Although it was not specifically urged in the Court below yet Mr. Rahim submits from oral evidence on record that the suit is barred by limitation. He submits that limitation will run either under article 91 or Article 120 of the Limitation Act. Since the evidence of the plaintiff's shows that by the year 1975 PW 2 came to know about the sale deed the suit for cancellation of the same was filed on 20.3.84 and. as such. it is hit under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. I find force in the above contention of Mr. Rahim.

<u>11. Mr. Rahim further submits that the registered deed of gift has got presumptive value unless contrary is proved. In this connection he has referred to the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner Revenue and Assistant Custodian Vested Property, Chandpur Vs. Tafurnessa & others 41 DLR (AD) 124 and the case of Haji Kari Abdur Rahman Vs. Abdur Rahim Gazi reported in 35 DLR 132. It is true by registered deed of transfer the title of the owner of the property is legally transferred to the transferee unless contrary is proved. Here in the present case I find that nothing can be proved to the effect that the registration of the deed of gift is illegal or fraudulent. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record I am of the view that the plaintiffs have totally failed to prove their case of fraud with regard to the deed of gift giving in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. It is the case of the defendant that the wife of late Hazi Abdur Rahman loved them very much and that is why she is not coming forward to depose in this case though she is the plaintiff No. 1. If that lady comes and deposes against defendant Nos. 1 and 2 some weight might have been given upon such evidence. It is observed in the judgment of the trial Court that wife of late Hazi Abdur Rahman is begging from door to door. This allegation is absolutely wrong in view of the evidence of PW 2 who stated that by earlier deed of gift Hazi Abdur Rahman had given some property and homestead to his wife plaintiff No. 1. So, the allegation of poverty against plaintiff No. 1 is belied by the evidence of PW 2 himself; Considering the facts and circumstance of the case and the material evidence on record I am of the view that plaintiffs have failed to make out a case of fraudulent document and as such both the courts below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. In the result this Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the judgment and decree passed by the lower Appellate Court affirming those of the trial Court are hereby set aside and the suit filed by the plaintiffs is hereby dismissed.</u>

End.
