Vs.
Haji Ashraf Ali Chowdhury and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: Appeal against the decree of Mr. A. K. Faizuddin Ahmed, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court of Zilla Chittagong dated the 16th day of February, 1966 passed in Money Appeal No. 13 of .1963 reversing the decree of Mr. Altaf Hossain Munsif 1st Court, Chittagong dated the 19th day of September, 1963 in Money Suit No. 35 of 1962.
full_judgment:
The question involved in this Second Appeal is, whether former ruling which is res judicata loses its force because it has been dissented from or overruled in another case.

The question arises out of the following circumstances:—

2. The plaintiff filed Money Suit No. 35 of 1962 for recovery of rent in respect of suit land for the period from 1363 B.S. to Kartick 1364 B.S. at a yearly rent of Rs. 1700/- with compensation. His case was that the defendants predecessor hired the suit land on the basis of Karayanama executed by him on 4-9-49 for a term of 30 years at a yearly rent of Rs. 1700/-. The plaintiff constituted a waqf in respect of the suit land along with other lands. He instituted Monry Suit No. 21 of 1958 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong as Mutwalli of the suit land and obtained a decree against the predecessor of the defendants for recovery of the rent from 1363 B.S. to Athar 1365 B.S. The predecessor of the defendants preferred an appeal and the Appellate Court notified the decree to the extent that the plaintiff's claim for rent for the period from 1363 BS to Kartick 1364 BS was disallowed inas-much as it was held that prior to that period no waqf was created. So the plaintiff filed the present suit to recover arrear rent of 1363 BS upto 20th Kartick, 1364 B.S. in his individual capacity.

3. The main ground on which the defendant No. 1 entered the contest was that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover rent from the defendants inasmuch as his interest, being that of a "lent receiver", within the meaning of sub-section (23) of section 2 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, hereinafter referred to as the said Act, had vested in the Government under provisions of the said Act.

4. The trial Court by judgment dated 19-9-63 upheld the contentions of the defendant and dismissed the suit holding that the rent receiving interest of the plaintiff having been acquired by the Government the plaintiff has lost his interest in the suit land and as such he is not entitled to recover rent.

5. The plaintiff preferred an appeal. In the meanwhile the predecessor of the defendant in the previous Money Suit No. 21 of 1954 preferred a Second Appeal to the then Dacca High Court against the judgment address of the first appellate Court modifying the decree of the trial Court. That appeal, being Second Appeal No. 281 of 1961, was heard and disposed of by Murshed, C.J. on the 4th June, 1965. It may be mentioned in this connection that the defence raised by the predecessor of the defendants in M.S. No. 21 of 1958 was the same as in the present suit, namely, that the plaintiff was a rent receiver. Murshed, C.J. quoted sub-section (23) of section 2 of the said Act as follows:—

"rent receiver" means a proprietor or a tenure holder, and includes a raiyat, or a non-agricultural tenant whose land has been let out and also the immediate landlord of a person who holds any land free of rent in consideration of some service to be rendered, but does not include a person in respect of such of his lands as has been let out, together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity.

"Thereafter his Lordship observed as follows: "Analysing the aforesaid definition of "rent receiver", it would be clear that if a proprietor or a tenure holder has a raiyat or an under-raiyat under him, than the said proprietor or tenure-holder becomes a rent-receiver, and, with regard to non-agricultural land, which has been leased out otherwise than in perpetuity, the holder of the land does not become a rent receiver."

6. Murshed, C.J. thus held that the plaintiff was not a rent-receiver. The appellate Court below in the present Appeal took into consideration the aforesaid judgment of Murshed, C.J. which has been reported in 17 DLR 329 On the view that in the previous M.S. No. 21 of 1958 and in the present M.S. No. 35 of the 1962 the same issue namely, whether the plaintiff was a rent-receiver or not was directly and substantially in issue between the same parties and their successors and that the same has been resolved in favour of the plain-tiff, the appellate Court below by its judgment dated 16-2-66 held that the defendants defence is barred by res judicata and decreed the suit.

The defendant No. 1 is the appellant in this appeal.

7. Mr. M.M. Hoque, the learned Advocate for the appellant has contended that the view of the law that Murshed, CJ. had taken in the previous suit between the parties failed to take note of the fact that if a non-agricultural tenant is to be kept out of the definition of "rent-receiver" contained in sub-section (23) of section 2 of the said Act he must lease out his land together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity. In the present case, he submits, the plaintiff has not let out any non-agricultural land with any building standing thereon. It appears from the facts of the case that the plaintiff has let out, non-agricultural land simplicitier, not with any building thereon. The decision reported in 17 DLR 329. Mr. M.M. Hoque further submits, has been arrived at without noticing the words "together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity" in the definition of the word "rent-receiver"

8. Mr.M. M. Hoque further submits that in a later decision of another Single Bench of the Dacca High Court, in the case of Suraton Nessa Vs. Debendra Nath, reported in 18 DLR 490 it was held that the words "otherwise than in perpetuity" inthe definition of the word rent-receiver" govern the words "a person in respect of such of his lands as has been let out, together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto." These words do not govern the earlier portion of the definition. Mr. M.M. Hoque submits that if this decision is followed then the plaintiff clearly becomes a rent-receiver because he has not let out non-agricultural land with any building thereon.

9. Mr. M. M. Hoque has further referred to a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court, namely case of Aminbagh Co-operative Society Ltd. vs. The Province of East Pakistan reported in 19 D.L.R. 50, wherein Murshed, C.J. sitting with Muksum-ul-Hakim, J. by a later judgment dated the 29th June, 1966 was pleased to hold that by letting out premises with structure the appellant is exempted from the definition of a rent-receiver unless the lease is in perpetuity. Mr. M.M. Hoque submits that Murshed, C.J. who had earlier decided the case reported in 17 D.L.R. 329 has been pleased to take note of the full version of the definition of the word "rent-receiver" and has come to a correct decision in the latter case.

10. Mr. M.M. Hoque has further referred to the case of M. H. Khandakar, Advocate Vs. Bangladesh, reported in 30 DLR (SC) 1, wherein the definition of "rent-receiver" as provided in the said Act has been considered and it has been observed by their Lordships as follows:

"The definition of "rent-receiver" and "khasland" kept the interest of the landlord letting out land together with building and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity, outside the mischief of acquisition"

11. From all the above Mr. M. M. Hoque argues that it is now the settled law that if a non-agricultural tenant is to be taken out of the ambit of rent-receiving interest he must let out his land with building thereon otherwise than in perpetuity. The present case presents a contrary picture. The plaintiff has let out non-agricultural land simplicities for a period of 30 years. He is therefore a rent-receiver.

12. Mr. M. M. Hoque submits on the authority of the case of Palaniappa Chettiar vs. Parvatibibi reported in A.I.R. 1972 Madras 52 that a former decision between the parties rendered in accordance with the case law then in force can be reopened by any of the parties at the subsequent stage of the proceeding on the ground of change in the case law rendering the former decision erroneous. He has also referred is support of his contention to a Single Bench decision of the Dacca High Court, the case of Habibur Rahman Vs. Sankar Bank Ltd. reported in 16 D.L.R. 516, wherein it has been held that a Civil Court may entertain a suit to execute any decree under changed circumstances. Any decision on the question of maintainability of a suit or a petition or execution of a decree or order will not operate as a res judicata for all time to come.

<u>13. It is no doubt apparent that in coming to a finding as to whether the plaintiff was a rent-receiver or not certain words in the definition of the word "rent-receiver" in 17 DLR 329. It is also apparent that subsequently the definition of "rent-receiver"has received fuller treatment in another Single Bench decision of the Dacca High Court and even in the hands of Murshed C. J. sitting later in a Division Bench. Our erstwhile Supreme Court has also endorsed the latter interpretation of the definition of "rent-receiver." The question now is, can this later development in the interpretation of the relevant provision on law render invalid the bar of res-judicata in a subsequent suit between the same parties or their successors?</u>

<u>14. I have my anxious thoughts to this question and have been unable to persuade myself as to why such changes or reversal in the interpretation of law or in the application of law to facts will render the bar of res judicata ineffective. The few occasions when the bar of res judicata are removed are inter alia when the law governing the earlier decision has been altered by a competent authority, when the decision relates to the jurisdiction of the Court to try the earlier proceeding and when the earlier decision declares valid a transaction which is prohibited by law. Barring these situations previous decision on an issue of law or a mixed issue of fact and law will be res judicata in a subsequent proceeding between the same parties, the reason being that the previous decision on a matter in issue alone is res judicata. The reasons for the decision are not res judicata.</u>

<u>15. The Supreme Court of India, in the case of Mathura Vs. Dossibai, (1970) 1 SCC 613, observed as follow:-</u>

<u>"A matter in issue between the parties is the right claimed by one party and denied by the other, and the claim of right from its very nature depends upon proof of facts and application of the relevant law thereto. A pure question of law unrelated to facts which gives rise to a right, cannot be deemed to be a matter in issue. When it is said that a previous decision is res judicata it is meant that the right claimed has been adjudicated upon and cannot again be placed in contest between the parties. A previous decision of a competent Court on facts which are the foundation of the right and the relevant law applicable to the determination of the transaction which is the source of the right is res judicata. A previous decision on a matter in issue is a composite decision; the decision on law cannot be dissociated from the decision on facts on which the right is founded. A decision on an issue of law will be as res judicata in a subsequent proceeding between the same parties if the cause of action of the subsequent proceeding be the same as in the previous proceeding, but not when the cause of action is different, nor when the law has since the earlier decision been altered by a competent authority, nor when the decision relates to the jurisdiction of the Court to try earlier proceeding nor when the earlier decision declares valid a transaction which is prohibited by law."</u>

16. I am in respectful agreement with the above observation. In the present case circumstances in the application of law have not changed and so the decision reported in 16 D.L.R. 576 has no application. The decision reported in A.I.R. 1972 Madras 52 merely say that in view of the subsequent contrary decision by the Supreme Court an erroneous decision of the High Court will not operate as a bar to the principle of res judicata, but fails to give any reason for the opinion given. Moreover the decision applies to subsequent stages of the same proceeding, not to a subsequent suit.

<u>17. I am clearly of the opinion that no matter whether a previous ruling is dissented from or reserved a concluded question of right between the parties in a previous suit will be binding on both the parties in a subsequent suit and will operate as res judicata. I am supported in my view by a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court, the case of Mofazal Ahmed Vs. Abdus Sattar reported in 16 D.L.R. 92, wherein it has been held that a ruling of a Supreme Court cannot undo the effect of a decision arrived at on the basis of the previous ruling. I am also supported in my view by a Division Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court, in the case of Ganesh Prasad vs. Mr. Makhan, reported in A.I R. 1948 All, 375, wherein it has been held that where a decision is res judicata it cannot lose its force by reason of a subsequent ruling in another case overruling the decision.</u>

<u>For the reason stated above the appeal is dismissed. The judgment and decree of the Appellate Court below are affirmed. There will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Faqueer Shahabuddin Ahmed with A.N.M. Gaziul Hoq M.A. Halim and Maleka Parveen ----- For the Petitioner.
Abdus Subhan. Additional Attorney General with M.M. Huq A.A. G. ----- For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Dr. Neelima Ibrahim ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
People's Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Women's Affairs, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dacca, ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
MH Rahman J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner has called in question the following order:—

"Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh"

Ministry of Women's Affairs Bangladesh Secretariat

Mo MWA/E-18/80. Dated, the 19th April 80.

ORDER

Whereas the Institution now called Bangladesh Mahila Samity has been in existence since before last January, 1972 and from Pakistan time when it was called APWA (All Pakistan Women's Association) and subsequently renamed as Bangladesh Mahila Samity after emergence of Bangladesh.

And whereas the Bangladesh Mahila Samity is indulging in political activities contrary to its aims and objects and against the public interest.

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by clause 1 of Article 3 of Bangladesh Committee of Management (Temporary Arrangement) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 117 of 1972) the Government is pleased to: (a) dissolve the Central Executive Committee (Committee of Management) of the Bangladesh Mahila Samity with immediate effect; and (b) appoint an Ad-hoc Committee.

By order of the President

Sd/-

(KGM Latiful Bari)

Additional Secretary-in-Charge."

2. The petitioner is a member of the Bangladesh Mahila Samity and she was the President of its Central Executive Committee on 19-4-80 when the above order was communicated to her. The Samity acquired assets and liabilities of All Pakistan Women's Association under the authority of Government order dated February 28, 1972. By the same order an Ad-hoc Committee was appointed for performing specified duties. After promulgation of PO 117 of 1972 another Ad-hoc Committee constituted by the Government under Article 3 of the Order framed a constitution and held election in 1973. After the expiry of term of that election another election was held in December, 1976. With due authority of the Samity the date for election of the Management Committee was fixed on the 28th April, 1980. In the evening of the 19th April the petitioner received the impugned order. The petitioner moved this application both as a member of the Samity as well as the President of its Management Committee.

3. The respondent's case is that the petitioner ceased to be the President of the Samity from 19-4-80. The term of the office of the Executive Committee was reduced from three to two years by a direction dated 4-8-77 of the Social Welfare Directorate. The impugned order was in accordance with law and not intended to postpone the election; that the Secretary of the Ad-hoc Committee, Mrs Moshfaqua Mahmood, had already assumed charge on 19-4-80; that on 22-4-80 in an emergent meeting of the Ad-hoc Committee it had been resolved that General Election of the Samity would held within six months.

4. Mr Faqueer Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has contended that President's Order No. 117 of 1972 is ultra vires to the Constitution as it has violated the freedom of association guaranteed under Article 38 of the Constitution, and, in the alternative, if the law is intra vires, the power under Article 3 of the President's Order is not available to the respondent as the Ad-hoc Committee that had earlier been appointed was replaced by a duly elected Committee of Management under Article 4 of the said order. Mr Ahmed has submitted that the impugned order is violative of principle of natural justice and it was passed mala fide on the eve of the election when all preparations for holding the election for the Central Executive Committee were set.

5. Mr MA Subhan the learned Additional Attorney-General, has challenged the locus standi of the petitioner. He has contended that the Petition is bad for not impleading necessary parties. He has submitted that the President's Order No. 117 of 1972 is not only an existing law at the time of the commencement of the Constitution but it was later amended by the Parliament by an Act, Act XXIX of 1973. He has also denied that there has been any violation of principle of natural justice or that the order was passed malafide.

6. Let us first take up the objections as to the petitioner's standing. It is contended that the term of the office of the petitioner had already expired. In absence of any authority given by the Samity to the President extending her term till the election of her successor or in absence of any such rules of the Samity, she cannot claim to exercise any power as the President, particularly, after the dissolution of Committee of Management. The Samity is not a statutory of public character and the rules of the Society are rules for its internal management and any infringement of an alleged right arising out of these rules cannot be questioned under Article 102 of the Constitution. The Samity, being registered under the Societies Act, 1860, and it ought to have been made a party in the case. The twelve members of the Ad-hoc Committee are interested parties and they were rightly, at first, impleaded by the petitioner, but on the petitioner's own application they were struck off from the petition.

7. Mr Faqueer Shahabuddin Ahmed has pointed out that to avoid complication and multiplicity of litigations he prayed for striking off the names of respondent Nos. 2 to 12. According to him this was done in his anxiety to get an expeditious hearing of the matter.

8. Let us briefly refer to the cases cited on behalf of the respondent with regard to the petitioner's standing. In Masudul Hasan vs Khadem Hussain PLD 1963 (SC) 203 Cornelius, CJ questioned whether it was appropriate in a proceeding of a writ of mandamus to make a finding on the validity of an order of dismissal by a Municipal authority, not a party of the case. However, in that case the order of the High Court was maintained on the ground of the circumstances casting a doubt upon the validity of the dismissal.

9. In the case of AFM Abul Fateh vs Province of East Pakistan 17 DLR 475 the Court refused to interfere where the heirs of a deceased allottee were not made parties by the petitioner challenging an order in respect of the allotment of the same plot of land.

10. In Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury vs Union of India AIR 1951 (SC) 41 Mukherjee, J observed that "it would not be open to an individual share-holder to complain of an Act which affects the fundamental rights of the Company except to the extent that it constitutes an infraction of his own rights as well." In that case by the majority decision the appeal of the share-holder was dismissed as he failed to discharge the prima facie burden to show that the impugned Act violated his right to property, but by the majority decision the appeal was allowed as the impugned Act denied him the protection of law relating to incorporated joint stock companies and it was prima facie within the inhibition of Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

11. In the State of Assam vs Ajit Kumar Sarma AIR 1965 (SC) 1196 the Indian Supreme Court held that it is only for the governing body of an aided college to decide whether to carry out any direction contained in mere administrative instructions laying down conditions for grant-in-aid under the Assam Aided Cottage Employees Rules (1960). Where the governing body chose to carry out an instruction, a teacher could not apply to the High Court for a mandamus against the State through the Director of Public Instruction for enforcement or non-enforcement of the rules, even if indirectly they might have some effect on him because of the grant-in-aid being with-held by the State in whole or in part.

12. It has been urged on behalf of the respondent that the petitioner is not entitled to seek restoration of her private office of the Presidentship. In support of this contention the following decisions are cited; Zainul Abedin vs Multan Co-operative Bank 18 DLR (SC)482; Chairman EPIDC vs Rustam Ali 19 DLR (SC) 106; Zeaul Huq vs The East Pakistan Co-Operative Society 19 DLR 498; Munshi Abdul Zabbar vs Barisal Municipal Committee 20 DLR 1186 and Shamsuzzaman vs Province of East Pakistan 22 DLR 52. These decisions have no manner of application in the present case. In each of them an employee's application for restoration to his office in an organization, not of public nature, was held as not maintainable. In the present case the petitioner is not seeking restoration to any office of employment.

13. Just before closing his arguments Mr Ahmed has very fairly brought to our notice the case of MR Khan vs Bangladesh and others reported in 27 DLR 603, which appears to have escaped the industry of the learned additional Attorney-General. In this case the governing body of the Bangladesh National Society for the Blind was suspended and a Care-taker Body was constituted by the Director, Social Welfare in pursuance to Section 9 (1) of the Voluntary Social Welfare Agencies (Registration and Control) Ordinance 1961. The Chairman of the suspended governing body alone moved an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. It was held by Fazle Munim, J and SM Hussain, J that the petitioner had no locus standi to prefer the petition. Reliance was placed by the Care-taker Body on Durayappoh vs Fernando and others (1967).

All ER 152. In that case the Municipal Council of Jaffna in Ceylon was dissolved by an order of the Minister of the Local Government under the provision of a subsisting law without hearing the Council. Their Lordships opined that the Minister's order was voidable and not a nullity, and it was voidable only at the instance of a person against whom the order was made, that is, the Council. Their Lordships observed;

"The appellant was no doubt mayor at the time of its dissolution, but that does not give him any right to complain independently of the council. He must show that he is representing the council or suing on its behalf or that by reason of certain circumstances such for example as that the council could not use its seal because it is in the possession of the municipal commissioner, or that for other reasons it has been impracticable for the members of council to meet to pass the necessary resolutions the council cannot be the plaintiff. Had that been shown then there are well-known procedures whereby the plaintiff can sue on behalf of himself and the other corporators making the council a defendant, and on pleading and proving necessary facts may be able to establish in the action that he is entitled to assert the rights of the council. That, however, is not suggested in this case. The appellant sets up the case that as mayor he is entitled to complain but as such he plainly is not. If the council is dissolved, the office of mayor is dissolved with it and he has no independent right of complaint, because he holds no office that is independent of the council. If the mayor were to be heard individually he could only deal with complaints against "the council with which ex-hypothesis the council itself did not wish to deal. So, accordingly, it seems to their Lordships that on this short ground the appellant cannot maintain this action."

14. The void-voidable question came up for critical examination before a number of superior courts within the Commonwealth. We like to refer only to one case. In Secretary of State for Trade and Industry vs F Hoffman La Roche & Co and others 1973. 3, All ER 945 in deciding a matter where the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry sought an ad interim injunction to restrain certain manufacturing companies from charging price above those specified in a statutory instrument for certain drugs Lord Denning, MR observed; "A failure to observe the rules of natural justice does not render a decision or order or report absolutely void in the sense that it is a nullity. The legal consequences are best told by recounting the remedies available in respect of it. A person who has been unfairly treated (by reason of a breach of the rules of natural justice) can go to the Courts, and ask for the decision or order or report, or whatever it is, to be quashed, or for a declaration that it is invalid, that it has not and never has had, any effect as against him. If he does not chose himself to query it and seek a remedy, no one else can do so; see Durayappah vs Fernando. But it is within the discretion of the court whether to grant him such a remedy or not."

15. On appeal by the manufacturing companies the case went up to the House of Lords (F Hoffman La Roche vs Secretary of State for Trade and Industry 1974 2 All ER 1128. Lord Diplock observed; "My Lords, I think it leads to confusion to use such terms as 'voidable ad initio, 'void' or a 'nullity' as descriptive of the legal status of sub-ordinate legislation alleged to be ultra vires for patent or latent defects, before its validity has been pronounced on by a court of competent jurisdiction. These are concepts developed in the private law of contract which are ill-adapted to the field of public law. All that can usefully be said is that the presumption that sub-ordinate legislation is intra vires prevails in the absence of rebuttal, and that it cannot be rebutted by a party to legal proceedings in a court of competent jurisdiction who has locus standi to challenge the validity of the sub-ordinate legislation in question."

16. With regard to the standing of a person questioning the validity of a sub-ordinate legislation. Lord Diplock opined;

"A part from express provision in the governing statute, locus standi to challenge the validity of sub-ordinate legislation the validity of sub-ordinate legislation may be restricted, under the court's inherent power to control its own procedure, to a particular category of persons affected by the sub-ordinate legislation, and if none of these persons chooses to challenge it the presumption of validity prevails. Such was the case in Durayappah vs Fernando where on an appeal from Ceylon, although the Privy Council was of opinion that an order of the Minister was ultra vires owing to a latent defect in the procedure prior to its being made, they nevertheless treated it as having legal effect because the party who sought to challenge it had, in their view, no locus standi to do so."

17. We also like to refer to the dissenting opinion of Lord Wilberforce;

"it is true enough that a piece of sub-ordinate legislation is presumed to be valid against persons who have no locus standi to challenge it; the puzzling case of Durayappah vs Fernando (1967) 2 All ER 152 can be understood as exemplifying this. But it is quite another matter to say. And I know of no supporting authority, that such a presumption exists when the validity of the sub-ordinate legislation is legitimately in question before a court and is challenged by a person who has locus standi to challenge it."

18-19. Before us the petitioner has come for a declaration that the impugned order is of no legal effect as it has been passed under a law that has violated Article 38 of the Constitution. The superior courts in our country have taken a liberal view of standing in relation to an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. Mr Ahmed has drawn our attention to the following observation of Hamoodur Rahman, J in Mian Fazal Din vs The Lahore Improvement Trust 19 DLR (SC) 225:

"That the right considered sufficient for maintaining a proceeding of this nature is not necessarily a right in the strict juristic sense but it is enough if the applicant discloses that he had a personal interest in the performance of the legal duty which if not performed or performed in a manner not permitted by law would result in the loss for some personal benefit or advantage or the curtailment of a privilege or liberty of franchise."

20. We also like to refer to an earlier observation, that of the Judicial Committee in Attorney-General of the Gambia vs N' Jle 1961 (AC) 617 (634). "The words "person aggrieved" of wide import and should not be subjected to a restrictive interpretation. They do not include, of course, a mere busybody who is interfering in things which do not concern him; but they would include a person who has a genuine grievance because an order has been made which prejudicially affects his interests."

21. Mr Ahmed has also referred to Kazi Mokhlesur Rahman vs Bangladesh 26 DLR (AD) 44 where the court decided to hear the petitioner who challenged the cession of southern half of south Berubari Union to India by the Government of Bangladesh though he was not a resident there. Sayem CJ observed;

"It appears to us that the question of locus standi does not involve the Courts jurisdiction to hear a person but of the competency of the person to claim a hearing, so that the question is one of discretion which the court exercises upon due consideration of the facts and circumstances of each case. The appellant has complained that he is under an impending threat of deprivation of his fundamental rights under Article 36 of the "Constitution and his right of franchise. Because of this as well as of the exceptional and extraordinary constitutional issues raised in this case involving consideration of an international agreement between this country and the friendly Republic of India, we decided to hear the appellant."

22. At one stage of the hearing the learned Additional Attorney-General has contended that the petitioner, if so aggrieved, may file a suit in a Civil Court. But Article 7 of the President's Order provides that no court shall entertain any suit or proceeding calling into question any action taken or deemed to have been taken under that Order.

23. In the earlier decision of this court in MR Khan vs Bangladesh the question of constitutionality of any legislation did not arise, and for that, we think that case is distinguishable from the instant one. In the present case the impugned order did adversely affect the petitioner's right as a member of the Samity to contest and participate in the election scheduled to be held on 20-4-80. The petitioner has challenged the vires of a law and sought enforcement of a right conferred by Part III of the Constitution. She is entitled to a hearing in this court.

24. Again, the application is not bad for non Joinder of necessary or proper parties, No one will be affected except the Government if the impugned law is held to be void and no one has any cause to grumble with regard to any supposed right under unenforceable law.

25. The reason for the impugned order is that the "Bangladesh Mahila Samity is indulging in political activities contrary to its aims and objects and against the public interest." Neither in the order nor in the affidavits of the respondent there is any material to show the nature or manner of alleged indulgence in politics. The only assertion is that the Samity is a non-political organization. There is no material before us to indicate what aims and objects of the association were contravened. There is no disclosure what compelling public interest necessitated the impugned order. There is no averment that it was meant to provide for proper functioning or reconstitution of an institution which is the avowed object of the impugned legislation.

26. There is no assertion in the respondent's affidavits that the order was made as the association could not hold the election of its executive committee according to its constitution. The learned additional Attorney-General has, however, laid emphasis on this aspect of the affairs of the Samity. The petitioner's statement that the date for election was fixed on 20th April, 1980 "with due authority of the Samity" has not been controverted. The only stress is on the assertion that the Petitioner ceased to hold her office on 19th April 1980 when the impugned order was passed and had no locus standi to move this application on her own.

27. If we accept the respondent's view that the term of the Committee expired in December, 1978 or if we prefer the petitioner's assertion that the term of the committee came to an end after December 1979, which is, we think, correct, as the amendment with regard to the term of election of the committee was not given any retrospective effect, then it is difficult to understand why the respondent waited till 19th April, 1980 to correct the alleged fault. It appears to us that the impugned order was intended to pre-empt the election which was scheduled to be held on the 20th April, 1980. The petitioner did not ascribe any particular ill motive to the respondent. In the facts and circumstances of the case it is clear that the impugned order is passed without any application of mind and it is malafide in law.

<u>28. We have indicated above that the impugned order has adversely affected the petitioner. It is now a settled law of our country, and for that we need not refer to any decision, that the principle of audi alteram partem unless expressly excluded by law or by the nature of the objects of any particular law, is to be implied to have been provided in every statute. In the facts of the case there was no urgency in the matter that called for an instant measure and exclusion of a pre-hearing of the petitioner. The petitioner's contention that the order violated the principle of audi alteram partem must be upheld.</u>

29. The learned Additional Attorney-General has urged that as the ad-hoc Committee had already on 22-4-80 resolved to hold the election within six months, a decision on the constitutionality of the President's Order may not be necessary. He has also submitted that this particular law can be administered manner which may not contravene any provision of the Constitution.

30. We have given our serious consideration to his submissions. The manner of administration of law is hardly material in examining the constitutionality of law. A constitutionally good law may be badly administered but that will not make that law unconstitutional. Again, a law inconsistent with Act 26 may be intelligently administered avoiding a collision course with any of the fundamental rights, but then, that will not make that law constitutionally enforceable. Besides, the complaint of the petitioner is that the President's order has violated Article 38 of the Constitution and that particular complaint of her's has a bearing on her standing. We have decided to hear her for that very complaint; otherwise we could have dis-posed the matter in the light of the earlier decision of this court in MR Khan vs Bangladesh.

31. We cannot pass by a complaint when it has been properly raised under clause (1) of Article 102 of the Constitution. We are aware of the well-established rule of interpretation that a law should be interpreted in such a manner that it would rather be saved than destroyed. The task is a delicate one and an unnecessary exercise of power to strike down a legislation on its being inconsistent with any of the fundamental rights described in Part III of the Constitution may result in serious consequences in the country.

<u>32. When a law is challenged as unconstitutional there is a presumption in favour of its constitutionality. There is also a presumption that the legislature knows best the needs, requirements and aspirations of the people on whose suffrage it comes into being. When the court examines the constitutionality of a legislation it does not claim that it is wiser than the legislature nor does it assume to exercise any right of veto on the power of the legislature. The Constitution has itself provided in Article 26 that all existing laws inconsistent with the provision of Part III shall to the extent of such inconsistency become void on its commencement, and the State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provision of Part III. (The combined effects of Articles 26, 44 and 102 of the Constitution is that the Court is required under the Constitution to enforce the fundamental rights conferred by Part III)</u>

33. Mr Ahmed has referred to Tamizuddin Ahmed vs The Government of East Pakistan, reported in PLD 1964 (Dad 795, and has also referred to Saiyyid Abul A'la Maudoodi vs Government of Pakistan, reported in (PLD) 1964 (SC) 673, and also in 17 DLR (SC) 209. In that case a political party, named, 'Jamaat-e-Islam' was declared unlawful, its properties were seized and its bank accounts were frozen under section 16 of the Criminal Law (Additional) Act of 1908 which was declared ultra vires to the freedom of association.

34. It is true, as Mr Additional Attorney-General has pointed out, that Maudoodi's case is distinguishable from the instant one as the Samity as such has not been dissolved, but in the decision of that case there is an illuminating discussion on a constitutional question not unsimilar to the present one.

35. Mr Additional Attorney-General has referred to Ratnaprova Devi vs State of Orissa AIR 1964 (SC) 1195. In this case the Indian Supreme Court refused to declare the Orissa Private Land of Rulers (Assessment of Rent) Act 1958 as unconstitutional because of Article 14 of the Constitution of India when the petitioners failed to displace the initial presumption of constitutionality of an Act, and it was found fair and equitable tests were laid down for determining the rent in section 6 of the Act.

36. Reliance has also been placed by the respondent on New York ex rel. Bryant vs Zimmerman 278 US 63. In that case a New York Statute requiring the Ku Klan to supply a list of its members was upheld by the Supreme Court. The decision was based on the peculiar feature of that case viz, the Klan's activities involving acts of unlawful intimidation and violence. Though there is no specific guarantee in the US Constitution of freedom of association, it is a settled principle of the US Supreme Court that freedom to engage in association for the advancement of beliefs and ideas is protected under the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment which embraces freedom of speech. We like to refer to only one case. In National Association for the Advancement of Colored People vs Alabama 357 US 449, the US Supreme Court held that an association could not be compelled by a State legislation to dis-close the list of its member as it was likely to affect adversely the ability of the petitioner and its members to purpose their collective efforts to foster beliefs which admittedly they had the right to advocate.

37. We like to refer to Smt Damyant Naranga vs The Union of India and others AIR 1971 (SC) 966, where the Supreme Court of India declared the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan Act, 1962 as ultra vices to the freedom of Association. The Hindi Sahitya Sammelan, a society registered in 1914, suffered a number of litigations toins and the UP legislature passed the aforesaid Act for taking over that society by new statutory Sammelan. Under the Act very wide powers were given to the first Governing body, to be constituted by the Central Government, to make rules in respect of matters relating to membership, and the rules framed could make provision for admission of persons as members whom the original members of the Sammelan might never have liked to admit in their Society. And the number of such members could even be so large as to leave the original members in a small minority with the result that those members would become totally ineffective in the society. This was, it was held, a clear interference with the right to form an association.

38. The offending legislation has been assailed with vehemence, and also defended boldly, but has somehow been forgotten to be placed before us. Let us have a close view of the President's Order.

39. The President's Order 117 of 1972 was promulgated on 20th September, 1972 to provide for an extraordinary situation obtaining then in the country. Because of non availability of members, for various reasons, of different organizations the President's Order was passed as a "temporary arrangement" to provide for proper functioning and reconstitution of various institutions. If we look at the preamble of the President's Order and its article 4 then it would be clear that this was meant to be a temporary measure. After the commencement of the Constitution when the country got its fundamental law this Order, instead of withering away, found a place on the Statute Book. In 1973 by Act XXIV the Order was further amended and a provision for appointment of an Administrator was also introduced, and powers wider than those given to the Ad-hoc Committee were conferred on the Administrator.

40. The relevant provisions of the President's Order as amended in 1973 are quoted below:

"3(1) "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any rule, regulation, bye law, document or in any memorandum or articles of association or any deed or instrument, the Government may if it is of the opinion that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, by an order in writing, dissolve a committee or of management of an institution and appoint an Ad-hoc Committee or Administration for that institution.

4. "The members of the Ad-hoc Committee shall, unless sooner replaced by another Ad-hoc Committee, hold office until replaced by a Committee of Management of the institution elected, nominated or appointed under the appropriate provision of law, rule, bye-law, document or memorandum of association, as the case may be.

5(2) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law, rule, bye-law, document, memorandum of association an Ad-hoc Committee of an institution set up by any rule, bye-law, document or memorandum of association whether registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (Act XXI of 1860), or not shall, with the approval of Government have power to make necessary amendments in such rule, bye-law, document or memorandum of association.

Under Article 5 (A) the Administrator shall..........

"1 (b) hold office for such period and on such terms and conditions and exercise such powers, perform such functions and dis-charge such duties, as the Government may determine;

(c) have power to make, with the approval of the Government, necessary amendment in any such rule, bye law, document or memorandum of association, as the case may be.

(2) The Government may appoint a commit-tee consisting of not more than five members to assist and advise, the Administrator in the exercise of his powers, performance of his functions and discharge of his duties.

(3) It shall be the duty of an Administrator to take such steps as may be necessary for the reconstitution of the Committee of Management of the institution in accordance with the rule, bye-law, document memorandum of association within such time as the Government may direct."

<u>41. It is a clear that the President's Order gives unfettered and unrestricted discretion to the Government to dissolve a Managing Committee of an association. The term "public interest" has not been defined. Its import is, no doubt, wider than the interests of morality or public order for which reasonable restrictions may be imposed on the freedom of association. An order under Article 3 of the Order can be made on the subjective satisfaction of the Government and there is no requirement of giving any reason or ground for that. There is no appeal on review to alleviate the rigours of such an order. Again, the Government has been given unrestricted powers to control the affairs of an association. The Government can change the very character of an institution and impose its own image on it. The members of an Ad-hoc Committee need not be the members of the association. A stranger to the institution may be appointed as member of the Ad-hoc Committee or as the Administrator. An Ad-hoc arrangement may be replaced by another ad-hoc measure. There is no restriction as such as to the duration of the term of the Ad-hoc Committee or that of the Administrator. The powers of the Ad-hoc Committee are, again, very wide. The constitution of an institution can be amended in any manner with the approval of the Government. This kind of plenary power can be called a reasonable restriction.</u>

42. Right to form an association must of necessity include a right to its continuance and a right to manage its affairs. By this, however, it is not meant that if there is any legislation which regulates the affairs of an association it will amount to a breach of freedom of association. The members of an association have no right to claim that they can carry on its activities in any manner they like. Only when a regulatory legislation interferes with the enjoyment of the right to form an association and it violates Article 38 of the Constitution it will be declared to be void.

<u>43. An incumbent of an elected office for a fixed period of time cannot hold on after the expiry of his term unless such action is either sanctioned or condoned by any law, or approved by the general constituents of an association. There may be a managing committee of an association that may attempt to perpetuate its existence and refuse to hold any election as per rules of the association. To meet such a situation if the Government intends to administer a remedial measure it may take recourse to an appropriate law, but that law must not however, cause any violence to freedom of association.</u>

44. We have considered whether the President's Order 117 of 1972 can be saved in part for whatsoever usefulness it may have, but its inconsistency with freedom of association is so pervasive that it ought to be held, and we hold, that the Act is wholly void under Article 26 of the Constitution.

45. In view of the above, we make the Rule absolute and declare that the impugned order is passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The Government is hereby directed to cancel and withdraw the said order. We, however, do not make any order as to costs.

On the prayer of Mr MM Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, the operation of this order is stayed for ten days.

End.

full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan J.- This rule has been referred to this Bench by the learned Chief Justice for a decision since contrary views with regard to the question whether an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) would fail in absence of a finding by the trial Court as to the eligibility of a pre-emptor u/s 90 of the Act to pre-empt a transfer have been expressed by some Single Benches of this Court.

2. The petitioners as pre-emptors filed an application u/s 96 of the Act to pre-empt the transfer. The said application was contested by the pre-emptee-opposite parties on the sole ground that the application was barred by limitation. The learned Munsif on hearing the petition allowed it. The learned Subordinate Judge, on appeal though upheld the findings of the learned Munsif on limitation, allowed the appeal and dismissed the pre-emption case on the ground, that the application was bad for defect of parties and that the learned Munsif failed to record any finding on the point as to whether the pre-emption petitioners are persons entitled to pre-empt the transfer under section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Upon these two grounds the appeal was allowed and the application for pre-emption was dismissed. This rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge.

<u>3. Mr. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners has submitted that the written objection filed before the learned Munsif does not contain any specific allegation that any co-sharer or contiguous tenant had not been impleaded or joined in the application. He has next submitted that although written objection contains a general allegation that the application for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties there is no specific allegation of non-joinder of a necessary party. Mr. Abdur Rahim has contended that the objection as to omission of a necessary party must be taken at the earliest opportunity and if no such objection is taken, it may be deemed that the defect had been waived. This controversy as to non-joinder of co-sharer or a contiguous tenant has been set at rest by a decision of the Appellate Division of this Court in the case of Akhtarun Nessa and another vs. Habibullah & ors. reported in 31 D.L.R. (A D)88. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division have stated the law on the question as follows:</u>

<u>"Any objection as to omission of necessary party must be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and such objection if not so taken may be deemed to have been waived."</u>

<u>We have not been shown any other decision in which these views have been departed from. No specific objection, having been taken at any stage of the proceeding in the instant case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the learned Munsif as to non-joinder of any particular co-sharer or contiguous tenant, the opposite party shall be deemed to have waived the objection as to non-joinder. It is seen that P.W. 1 in his cross-examination disclosed the names of some contiguous tenants. Disclosure of the names of some persons who ought to have been impleaded in the proceeding would not make the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act bad on ground of defect of parties unless the pre-empee-opposite parties has raised the question of non- joinder of some co-sharer or contiguous tenant at the earliest opportunity before the learned Munsif. An issue for determination in a proceeding arises when a proposition of law and fact is asserted by one party and denied by other. The pre-emptee-opposite parties having not raised the issue as to non-joinder in their objection they cannot take advantage of any disclosure of such absence of any co-sharer at the trial and the learned Munsif as well is not required under law to decide the question of non-joinder. Since there was no contest between the parties as to the question of non-joinder in the pleading of the parties the application cannot fail for non-joinder of some contiguous tenants though disclosure about them were made during the cross-examination of the petitioner.</u>

4. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate for petitioner has next attacked the findings of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the application for pre-emption must fail because the learned Munsif made no finding on the question as to whether the pre-emptor-petitioners are persons to whom transfer by pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act could be made or in other words whether the pre-emptor petitioners were the person to whom transfer of the pre-empted land can be made under section 90 of the Act. The learned Subordinate Judge has also taken exception that no evidence was led by the pre-emptor- petitioners to prove that they were persons who are entitled to pre-empt the land in question under section 90 of the Act. The relevant portion of section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act runs as follows;

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any under Jaw for the time being in force, no person shall, after the commencement of this part be entitled to purchase or otherwise, acquire, except in accordance with the provisions of this part, any quantity of land which added to the total quantity of land already held by him for himself and his family, exceeds three hundred and seventy five standard bighas have been substituted by hundred bighas under the' provision of P.O. 98 of 1972".

5. The pre-emptor-petitioners have averred in their application claiming pre-emption that they were persons who would be entitled to purchase by pre-emption the land in question and that the quantity of land sought to be pre-empted if added to the quantity already held by them for themselves and families shall not exceed 100 standard bighas. The pre-emptor-petitioners in this connection have averred in the application as follows:

"The petitioners are agriculturists and they owned 15/16 bighas of land, If pre-emption of the land is allowed the total land will not exceed the standard limit........................"

The pre-emptee opposite parties in their written objection averred as follows:

"The statement to the effect that the petitioners are agriculturists and they owned 15/16 bighas of land and are entitled to pre-emption are false, fraudulent and collusive."

6. The pre-emptor petitioners, it appears, did not adduce any evidence in support of their averment that they owned 15/16 bighas of land. The opposite parties, on the other hand, also did not lead any evidence that the pre-emptor-petitioners owned more then 15/16 bighas of land or that the quantity of land sought to be pre-empted if added with the total quantity of land held by them would exeed 100 bighas. The learned Munsif did not record any finding as to the question whether the pre-emptor-petitioners were competent persons to whom the land could be transferred by pre-emption under section 90 of the Act. The question is whether the failure of the learned Munsif to record a finding on the petitioner’s competency to get the pre-emption under section 90 of the Act was fatal to the proceeding

<u>7. Let us consider the question in the back-ground of various provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to procedure in Civil Courts for disposal of suits and proceedings and in this connection we may refer to the provisions of rules 3 and 5 of Order 8 of the Codeof Civil Procedure and rule 1 of Order 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure, The provision of rule 1 of Order 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure are as follows:</u>

<u>"1(1) Issues arise when a material proposition of fact or law is affirmed by the one party and denied by the other.</u>

<u>(2) Material propositions are those propositions of law or fact which a plaintiff must allege in order to show a right to sue or a defendant must allege in order to constitute his defence</u>

<u>Now turning to the provisions of rules 3 and 5 of Order 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure we find in the said rules as follows:</u>

<u>"3. It shall not be sufficient for a defendant in his written statement to deny generally the grounds alleged by the plaintiff but the defendant must deal specifically with each allegation of fact of which he does not admit the truth, except damages."</u>

<u>4. Every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability. Provided that the court may in its discretion require any fact so admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admission."</u>

8. It has been settled by several decisions of this court that procedure of trial of an application under section 96 of the Act would be governed by the procedure as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure. In this view the provision of the Orders in C.P. Code shall be applicable to the instant proceeding. It appears from the written objection referred to above that the objection of the pre-emptee-opposite parties does not contain any specific and clear expressive denial of the averments of the pre-emptor-petitioners. The pre-emptee opposite parties in their written objection merely denied the averments of the pre-emptor- petitioners but they gave no specific denial or set up any plea that if the pre-emption application was allowed the added land would exceed the permissible limit of 100 standard bighas. The denial in this case appears to be evasive and vague and as such in view of the provisions of rule 1 of Order 14 read with the provisions of Rules 3 and 5 of Order 8 of the Cede of Civil Procedure the assertion of the pre-emptor petitioners that they are competent persons to get pre-emption under section 90 of the Act may be taken to have been admitted by the pre-emptee-opposite parties and the pre-emptor petitioners need not lead any evidence in support of their averments that they are competent persons to get pre-emption under section 90 of the Act.

9. As to the question whether the failure of the learned Munsif to record a finding about the petitioners competency under section 90 of the Act to get pre-emption would be fatal to the proceeding or not the learned Advocates for the parties have referred to several decisions of this court in support of their respective submissions. A Division Bench of this Court in the case of Satya Ranjan Halder and others vs. Surendra Nath Das and others reported in 13 D.L.R. (Dacca) 338 has held that the application for pre-emption must fail on the ground that the learned subordinate Judge without establishment-of the fact as to whether the pre-emptor petitioner was a competent person under section 90 of the Act to get pre-emption allowed the application, 1 his is a case where the pre-emptees, in their written objection, specifically asserted that the pre-emptor was in possession of lands more than statutory limit and in fact the pre-emptees challenged the assertion of the pre-emptor as to his capacity to get pre-emption under section 90 of the Act. In this view the aforesaid decision of the Division Bench is not applicable to the facts of this case and thus is of no help in deciding this case. Another decision of single Bench of this Court in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali and others reported in 21 D.L.R. (Dacca) 599 has been referred to us. In that case reference was made to the decision reported in 13 D.L.R. (Dacca) 338 but it was not followed since there was a specific pleading of the pre-emptee opposite party that if pre-emption was allowed the total land would exceed the limit. Such pleading by the pre-emptee in his written objection being absent in that case before the learned single Judge (case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali and others) the order of pre-emption was upheld although the trial court did not record any findings as regard fulfillment of the requirement under section 90 of the Act. In another case, namely, the case, of Tamizuddin Ahmed Vs. Guljan Bibi and others reported in 26 D.L.R. (High Court Division) 93 the application for pre-emption was allowed since the assertion in the deposition of the pre-emptor that the land in question if added would not exceed the statutory limit was not challenged in cross-examination.

<u>10. The case of Nayeb Ali and others Vs. Aktar Rahman and others reported in 29 D.L.R. (High Court Division) 153 the learned Single Judge of this Court took a contrary view from that taken earlier in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali and others. In the last cited case the pre-emptor asserted that section 90 of the Act was not an impediment in getting pre-emption. The pre-emptee did not deny the claim of the pre-emptor in his written objection. The learned Judge of this Division took the view that although there has been no denial of the statements as to the competency of the pre-emptor petitioner to get pre-emption still the pre-emptor was obliged to prove that the land if transferred to him by pre-emption will not exceed the statutory limit." The learned Single Judge held as follows:</u>

<u>"That the burden to prove that the pre-emptor is entitled to get pre-emption in his favour, is on the pre-emptor and as such he is required to prove that the land sought to be pre-empted, if allowed to pre-empt, will not exceed the ceiling. Therefore, it was not the burden of the pre-emptee to say how much land the pre-emptor had.</u>

<u>The pre-emptor came to court for, pre-emption and it is he who is to satisfy the requirements of law, He cannot steal a march ever the silence of his adversary."</u>

11. The learned Judge departing from the decision reported in 21 D.L.R. (Dacca) page 599 took the view that the court while granting pre-emption was required under law to record a finding that the pre-emptor is a competent person under section 90 of the Act to get an order of pre-emption or that the pre-emptor was required to prove that if the land sought to be pre-empted was added the total quantity of land would not exceed the statutory limit of 100 standard bighas. We have also been referred to another decision of this court reported in 1 B.L.D. (High Court Division) 121 in the case of Anwara Begum Vs. Maimuna Khotun Chowdhury and others. In that decision A.T.M Afzal J. has agreed with the view expressed in the case reported in 21 D.L.R. (Dacca) and has differed from the view taken in 29 D.L.R. (High Court Division) 153 referred to above. A.T.M. Afzal, J. has held that if the statement as to competency of the petitioner had not been controverted by the pre-emptee opposite party the pre- emption cannot be denied on the ground that the court failed to record the necessary findings under section 90 of the Act. In the aforesaid case reported in 1 B.L.D. (H.C.D) 121 the learned Judge has also held that if the court failed to determine the issue the revisional court may determine the issue and record the necessary finding. The question is whether in the absence of any finding by the trial court as to whether pre-emptor is a person to whom transfer of the holding or a portion or share thereof as the case may be can be made under section 90, should the application for pre-emption fail. This question has been settled by a decision of Appellate Division of this Court in the case of Md. Matiur Rahman Vs. Md. Iman Ali @ Md. Iman Miah & others reported in 1 B.L.D (A.D) 280. In that decision their Lordships of the Appellate Division have held that in the absence of any finding by the trial Court as to whether the pre-emptor is a person to whom transfer by pre-emption can be made as envisaged under section 90 of the Act the application for pre-emption would not fail. Their Lordship have held that omission to record a finding to the effect that the pre-emptors were entitled to purchase or acquire the land by pre-emption and the total quantity of the land together with the land sought to be pre-empted would not execeed the maximum ceiling as set out in section 90 of the Act cannot be a ground for dismis3al of the pre-emption application. Their Lordships, however, remanded the case to the lower court for taking evidence on the point whether the petitioner was entitled to pre-empt the land under section 90 of the Act. This order of remand for taking evidence was made on the basis, it appears to us, on a prayer for remand by the pre-emptor stating that he would adduce evidence to support his case that he possessed only 10 bighas of land. This order of remand in the situation passed in that case in not applicable in the instant case before us.

12. In the instant case the pre-emptors averments regarding competency to get pre-emption as envisaged under section 90 have not been specifically denied. We are of opinion that under rule 1 of Order 14 and rules 3 and 5 of Order 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure absence of denial by the pre-emptee opposite party as to the assertion of the pre-emptor petition that they did not own more than 15/16 bighas of land the case does not call for any remand for the purpose of adducing any evidence on the point as envisaged under section 90 of the Act because the pre-emptee opposite parties have not pleaded that the total land added up to the land sought to be pre-empted would exceed the ceiling as set out under section 90 of the Act The pleadings of the pre-emptor as envisaged under section 90 of the Act as to ceiling of land having not been specifically denied or set up-as a defence the pre-emptee opposite party would be precluded under law to adduce evidence to controvert the assertion made by the pre-emptor This view has also been taken, by Mustafa Kamal J. in his reference to the learned Chief Justice for a decision by a Divisional Bench. In the facts and circumstances of the case an order or remand to enable the pre-emptors to adduce evidence in support of their assertion of fact as envisaged under the provision under section 90 of the Act would be a fruitless endeavor and without any purpose. The parties on the point in question being not in variance there is no point for remand for decision by-the trial Court. Under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure this Court is competent to make a finding on the basis of materials available in the record The assertions that the pre-emptor petitioners would not own a total of more than 100 standard bighas together with the land sought to be pre-empted having not been denied and specifically set up in defence the statement in the application for pre-emption may be taken to have been admitted by the pre-emptee petitioners as being competent persons to whom transfer of the land or a portion or share thereof can be made under section 90 of the Act. In this view the application for pre- emption must succeed.

13. In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the judgment and order dated 28.11.1977 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Jessore in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 47 of 1976 are set aside and those of the learned Munsif 3rd Court. Narait passed in Misc. Judicial Case No. 106 of 1974 dated 30.4.76 are restored. The judgment and order of the learned Munsif allowing the application for pre-emption are affirmed. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

Abdul Wadud Chowdhury J.-I agree.

End.
